Element / structure Role in English Application example
can present ability and possibility she can run the audit
could general past ability he could read at four
was able to / managed to single past achievement we were able to finish
will be able to future ability we will be able to start on Monday
have been able to ability up to now they have been able to cope
couldn't / wasn't able to past inability they weren't able to finish

Formula / rule: Decide the time first. Present: can. General past skill: could. One specific past success: was able to. Future or perfect: be able to with the tense. Negative forms follow the same logic.

★ Why it matters

The distinction between could and was able to is the difference between a capability and an achievement: he could swim as a child, but he was able to swim across the lake last summer. In performance reports, that is the difference between potential and delivery.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use can and could for permission and requests far more than for ability (can I borrow this?), and use be able to when the tense demands it without thinking.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Can is unstressed and reduced to /kən/; the negative can't is stressed and distinguishes British /kɑːnt/ from American /kænt/.

Additional example bank
  • Future: The team will be able to report by June.
  • Achievement: They managed to close the gap in one quarter.
  • Perfect: We have been able to hold the price.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: We will can start on Monday (can has no future form)

✅ Right: We will be able to start on Monday

❌ Wrong: We could finish the audit yesterday (could for a single achievement)

✅ Right: We were able to finish the audit yesterday

Permission, obligation and prohibition · Needn't, didn't need to

135 Causative: Have and Get Something Done

Causatives

Who did the work? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. We
    gaphad
    the report translated.
  2. She
    gapgot
    the contract checked.
  3. I need to
    gaphave
    my laptop repaired.
  4. They
    gaphad
    the office painted.
HAVE / GET→+ object + past participle
Level B1 Grammar

Causative: Have and Get Something Done

Say that someone else did the work for you.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use have and get with an object and a past participle.
Examples in context
  • We had the report translated. Someone else translated it. — Have + object + participle.
  • She got the contract checked. Same meaning, more informal. — Get + object + participle.
  • I had my laptop stolen. Something happened to me, not arranged. — Have + object + participle, bad event.

👀 What do you observe?

The causative have something done means that someone else performs the action: we had the report translated, I need to have my laptop repaired. Get does the same job in a more conversational register. The same pattern with an unwanted event means that something happened to the subject: he had his laptop stolen. The object is the thing acted on, and the participle carries the action.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
have + object + participle arranged service we had the report translated
get + object + participle same, more informal she got the contract checked
have + object + participle, bad event something happened to the subject he had his wallet stolen
have + object + base verb cause someone to act they had the courier wait
get + object + to-infinitive persuade someone I got the supplier to reissue the invoice
need / want + have + participle future arrangement I need to have the car serviced

Formula / rule: Ask who did the work. If the subject arranged it, use have or get plus object plus past participle. If the subject did it, use the active voice. If the subject caused another person to act, use have plus object plus base verb, or get plus object plus to-infinitive.

★ Why it matters

This is the structure of service and delegation, and English uses it constantly: I had the figures checked, we got the room cleaned. Without it, learners describe arrangements by naming the agent, which sounds unnecessarily specific, or by using the passive, which loses the fact that the subject arranged it.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers prefer have in writing and get in speech, and they use the unpleasant-event pattern without any sense of arrangement: she had her bike stolen. Get is avoided in formal reports for this reason: it can suggest the subject was careless.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Have is unstressed in the causative (we had the report transLAted), and the participle carries the main stress.

Additional example bank
  • Service: We had the audit reviewed by an external firm.
  • Arrangement: She is getting the signage replaced.
  • Bad event: They had their offices flooded in June.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: We had translated the report by someone (active voice where the causative is meant)

✅ Right: We had the report translated

❌ Wrong: She got the contract check (base verb where a participle is needed)

✅ Right: She got the contract checked

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Passive: simple and future tenses · Verb + preposition

🎯 Can you already use this?

Level B1 Grammar Reference

B1 Intermediate Confusing Grammar Master Guide

A vs B (vs C) structural contrasts, logic maps, and usage guides for intermediate English learners

🎯 Master Goal: Express subtle differences in past experience, continuous duration, necessity, preference, and degree with intermediate fluency.

👀 What do you notice?

Compare these two intermediate sentences:

  • "I have painted the kitchen." (Result / finished action → kitchen is ready now)
  • "I have been painting the kitchen." (Duration / activity focus → my hands are covered in paint!)

Score: 0 / 2

Correct · Present Perfect Continuous emphasizes the duration and continuous activity up to now.
2. Form check: What is the difference between 'so beautiful' and 'such a beautiful day'?
Correct · 'So' modifies adjectives alone (so warm); 'Such' modifies noun phrases (such a warm day).

🧠 Logic Map: Core B1 Grammar Contrasts

Structure AStructure B (vs C)Core Logic DifferenceKey Examples
Past Simple Present Perfect Simple Finished specific past time vs. Unspecified past time connected to now I lived in Rome in 2018. vs. I have lived in Rome for 3 years.
Present Perfect Simple Present Perfect Continuous Completed result / quantity vs. Duration of activity / ongoing action I have written 5 emails. vs. I have been writing emails all morning.
For Since / From Duration length vs. Specific starting point in time for 3 months | since March | from 9 AM to 5 PM
Didn't need to Needn't have Action was not necessary, so maybe not done vs. Action was done, but was unnecessary I didn't need to buy milk (so I didn't). vs. I needn't have bought milk (I bought it, but we had plenty).
So Such (a/an) So + adjective/adverb vs. Such + (a/an) + adjective + noun She is so smart. vs. She is such a smart person.
Another Other / The other / Others Another + singular countable vs. Other + plural vs. The other = remaining one another cup | other places | the other shoe | others agree
Wish + Past Simple Wish + Would Desire to change a present state vs. Desire for someone else to change annoying behavior I wish I was taller. vs. I wish you would stop tapping your pen!
⚠️ Common B1 Mistake Flips
❌I have seen him yesterday.
tap to see the correct form
✅I saw him yesterday.
('Yesterday' is a finished past time marker → Past Simple)
❌It was so good day!
tap to see the correct form
✅It was such a good day! / The day was so good!
('Such a + adjective + noun' vs 'So + adjective')
❌I have lived here since 5 years.
tap to see the correct form
✅I have lived here for 5 years. / ...since 2021.
('For' + duration; 'Since' + starting point)

137 Connectors and Linking Words

Text connectors

What job does the connector do? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The bid was late.
    gapMoreover
    , it was over budget.
  2. The delay was avoidable.
    gapTherefore
    , we are claiming costs.
  3. The plan is sound.
    gapHowever
    , the timetable is not.
  4. Three risks stand out.
    gapFirstly
    , the supplier.
CONNECTOR→+ comma, at the start of the sentence
Level B1 Grammar

Connectors and Linking Words

Link sentences and paragraphs, not only clauses.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use connectors that open sentences and hold a longer text together.
Examples in context
  • The bid was late. Moreover, it was over budget. Adds a second point. — Moreover opens a sentence.
  • The delay was avoidable. Therefore, we are claiming costs. Draws a conclusion. — Therefore marks result.
  • Three risks stand out. Firstly, the supplier. Orders the points. — Firstly marks sequence.

👀 What do you observe?

Sentence connectors hold a text together across sentence boundaries: addition (moreover, furthermore, in addition, similarly), contrast (however, nevertheless, on the other hand, by contrast), result (therefore, consequently, as a result), sequence (firstly, secondly, finally), and summary (in conclusion, overall, to sum up). They are adverbs, so they take a comma after them and a full stop or semicolon before them.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What punctuation follows a sentence connector?
However, the timetable is not.
2. Which connector marks a conclusion?
Therefore marks result.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
addition moreover, furthermore, in addition moreover, it was over budget
contrast however, nevertheless, on the other hand however, the timetable is not
result therefore, consequently, as a result therefore, we are claiming costs
sequence firstly, secondly, finally firstly, the supplier
summary in conclusion, overall overall, the plan is sound
punctuation full stop or semicolon before, comma after late. Moreover, it was over budget.

Formula / rule: Decide the relation, then place the connector at the start of the sentence with a comma after it. Use a full stop or a semicolon before it, never a comma alone. Keep one connector per relation per paragraph, since two addition connectors in a row read as padding.

★ Why it matters

At B1 the clause-level links are already known, and the step up is managing a paragraph: a reader follows an argument because however signals a reversal and therefore signals a conclusion. Without them a report is a list of true statements with no claim about how they relate.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use these connectors far more in writing than in speech, where and, but and so do the work. Overusing moreover and furthermore in speech sounds like a memo being read aloud.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The connector is stressed and followed by a pause: the bid was late. moreOVER, it was over budget.

Additional example bank
  • Contrast: The trial succeeded. Nevertheless, the cost is prohibitive.
  • Result: Two suppliers withdrew. As a result, the tender reopened.
  • Summary: Overall, the audit found no material error.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The bid was late, moreover it was over budget (comma splice before a sentence connector)

✅ Right: The bid was late. Moreover, it was over budget

❌ Wrong: However the timetable is not (missing comma after the connector)

✅ Right: However, the timetable is not

138 Defining and Non-Defining Relative Clauses

Relative clauses

Which clause, and does it take commas? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The report
    gapthat
    we sent is out of date.
  2. The report
    gap, which
    we sent in June, is out of date.
  3. My manager
    gap, who
    joined in May, approved it.
  4. The team
    gapthat
    won the bid has disbanded.
DEFINING→→ no commas, that or which · NON-DEFINING → commas, never that
Level B1 Grammar

Defining and Non-Defining Relative Clauses

Decide whether the clause identifies or merely adds.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use defining and non-defining relative clauses with the right punctuation and pronouns.
Examples in context
  • The report that we sent is late. Defining: tells you which report. — No commas, that is allowed.
  • The report, which we sent in June, is late. Non-defining: extra information. — Commas, never that.
  • The team that won the bid has disbanded. Defining: identifies the team. — Removing it changes the meaning.

👀 What do you observe?

A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing is meant, so it carries no commas and that is allowed. A non-defining clause adds information about something already identified, so it sits between commas, that is not allowed, and who or which is required. In a defining clause the pronoun can be left out when it is the object: the report we sent. It cannot be left out in a non-defining clause.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which clause can use that?
Commas and that never go together.
2. Does removing a non-defining clause change which thing you mean?
That is why it takes commas.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
defining, no commas identifies the noun the report that we sent
non-defining, commas adds information the report, which we sent in June,
that defining only the team that won the bid
who / which both types, people and things my manager, who joined in May,
pronoun omitted defining, object the report we sent
whose possession, both types the analyst whose model failed

Formula / rule: Ask whether the reader already knows which thing you mean. If not, the clause identifies it: no commas, that is fine, and the pronoun can vanish when it is the object. If yes, the clause only adds: commas, no that, and the pronoun must stay.

★ Why it matters

The comma is not decoration; it decides what the sentence asserts. The staff who passed the audit were promoted says only some passed. The staff, who passed the audit, were promoted says all of them did, and the audit is a side note. In a report that distinction is the finding.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers drop the object pronoun in defining clauses without thinking (the file we sent) and almost never make the reverse error, because the comma is audible as a pause and a pitch change when the clause is non-defining.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

A non-defining clause is spoken as a separate tone unit: the report, / which we sent in June, / is late. The defining clause runs as one unit with no pause.

Additional example bank
  • Defining, object omitted: The figures we published in March were revised.
  • Non-defining, added fact: The figures, which we published in March, were revised.
  • Whose: The client whose contract lapsed has reappeared.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: My manager, that joined in May, approved it (that in a non-defining clause)

✅ Right: My manager, who joined in May, approved it

❌ Wrong: The report which we sent in June is late and out of date (missing commas around a non-defining clause)

✅ Right: The report, which we sent in June, is late and out of date

🔗 Connects to what you already know

139 During, For, While

Time words

Noun or clause after the word? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The alarm rang
    gapduring
    the meeting.
  2. We waited
    gapfor
    two hours.
  3. The phone rang
    gapwhile
    we were talking.
  4. Nothing changed
    gapduring
    the audit.
DURING + noun→→ FOR + length · WHILE + clause
Level B1 Grammar

During, For, While

Separate a period, a length and a background action.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use during with a noun, for with a length and while with a clause.
Examples in context
  • during the meeting a period, with a noun — the alarm rang during the meeting
  • for two hours a length of time — we waited for two hours
  • while we were talking two actions at once, with a clause — the phone rang while we were talking

👀 What do you observe?

During takes a noun and means inside a period: during the meeting, during the audit. For takes a length of time: for two hours, for three weeks. While takes a clause and marks two actions happening at the same time: while we were talking. During and for answer different questions, and while cannot take a noun.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which word takes a clause?
While we were talking.
2. Which word marks a length of time?
For two hours.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
during + noun inside a period during the meeting
for + length duration for two hours
while + clause simultaneous actions while we were talking
during which formal relative use the audit, during which the file vanished
for + period noun also possible for the duration of the meeting
not during + clause during cannot take a clause during we talked is wrong

Formula / rule: Look at what follows the word. A noun means during or for, and the choice is period versus length. A subject and verb means while. Then check the verb in the while-clause: it is usually continuous when the action is background.

★ Why it matters

These three are the most frequent time-word confusion at B1 because many languages use one word for all of them. In writing, the difference between during the audit and for the audit is the difference between an event inside a period and a period itself.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use while and during freely, and they often drop the subject and verb after while in informal speech (while eating, while on the phone), which is standard in reduced clauses.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

During is unstressed (/ˈdjʊərɪŋ/), for reduces to /fə/ before a length, and while is /waɪl/ with a full vowel.

Additional example bank
  • Period: Nothing was recorded during the hearing.
  • Length: The panel deliberated for three hours.
  • Simultaneous: The line dropped while I was presenting.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: during we talked (clause after during)

✅ Right: while we talked

❌ Wrong: we waited during two hours (during with a length)

✅ Right: we waited for two hours

140 -ed and -ing Adjectives

Adjectives

Who feels it, and what causes it? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. I was
    gapbored
    by the presentation.
  2. The presentation was
    gapboring
    .
  3. The team was
    gapexhausted
    after the audit.
  4. The audit was
    gapexhausting
    .
PERSON FEELS→→ -ed · THING CAUSES → -ing
Level B1 Grammar

-ed and -ing Adjectives

Match the adjective to who feels and who causes.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use -ed for the person who feels and -ing for the thing that causes the feeling.
Examples in context
  • I was bored. The subject feels the feeling. — -ed for people.
  • The talk was boring. The subject causes it. — -ing for things.
  • We were confused by the form. Cause: the form. — Confusing form, confused people.

👀 What do you observe?

Adjectives ending in -ed describe how a person or animal feels: bored, confused, exhausted, interested. Adjectives ending in -ing describe what produces that feeling: a boring talk, a confusing form, an exhausting audit. The -ed form is not a passive; it is a state. A thing can be -ed only if something acted on it: a closed door, a bored student.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form describes the thing that causes the feeling?

2. Which sentence is correct for a person?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
-ed the feeler I was bored
-ing the cause the talk was boring
pairs feel versus cause confused / confusing, interested / interesting
state, not passive -ed is an adjective a bored student
things with -ed only if something acted on them a closed door, a broken window
intensifiers very, really, absolutely absolutely exhausted, really boring

Formula / rule: Ask who holds the feeling. If it is the subject, use -ed. If the subject causes the feeling in someone else, use -ing. Then check the intensifier, because exhausted and fascinating behave like extreme adjectives and take absolutely rather than very.

★ Why it matters

The pair is a small window onto English's habit of putting the experiencer in the subject slot: the news is depressing, the staff are depressed. Confusing them reverses who is affected, which in a report about morale is not a small error.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use the -ing form for things and situations without thinking, and they extend -ing to people when describing their effect: he is exhausting to work with. That extension is normal and idiomatic.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

-ed is weak and quick (/bɔːd/), while -ing keeps a full ending (/ˈbɔːrɪŋ/), and the -ing form is longer by a syllable, which matches its 'more' meaning.

Additional example bank
  • Feeling: The panel seemed satisfied with the audit.
  • Cause: The timetable was demanding.
  • Pair: a tiring week, a tired team
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: I was boring by the presentation (the feeler takes -ed)

✅ Right: I was bored by the presentation

❌ Wrong: The presentation was bored (the cause takes -ing)

✅ Right: The presentation was boring

141 Embedded and Indirect Questions

Indirect questions

Is the word order inverted? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. Could you tell me
    gapwhere the office is
    ?
  2. I wonder
    gapif the file arrived
    .
  3. Do you know
    gapwhen the panel meets
    ?
  4. She asked
    gapwhat the deadline was
    .
FRAME→+ question word + SUBJECT + VERB
Level B1 Grammar

Embedded and Indirect Questions

Put a question inside a sentence without inverting it.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can embed a question inside another clause with correct word order.
Examples in context
  • Where is the office? → Could you tell me where the office is? Inversion disappears. — Subject before verb.
  • Did the file arrive? → I wonder if the file arrived. Yes/no takes if. — No auxiliary in the clause.
  • When does the panel meet? → Do you know when the panel meets? Do disappears. — The verb takes its normal ending.

👀 What do you observe?

When a question is embedded in another clause, the word order becomes statement order: subject before verb, and no do or did. The frame can be a polite opener (could you tell me, do you know, I wonder), a reporting verb (she asked, he wanted to know), or a statement (the question is). Yes/no questions take if or whether, and the auxiliary moves into the tense rather than vanishing.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What happens to the word order in an embedded question?

2. What introduces an embedded yes/no question?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
polite frame could you tell me, do you know could you tell me where the office is
reporting frame she asked, he wanted to know she asked what the deadline was
yes/no if or whether I wonder if the file arrived
no do / did auxiliary absorbed do you know when the panel meets
statement order subject before verb where the office is, not where is the office
tense shift in reporting backshift after a past verb she asked what the deadline was

Formula / rule: Build the question first, then strip the inversion: move the subject before the verb, remove do or did and put the tense on the main verb, and add if for a yes/no question. Keep the question mark only when the frame itself is a question.

★ Why it matters

Indirect questions are the grammar of politeness and of reported enquiry. Where is the office? is a demand for information; could you tell me where the office is? is a request, and the difference matters in every email a learner writes. The same structure is what makes minutes report questions without quoting them.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use indirect questions constantly as politeness, and they often keep the inversion in very informal speech (could you tell me where's the office?), which is common but not standard written English.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The frame carries a rising tone and the embedded clause falls: could you TELL me / where the OFFice is.

Additional example bank
  • Polite: Do you know whether the deadline has moved?
  • Reported: He asked when the audit would close.
  • Statement: The question is whether the file was ever sent.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: Could you tell me where is the office (inversion kept in an embedded question)

✅ Right: Could you tell me where the office is

❌ Wrong: I wonder if did the file arrive (do kept inside the clause)

✅ Right: I wonder if the file arrived

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Question tags · Reported questions and commands

142 For, Since, From

Time prepositions

Length, start or range? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. We have waited
    gapfor
    three weeks.
  2. She has worked here
    gapsince
    2019.
  3. The office is open
    gapfrom
    nine to five.
  4. The rule applies
    gapfrom
    June.
FOR + length→→ SINCE + starting point · FROM + range
Level B1 Grammar

For, Since, From

Mark a length, a starting point and a range.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use for with a length, since with a starting point and from with a range.
Examples in context
  • for three weeks a length of time — we have waited for three weeks
  • since 2019 a starting point, up to now — she has worked here since 2019
  • from nine to five a range with a start and end — open from nine to five

👀 What do you observe?

For marks a length of time and works with any tense: for three weeks, for two hours. Since marks a starting point and requires a perfect tense when the period runs to now: since 2019, since Monday. From marks the start of a range and looks forward: from nine to five, from June onwards. From does not run to the present on its own.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which word needs a perfect tense?

2. Which word marks a start and an end?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
for + length any tense we waited for two hours
since + point perfect tense to now she has worked here since 2019
from + point range, forwards the office is open from nine
from ... to start and end from nine to five
since + clause point in time as a clause since the merger closed
for + period noun also used with perfects for three years

Formula / rule: Ask whether you are measuring a length, naming a starting point, or marking a range. Length takes for with any tense. A start that runs to now takes since with a perfect. A range takes from, usually paired with to or until.

★ Why it matters

For and since track the two things a schedule needs: how long something lasts and when it began. From is the only one that describes a future range, which is why it appears on every notice and timetable.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use since with a clause freely (since we moved) and use from in speech mainly for ranges. Since with a past simple is a common error that natives never make.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

For is weak /fə/ before a length, since is unstressed /sɪns/, and from reduces to /frəm/ in the range pattern.

Additional example bank
  • Length: The panel has been sitting for six hours.
  • Start: Nothing has changed since the audit.
  • Range: The window is open from March to June.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: She has worked here for 2019 (for with a starting point)

✅ Right: She has worked here since 2019

❌ Wrong: I have known him since three years (since with a length)

✅ Right: I have known him for three years

WILL BE + -ING→→ in progress at a future point
Level B1 Grammar

Future Continuous

Say what will be happening at a future moment.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use will be + -ing for an action in progress at a future time.
Examples in context
  • At ten, we will be presenting. In progress at ten. — Will be + -ing.
  • This time tomorrow, I will be travelling. In progress at that moment. — Time phrase fixes the point.
  • Will you be using the room at three? Polite enquiry about a plan. — Question form.

👀 What do you observe?

The future continuous describes an action that will be in progress at a future moment. It is built with will be plus the -ing form, and it usually comes with a time expression (at ten, this time tomorrow, at three). It also softens an enquiry about someone's plans, and it presents a future event as a matter of course rather than as a decision.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

2. Why use it in 'Will you be using the room at three?'

Element / structure Role in English Application example
will be + -ing in progress at a future point at ten, we will be presenting
time phrase fixes the point this time tomorrow
negative won't be + -ing they won't be working on Friday
question will + subject + be + -ing will you be using the room?
polite enquiry softens the question will you be joining us?
contrast with future perfect in progress versus completed will be finishing / will have finished

Formula / rule: Fix the future moment first, then decide whether the action will be in progress or completed. In progress: will be plus -ing. Completed: will have plus the participle. Use the continuous for polite enquiries about plans, which asks what someone will be doing rather than what they have decided.

★ Why it matters

The future continuous is how English talks about a moment rather than an event, which is what most schedules need: at ten we will be presenting says where to find us, while we will present at ten commits the team to starting then. It is also the politest way to ask about someone's availability.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use it for assumptions about the present too (they'll be arriving about now), and for polite requests (will you be needing the car?), which is a marker of British politeness.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The -ing form carries the stress: at ten, we will be preSENTing; the auxiliaries run together as /wɪlbi/.

Additional example bank
  • Moment: At noon, the auditors will be checking the accounts.
  • Polite: Will you be attending the briefing?
  • Negative: We won't be accepting new bids until March.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: At ten, we will presenting (missing be after will)

✅ Right: At ten, we will be presenting

❌ Wrong: This time tomorrow I will be travel (base verb instead of -ing)

✅ Right: This time tomorrow I will be travelling

Future forms

Plan, prediction or timetable? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapwill

    gapam meeting

    gapleaves

INTENTION→→ going to / present continuous · DECISION → will · TIMETABLE → present simple
Level B1 Grammar

Future Forms Review

Choose will, going to, the present continuous or the present simple.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can pick the future form that matches the plan, the prediction or the timetable.
Examples in context
  • I'll call you tonight. Decision made now. — Will for spontaneous offers.
  • We're going to move the office. Plan decided earlier. — Going to for intentions.
  • I'm meeting the auditor at ten. Fixed arrangement. — Present continuous for appointments.

👀 What do you observe?

Four forms divide the future work. Will for decisions made at the moment of speaking, promises and predictions based on opinion. Going to for intentions decided before and for predictions based on visible evidence. Present continuous for fixed arrangements with a time. Present simple for timetables and schedules. Shall appears in offers and suggestions in British English.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
will spontaneous decision, promise, opinion I'll call you tonight
going to prior intention, evidence-based prediction we're going to move the office
present continuous fixed arrangement I'm meeting the auditor at ten
present simple timetable, schedule the train leaves at 07:40
shall offers and suggestions, British shall I open the window?
future continuous / perfect in progress or completed by a future point I'll be working / I'll have finished

Formula / rule: Ask what kind of future it is. A decision made now takes will. An intention made earlier takes going to. An arrangement with a time and a person takes the present continuous. A published timetable takes the present simple. Then refine with the continuous or perfect future if the action will be in progress or finished by a future point.

★ Why it matters

The choice signals commitment. I'm seeing the client on Tuesday tells a colleague the appointment exists, while I'll see the client suggests it is still a matter of intention. In scheduling and project work the difference decides whether a date is real.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use will and going to almost interchangeably in speech when the distinction is not at stake, and they use the present continuous constantly for arrangements. Shall survives mainly in questions and in the north of England.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Contractions carry the future meaning: I'll /aɪl/, we're going to /ˈɡənə/ in fast speech, and the arrangement form is stressed on the verb.

Additional example bank
  • Decision: I'll send it now.
  • Intention: We're going to redesign the form.
  • Timetable: The panel sits on the first Thursday.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: I am knowing the answer tomorrow (stative verb in the continuous)

✅ Right: I'll know the answer tomorrow

❌ Wrong: We will moving the office in June (missing be)

✅ Right: We are going to move the office in June

145 Future Perfect

Deadlines ahead

Will it be finished by then? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapwill have
    completed the audit.

    by the time you arrive.

    the report by Friday.
  4. Will you
    gaphave signed
    it by then?
WILL HAVE + PAST PARTICIPLE→→ completed before a future point
Level B1 Grammar

Future Perfect

Say what will be finished by a future point.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use will have + past participle with by and by the time.
Examples in context
  • By June, we will have completed the audit. Finished before June. — Will have + participle.
  • She will have left by the time you arrive. Earlier than your arrival. — By the time marks the point.
  • Will you have signed it by then? Question form. — Will + subject + have + participle.

👀 What do you observe?

The future perfect describes an action that will be complete before a specified future time. It is built with will have plus the past participle, and it almost always appears with by, by the time, before or a date. It is the future counterpart of the past perfect, and it is common in project planning and in promises with a deadline.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
will have + participle completed before a future point by June, we will have completed the audit
by / by the time the future reference point by the time you arrive
negative won't have + participle they won't have finished by Friday
question will + subject + have + participle will you have signed it by then?
with before the point may be an event we will have left before the panel sits
contrast with future continuous finished versus in progress will have finished / will be finishing

Formula / rule: Set the future deadline first, then say what will be finished by then: will have plus the participle. If the action will be in progress rather than complete, use the future continuous; if it is simply later, use will.

★ Why it matters

The future perfect is the tense of commitments: we will have delivered by June is a promise with a date attached, and it is checkable in a way that we will deliver is not. That is why it appears in contracts, project plans and performance reviews.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use it less than the past perfect, and often replace it in speech with will be done by or should have finished by. In writing it signals a firm commitment.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The stress falls on the participle: by June, we will have comPLETED the audit; the auxiliary strings are weak.

Additional example bank
  • Deadline: By the end of the quarter, the migration will have finished.
  • Earlier than an event: The panel will have reported before the board meets.
  • Question: Will the auditors have signed off by then?
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: By June, we will complete the audit (simple future where completion by a point is meant)

✅ Right: By June, we will have completed the audit

❌ Wrong: She will has left by the time you arrive (have after will)

✅ Right: She will have left by the time you arrive

146 Have To, Must, Should, Had Better

Obligation

How strong, and who says so? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. You
    gapmust
    submit the form today.
  2. We
    gaphave to
    file by 31 March.
  3. You
    gapshould
    check the figures.
  4. You
    gaphad better
    tell them before Friday.
MODAL→→ strength and source
Level B1 Grammar

Have To, Must, Should, Had Better

Grade the pressure from a rule to a piece of advice.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can choose the modal that matches how strong the obligation is and who imposed it.
Examples in context
  • You must submit it today. Strong, speaker's authority. — Must.
  • We have to file by 31 March. External rule. — Have to.
  • You should check the figures. Advice. — Should.

👀 What do you observe?

Must and have to both express obligation, but must usually carries the speaker's authority while have to reports a rule imposed from outside. Should gives advice with no compulsion. Had better gives advice with a warning of consequences and takes the base verb. Ought to sits with should but is slightly more formal and less common in speech.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form reports an external rule?

2. What does had better add to advice?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
must strong obligation, speaker's authority you must submit the form today
have to external rule or necessity we have to file by 31 March
should / ought to advice, expectation you should check the figures
had better + base advice with a warning you'd better tell them
don't have to no obligation you don't have to attend
mustn't prohibition you mustn't share the file

Formula / rule: Decide the strength first: obligation, advice or warning. Then decide the source: the speaker (must), an institution (have to), or nobody in particular (should). Keep mustn't apart from don't have to, since one forbids and the other releases.

★ Why it matters

These four carry the difference between a rule and a suggestion, which is the difference between a compliance failure and a missed improvement. In a workplace, a task described with should is optional in practice, and a task described with must is auditable, so the choice has consequences.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers keep must for written rules and self-imposed duties, and use have to for everything institutional in speech. Had better is usually contracted and can sound like a threat when the stress falls on better.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Have to reduces to /hæftə/ and had better to /ˈbetə/, with the auxiliary almost lost; should is unstressed unless it corrects.

Additional example bank
  • Rule: Visitors must sign in at reception.
  • Necessity: We have to resubmit the whole application.
  • Advice: You should ask for the minutes in writing.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: You don't have to share the file; it is confidential (no obligation where a prohibition is meant)

✅ Right: You mustn't share the file; it is confidential

❌ Wrong: You had better to check the figures (to after had better)

✅ Right: You had better check the figures

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Needn't, didn't need to · Can, could, be able to

Impersonal reporting

Who says it, and how is it framed? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapthat
    the merger will close in June.

IT IS SAID / THOUGHT / BELIEVED→+ that + clause
Level B1 Grammar

It Is Said That

Report general opinion without naming the source.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use it is said that and the passive reporting patterns.
Examples in context
  • It is said that the merger will close. Opinion without a source. — It + passive + that.
  • The company is said to be restructuring. Subject + passive + to-infinitive. — Same meaning, tighter.
  • He is believed to have left. Earlier action with a perfect infinitive. — To have + participle.

👀 What do you observe?

These patterns report what people generally say without naming them. Two forms are equivalent: it is said that the merger will close, and the merger is said to be closing. Verbs used this way include say, think, believe, report, consider, expect and understand. When the reported action is earlier than the reporting, the infinitive is perfect: he is believed to have left.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

2. Which infinitive marks an earlier action?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
it is said that + clause impersonal framing it is said that the merger will close
subject + is said to + base same meaning, subject first the company is said to be restructuring
to have + participle earlier action he is believed to have left
it is thought / believed / reported other reporting verbs it is thought that the delay was avoidable
it is understood that formal, in minutes it is understood that the terms still hold
there is said to be existence framing there is said to be a second file

Formula / rule: Choose the framing: impersonal (it is said that) when the source is irrelevant or unknown, or subject-first (the subject is said to) when the topic matters. Then set the infinitive: to do for simultaneous, to have done for earlier.

★ Why it matters

This is the register of journalism and of official prose that must not attribute: it is believed that reports a consensus without a witness. It also protects the writer, which is why it appears in reports where a claim cannot be sourced.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use these patterns chiefly in news and formal writing, and they say people say or apparently in speech. Is said to is also used to distance a rumour politely.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The reporting verb is unstressed and the infinitive carries the stress: the company is said to be reSTRUCturing.

Additional example bank
  • News: The firm is reported to be seeking a buyer.
  • Rumour: He is understood to have resigned.
  • Existence: There is said to be a second version.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The company is said restructuring (missing to be)

✅ Right: The company is said to be restructuring

❌ Wrong: He is believed to left the country (base verb where a perfect infinitive is needed)

✅ Right: He is believed to have left the country

148 Linking Words

Connectors

What is the relation between the two ideas? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The bid was late
    gapand
    incomplete.
  2. It was expensive
    gap, but
    it worked.
  3. The audit failed
    gapbecause
    the file was missing.
  4. Costs rose
    gap, so
    we cut the scope.
RELATION→→ connector + punctuation
Level B1 Grammar

Linking Words

Connect ideas and show the relation between them.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can choose connectors for addition, contrast, cause, result and example.
Examples in context
  • The bid was late and incomplete. Addition, same direction. — And joins equal ideas.
  • It was expensive, but it worked. Contrast. — But takes a comma before it.
  • Costs rose, so we cut the scope. Result. — So introduces the consequence.

👀 What do you observe?

Linking words fall into five relations: addition (and, moreover, in addition), contrast (but, however, although, whereas), cause (because, since, as), result (so, therefore, consequently), and example (for example, for instance, such as). Some join clauses inside a sentence, others open a new sentence with a comma. However and therefore are adverbs, not conjunctions, so they need a full stop or a semicolon before them.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Can however join two clauses with a comma alone?
It was expensive. However, it worked.
2. Which connector marks a result?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
addition and, moreover, in addition the bid was late and incomplete
contrast but, although, whereas, however expensive, but it worked
cause because, since, as failed because the file was missing
result so, therefore, consequently costs rose, so we cut the scope
example for example, such as software such as the audit tool
punctuation however and therefore are adverbs it failed. However, we retried.

Formula / rule: Name the relation first, then pick the connector: same direction, opposite, reason, consequence, illustration. Then check the punctuation, because the adverb connectors need a boundary before them while the conjunctions do not.

★ Why it matters

Connectors are the argument. Two facts joined by because make a claim about causation, the same two joined by and make no claim at all. A reader follows the reasoning through these words, which is why a report with no connectors reads as a list and a report with the wrong ones reads as a non sequitur.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers overuse so and but in speech and switch to therefore and however in writing; using however in conversation sounds formal. In academic writing, moreover and consequently are frequent and rarely wrong.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The connector usually carries a light stress at the start of its clause: it was expensive, BUT it worked; costs rose, SO we cut the scope.

Additional example bank
  • Contrast in writing: The timetable was met. However, the budget was not.
  • Cause: Since the file is missing, the audit cannot close.
  • Example: We use tools such as the audit log.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: It was expensive, however it worked (comma splice with an adverb connector)

✅ Right: It was expensive. However, it worked.

❌ Wrong: The audit failed, because of the file was missing (preposition used as a conjunction)

✅ Right: The audit failed because the file was missing

149 Mixed Conditionals

Time and condition

Which time does each half refer to? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. If I had taken
    gapthe job
    , I would live in Berlin now.
  2. If she were
    gapmore careful
    , the error would not have happened.
  3. If we had invested
    gapin 2019
    , we would own the market today.
  4. If he spoke
    gapGerman
    , he would have got the post.
PAST CONDITION→→ would + base (present result)
Level B1 Grammar

Mixed Conditionals

Join a condition in one time to a result in another.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use a past condition with a present result, or a present condition with a past result.
Examples in context
  • If I had studied law, I would be a solicitor now. Past condition, present result. — Past perfect, then would + base.
  • If she were tidier, the file would not have been lost. Present condition, past result. — Past simple, then would have + participle.
  • If they had listened, we would not be here. The classic mixed pair. — Same shape as the first.

👀 What do you observe?

A mixed conditional joins two time frames. Past condition with present result: if + past perfect, would + base verb. Present condition with past result: if + past simple, would have + past participle. The half that carries the condition sets the tense of the other half's auxiliary, and would never appears in the if-clause.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. In 'If I had taken the job, I would live in Berlin now', when is the result?

2. Which half is unreal in 'If she were more careful'?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
past condition + present result if + past perfect, would + base if I had taken it, I would live there now
present condition + past result if + past simple, would have + participle if she were careful, it would not have happened
past condition + past result third conditional if I had known, I would have called
present condition + present result second conditional if I knew, I would tell you
unreal present with be were for all persons if he were here
inverted mixed conditional Had + subject, would + base had we known, we would be prepared

Formula / rule: Choose the time of each half separately: the condition by when it is unreal, the result by when it lands. Past condition, present result takes if + past perfect and would + base. Present condition, past result takes if + past simple and would have + participle.

★ Why it matters

Mixed conditionals are how English argues about consequences that outlive their causes. A decision in 2019 explains a present shortfall, and the third conditional alone cannot say that. The mix is also what makes a history essay sound analytic rather than narrative.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers mix conditionals freely in speech and rarely notice the time shift; what they notice is would in the if-clause, which marks a learner. In writing, the mixed form signals deliberate analysis.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The time marker carries the stress, which is what makes the mix audible: I would LIVE there NOW; it would not HAVE happened.

Additional example bank
  • Past to present: If the factory had stayed open, the town would still have work.
  • Present to past: If he were better organised, the deadline would have been met.
  • Inverted: Had the warning been heeded, we would not be in this position.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: If I would have taken the job, I would live in Berlin (would in the if-clause)

✅ Right: If I had taken the job, I would live in Berlin

❌ Wrong: If she was more careful, the error would not have happened (indicative for an unreal present)

✅ Right: If she were more careful, the error would not have happened

150 Modals of Deduction: Past

Past deduction

How certain is the speaker? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The file
    gapmust have been
    deleted.
  2. She
    gapmight have missed
    the email.
  3. They
    gapcan't have known
    the result.
  4. He
    gapcould have signed
    it already.
MODAL + HAVE + PAST PARTICIPLE→→ judgement about a past event
Level B1 Grammar

Modals of Deduction: Past

Say how certain a past event is.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use must have, might have and can't have to judge past events.
Examples in context
  • The file must have been deleted. Almost certain. — Must have + participle.
  • She might have missed the email. Possible. — Might have + participle.
  • They can't have known. Almost impossible. — Can't have + participle.

👀 What do you observe?

Past deduction uses a modal plus have plus the past participle. Must have marks near certainty that something happened. Might have, may have and could have mark possibility. Can't have and couldn't have mark near certainty that it did not happen. Should have and ought to have add expectation or regret, and needn't have marks something done that was unnecessary.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form marks near certainty that something happened?
The file must have been deleted.
2. Which form marks near certainty that something did not happen?
They can't have known.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
must have near certainty, affirmative the file must have been deleted
might / may / could have possibility she might have missed the email
can't / couldn't have near certainty, negative they can't have known
should have expectation, often criticism you should have told me
needn't have unnecessary but done you needn't have waited
modal + have + participle never a past form after the modal must have been, not must was

Formula / rule: Judge the evidence first, then pick the modal: strong positive evidence takes must have, possible evidence takes might have, strong contrary evidence takes can't have. The verb after the modal is always have plus the participle, whatever the tense of the story.

★ Why it matters

Past deduction is how English reasons aloud about what it cannot see: the file must have been deleted says the evidence is overwhelming without saying who did it. That is a useful move in an audit and a dangerous one in a disciplinary hearing, which is why the modal choice is scrutinised.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers contract the pattern heavily (must've, might've, can't've) and the contracted forms sound identical to must of, might of, which is a common spelling error even among natives.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Have is weak /əv/ in all four, and the modal carries the stress: it MUST have been deleted; they CAN'T have known.

Additional example bank
  • Certain: The panel must have received the report late.
  • Possible: The supplier may have misread the specification.
  • Impossible: They couldn't have finished in one day.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The file must was deleted (past form after a modal)

✅ Right: The file must have been deleted

❌ Wrong: They mustn't have known (mustn't for a negative deduction)

✅ Right: They can't have known

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Modals of Deduction: Present (Must, Can't, Might/Could)

might / may / could50% possible (maybe yes, maybe no)He's not answering. He might be busy.

🔊 Pronunciation

In deductions, "must" is usually pronounced in its weak form /məst/ or /məs/ in fast connected speech (He must be tired), but stressed to /mʌst/ when emphasizing certainty (He MUST be joking!).

152 Modifying Comparatives

Degrees of difference

Which modifier fits the size of the gap? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapfar
    faster.

    gapslightly
    clearer.

    gapno

MODIFIER→+ comparative adjective
Level B1 Grammar

Modifying Comparatives

Say how much bigger, how much better, how much less.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can modify a comparative with much, far, slightly, a bit and no.
Examples in context
  • much faster a large difference — The new system is much faster.
  • slightly clearer a small difference — This draft is slightly clearer.
  • no better no difference at all — The second offer is no better.

👀 What do you observe?

A comparative can be graded by the size of the gap. Large: much, far, considerably, significantly, a great deal. Small: slightly, a little, a bit, marginally. None: no, not any. The modifier goes before the comparative adjective or adverb, and much and far work with both short and long forms.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
much / far large difference much faster, far more expensive
considerably / significantly large, formal considerably higher
slightly / marginally small difference slightly clearer
a bit / a little small, informal a bit cheaper
no / not any no difference no better, not any worse
even surprising extra degree even faster than expected

Formula / rule: Judge the gap, then pick the modifier: much or far for a large one, slightly or marginally for a small one, no for none. Keep the comparative form intact after the modifier: much more expensive, not much expensive.

★ Why it matters

These modifiers are the vocabulary of comparison in reports, where the size of a difference is the finding: marginally higher and far higher describe two different worlds. Learners often overstate with very, which cannot modify a comparative at all.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use way in speech for a large difference (way faster) and avoid it in writing. A bit and a little soften criticism, which makes them frequent in feedback.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The modifier is stressed when the size is the point: FAR faster, SLIGHTly clearer, NO better.

Additional example bank
  • Large: The second version is significantly cheaper to run.
  • Small: Response times are marginally slower.
  • None: The revised offer is no more attractive than the first.

❌ Wrong: The new system is very faster (very with a comparative)

✅ Right: The new system is much faster

❌ Wrong: This draft is slightly more clear (double comparative form)

✅ Right: This draft is slightly clearer

154 Needn't, Didn't Need To, Needn't Have

Need

Was it unnecessary, or just not required? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. You
    gapneedn't
    attend the briefing.
  2. We
    gapdidn't need to
    resubmit the form.
  3. You
    gapneedn't have
    waited outside.
  4. She needn't
    gaphave paid
    in advance.
NEEDN'T + base→→ no obligation, now or future
Level B1 Grammar

Needn't, Didn't Need To, Needn't Have

Separate no obligation from unnecessary action.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use needn't, didn't need to and needn't have with the right meaning.
Examples in context
  • You needn't attend the briefing. No obligation, present or future. — Needn't + base verb.
  • We didn't need to resubmit. No obligation, and it was not done. — Didn't need to + base.
  • You needn't have waited. It was done, but unnecessary. — Needn't have + participle.

👀 What do you observe?

Needn't plus the base verb removes an obligation: you needn't attend, meaning you are not required to. Didn't need to says the same about the past and usually implies it was not done. Needn't have plus the past participle says it was done but did not need to be: you needn't have waited means you did wait. Didn't need to and needn't have are the pair that learners mix.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form says the action was done unnecessarily?
You needn't have waited: you did wait.
2. Which form removes an obligation?
Mustn't prohibits; needn't releases.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
needn't + base no obligation you needn't attend
didn't need to + base no obligation in the past, action not done we didn't need to resubmit
needn't have + participle action done, unnecessarily you needn't have waited
mustn't prohibition, not the same you mustn't sign without authority
don't have to neutral form of needn't you don't have to attend
need as a normal verb questions and negatives with do do we need to resubmit?

Formula / rule: Ask two things: is the obligation removed, and was the action done? Not required now or later: needn't. Not required then, not done: didn't need to. Done but not required: needn't have. Keep mustn't apart, since it forbids rather than releases.

★ Why it matters

This set is where permission and obligation meet, and the difference has consequences in a workplace: you needn't attend is an option, you mustn't attend is a ban, and you needn't have attended means the room was empty. Using one for another creates either annoyance or a compliance risk.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use didn't need to and didn't have to interchangeably, and they use needn't mostly in British English; Americans prefer don't have to. Needn't have is common in British speech as gentle criticism.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Needn't contracts heavily (/ˈniːdnt/) and the participle is stressed in the reproach: you needn't HAVE waited.

Additional example bank
  • Option: You needn't include the annex.
  • Not done: We didn't need to book in advance.
  • Unnecessary: You needn't have sent it twice.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: You mustn't attend if you are busy (prohibition where an option is meant)

✅ Right: You needn't attend if you are busy

❌ Wrong: You needn't have waited if it was closed (the action was not done)

✅ Right: You didn't need to wait

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Have to, must, should, had better · Can, could, be able to

155 Passive: Continuous and Perfect

Passive forms

Ongoing or completed? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapis being
    repainted.
  2. The file
    gapwas being
    checked when the system failed.
  3. The report
    gaphas been
    published.
  4. The room
    gaphad been
    cleaned before we arrived.
BEING→→ action in progress · BEEN → action completed
Level B1 Grammar

Passive: Continuous and Perfect

Put an ongoing or completed action in the passive.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use is being, was being, has been and had been in the passive.
Examples in context
  • The office is being repainted. Present continuous passive. — Is being + participle.
  • The report has been published. Present perfect passive. — Has been + participle.
  • The room had been cleaned. Past perfect passive. — Had been + participle.

👀 What do you observe?

The continuous passive uses being plus the participle: is being repainted, was being checked. The perfect passive uses been plus the participle: has been published, had been cleaned, will have been finished. Both keep the tense on the auxiliary, and both keep the participle unchanged.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

2. Which form marks a completed action before a past point?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
is / are being + participle present continuous passive the office is being repainted
was / were being + participle past continuous passive the file was being checked
has / have been + participle present perfect passive the report has been published
had been + participle past perfect passive the room had been cleaned
will have been + participle future perfect passive it will have been finished by June
being versus been in progress versus completed is being checked / has been checked

Formula / rule: Choose the time and the aspect first, then build: progressive takes being, perfect takes been, and the participle never changes. The single most common error is writing been where being belongs.

★ Why it matters

The continuous passive is the tense of work in progress (the system is being migrated), and the perfect passive is the tense of results (the system has been migrated). In status reporting those two sentences describe completely different states.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use the continuous passive mainly in writing and formal speech; in conversation they prefer the active (they're repainting the office). The perfect passive is common everywhere.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Being is stressed when the progress is the point: the office is BEING repainted; been is weak and the participle carries the stress.

Additional example bank
  • In progress: The accounts are being audited this week.
  • Completed: The accounts have been audited.
  • Earlier: The site had been cleared before the survey.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The office is been repainted (been where being belongs)

✅ Right: The office is being repainted

❌ Wrong: The report has being published (being where been belongs)

✅ Right: The report has been published

BE + PAST PARTICIPLE→→ tense carried by be
Level B1 Grammar

Passive: Simple and Future Tenses

Put the object first in the present, past and future.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can form the passive in present simple, past simple and future.
Examples in context
  • The file is checked daily. Present simple passive. — Is + participle.
  • The contract was signed in June. Past simple passive. — Was + participle.
  • The results will be published. Future passive. — Will be + participle.

👀 What do you observe?

The passive takes the tense on be and leaves the main verb as a past participle. Present simple: is checked. Past simple: was signed. Future: will be published. Present continuous: is being repainted. Past continuous: was being checked. The agent appears in a by-phrase only when it matters: the contract was signed by both directors.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

Element / structure Role in English Application example
present simple is / are + participle the file is checked daily
past simple was / were + participle the contract was signed in June
future will be + participle the results will be published
present continuous is / are being + participle the office is being repainted
past continuous was / were being + participle the room was being cleaned
agent with by only when it matters signed by both directors

Formula / rule: Find the tense the sentence needs, put it on be, and leave the participle alone. Then decide whether the agent earns a by-phrase: it does when the reader needs to know who acted, and it does not when the actor is obvious, unknown or irrelevant.

★ Why it matters

The passive lets a writer keep the topic in front: the file is checked daily puts the file first because the file is what the paragraph is about. It also hides the agent, which is a service in a process description and a problem in an accountability report.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use the passive freely in process talk (the forms are sent out automatically) and avoid it in personal statements. In speech, the agent is usually dropped: it was cancelled, nobody knows by whom.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The auxiliary is unstressed and the participle carries the information stress: the file is CHECKED every morning; the results will be PUBlished.

  • Past: The minutes were circulated after the meeting.
  • Future: The panels will be replaced in April.

✅ Right: The contract was signed in June

Level B1 Grammar

Passive with Modals

Keep the modal and put the verb in the passive.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use must be, can be, should have been and might be in the passive.
Examples in context
  • The form must be signed today. Present obligation, passive. — Must be + participle.
  • The file should have been checked. Past criticism, passive. — Should have been + participle.
  • The room can be booked online. Possibility, passive. — Can be + participle.

👀 What do you observe?

In a modal passive the modal stays first, be follows it, and the main verb is a past participle: must be signed, can be booked, might be shared. For a past judgement the pattern is modal plus have been plus the participle: should have been checked, must have been sent. The agent, if named, comes in a by-phrase.

★ Why it matters

The modal passive is the register of rules and procedures: forms must be signed, rooms can be booked, figures should have been checked. It states an obligation or a possibility without naming the person, which is exactly what a policy needs and exactly what an accountability report must avoid.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use the present modal passive constantly in instructions and hedge with it: this should be checked before publication. The past form, should have been, is the standard written form of criticism.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Be is weak after the modal, and the participle carries the stress: the form must be SIGNED today; the file should have been CHECKED.

158 Past Perfect: Had + Past Participle

Sequence

Which action came first? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The train
    gaphad left
    before we arrived.
  2. She
    gaphad finished
    the report by noon.
  3. We
    gaphad not seen
    the memo until Friday.
  4. After he
    gaphad signed
    , the terms changed.
EARLIER ACTION→→ had + past participle · LATER → past simple
Level B1 Grammar

Past Perfect: Had + Past Participle

Show which of two past events happened first.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use the past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.
Examples in context
  • The train had left before we arrived. Leaving came first. — Had left, then arrived.
  • She had finished by noon. Completed before a past point. — Had + participle with by.
  • After he had signed, the terms changed. After marks the earlier clause. — Had signed, then changed.

👀 What do you observe?

The past perfect marks an action completed before another past action or before a past moment. The reference point stays in the past simple: had left before we arrived, had finished by noon. It is used with before, after, by the time, already, never and until. In a sequence where the order is already clear, the past simple is enough and the past perfect can sound heavy.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which action does the past perfect describe?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
had + participle earlier past action the train had left
before / after explicit order after he had signed
by the time deadline in the past by the time we arrived, it had closed
already / never / just position with the perfect she had already left
negative had not + participle we had not seen the memo
past simple for clear sequence avoid overusing the perfect he opened the door and walked in

Formula / rule: Place the two events on a line, choose the reference point, and give the earlier one had plus the participle. If the order is already carried by before or after, the simple past is acceptable and often better, especially in speech and in narrative with then.

★ Why it matters

The past perfect is the only tense that can step back from a past moment, which is why it carries explanation: the figures had been revised before the board met tells you why the board's decision looks odd. Without it, the reader has to infer the order, and the inference is often wrong.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers underuse the past perfect rather than overuse it, and rely on before, after and then to order events. In British English it appears more often in writing than in speech.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The auxiliary is contracted in speech (they'd left), and the participle is stressed when the order is the point: the train had LEFT before we arrived.

Additional example bank
  • Earlier: The file had already been deleted when the auditor asked for it.
  • Deadline: By Friday, the panel had received only two replies.
  • Negative: I had never seen the annex before that meeting.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: When I arrived, she already left (past simple where the earlier event needs the perfect)

✅ Right: When I arrived, she had already left

❌ Wrong: After he has signed, the terms changed (present perfect in a past narrative)

✅ Right: After he had signed, the terms changed

Level B1 Grammar

Past Perfect Continuous

Say how long something had been going on before a past event.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use had been + -ing for an activity in progress before a past point.
Examples in context
  • They had been negotiating for weeks. Duration before a past event. — Had been + -ing.
  • The line had been running since dawn. Started earlier, still true at the point. — Since marks the start.
  • She had been working there for a year. Duration, with a visible result. — For marks the length.

👀 What do you observe?

The past perfect continuous describes an activity that had been going on up to a past moment, often explaining a visible result: the ground was wet because it had been raining. It takes for with a length of time and since with a starting point, and it is the past counterpart of the present perfect continuous.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
had been + -ing activity up to a past point they had been negotiating for weeks
for + duration length of time for a year
since + starting point when it began since dawn
visible result explains the state at the moment the ground was wet because it had been raining
negative hadn't been + -ing the system hadn't been working for days
contrast with past perfect activity versus completed action had been writing / had written

Formula / rule: Fix the past moment, then ask whether the activity was completed by it or still running into it. Completed: past perfect. Still running, with duration: past perfect continuous. Add for or since to make the duration explicit.

★ Why it matters

This tense is the grammar of explanation in reports: the figures were unreliable because the system had been running on a patched version for months. It carries the cause and the duration in one clause, which is why incident reports lean on it.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use it freely in speech when explaining a state (I'd been waiting for an hour), and often reduce had been to /ɪdbɪn/ or /bɪn/.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Been is weak and the -ing form carries the stress: they had been neGOtiating for WEEKS.

Additional example bank
  • Duration: The team had been pressing for a decision since March.
  • Explanation: The file was incomplete because it had been edited offline.
  • Negative: The alarm hadn't been working for days.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: They had been negotiate for weeks (base verb instead of -ing)

✅ Right: They had been negotiating for weeks

❌ Wrong: She had been working there since a year (since with a duration)

✅ Right: She had been working there for a year

Phrasal verbs

Can the object move? tap the line.write it on the line.

SEPARABLE→→ object before or after · INSEPARABLE → keep together
Level B1 Grammar

Phrasal Verbs: Grammar Patterns

Know whether the object goes before or after the particle.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can separate transitive phrasal verbs correctly and keep inseparable ones together.
Examples in context
  • They turned down the offer. Separable: the object can follow. — Turn the offer down.
  • She looks after the archive. Inseparable: the particle stays. — Never look the archive after.
  • We ran into the client. Inseparable, and idiomatic. — Ran into = met by chance.

👀 What do you observe?

Separable phrasal verbs allow the object between the verb and the particle, or after both: turn down the offer, turn the offer down. A pronoun must go between: turn it down. Inseparable verbs keep the particle next to the verb: look after the archive, run into a client. Three-part verbs are always inseparable: put up with the delay.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

2. Can an inseparable verb be split by its object?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
separable object before or after the particle turn down the offer / turn the offer down
pronoun with separable always between turn it down
inseparable particle stays with the verb look after the archive
three-part inseparable put up with the delay
intransitive no object the plan fell through
register single verb in formal writing reject, tolerate, investigate

Formula / rule: Check the pattern in a dictionary before you split. If the verb is separable, put a pronoun inside and a noun either side. If it is inseparable, keep the particle attached. In formal writing, replace the whole thing with a single verb.

★ Why it matters

The pattern decides where the object goes, and the error is audible: turn off it is a learner error, while turn it off is automatic for a native. In writing, the phrasal verb is also a register marker, which is why reports say postpone rather than put off.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers split separable verbs freely in speech (turn the light off) and often keep the object first in writing (turn off the light). Inseparable verbs are learned as single words.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The particle is stressed when it carries the meaning: turn it DOWN; the plan fell THROUGH.

Additional example bank
  • Separable: They called the meeting off at short notice.
  • Inseparable: The lawyer looked into the complaint.
  • Three-part: Nobody will put up with that behaviour.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: They turned down it (pronoun after the particle)

✅ Right: They turned it down

❌ Wrong: She looks the archive after (inseparable verb split)

✅ Right: She looks after the archive

162 Present Perfect Simple vs Continuous

Perfect forms

Result or activity? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. I
    gaphave sent
    the file.
  2. I
    gaphave been sending
    reminders all week.
  3. She
    gaphas written
    three reports.
  4. She
    gaphas been writing
    since eight.
RESULT→→ have + participle · ACTIVITY → have been + -ing
Level B1 Grammar

Present Perfect Simple vs Continuous

Choose between the result and the activity.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can tell a finished result from an activity that has been going on.
Examples in context
  • I have sent the file. Completed action, result now. — Simple: the job is done.
  • I have been sending reminders all week. Repeated activity up to now. — Continuous: the activity continues.
  • She has written three reports. Completed, counted. — Simple with a quantity.

👀 What do you observe?

The present perfect simple reports a completed action with a present result, and it is the form used with quantities: I have sent it, she has written three reports. The present perfect continuous reports an activity that has been going on up to now, often without a result: I have been sending reminders, she has been writing since eight. With for and since, both are possible, and the continuous emphasises duration.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form reports a completed result?

2. Which form goes with 'three reports'?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
have + participle completed action, result I have sent the file
have been + -ing activity continuing to now I have been sending reminders
simple + quantity counted results she has written three reports
continuous + duration how long the activity lasted she has been writing since eight
simple with stative verbs no continuous form I have known her for years
both with for / since simple for result, continuous for duration I have worked here since 2019 / I have been working here since 2019

Formula / rule: Ask whether the sentence reports a result or an activity. A result, especially with a number, takes the simple form. An activity that is still going, especially with a duration, takes the continuous. Stative verbs stay in the simple form.

★ Why it matters

The pair carries a claim about completion: I have written the report tells the reader it exists, I have been writing it tells them it is not finished. In a work context that difference is the point of the sentence, which is why the choice is worth getting right.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use the continuous for complaints and explanations (I have been waiting for an hour) and the simple for announcements (I have finished). In American English the simple is used where British English would use the continuous with just and already.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The auxiliary contracts (I've sent, I've been sending) and the stress falls on the participle or on the duration phrase: I've been WAITing for an HOUR.

Additional example bank
  • Result: We have published the figures.
  • Activity: We have been reviewing the figures since Monday.
  • Quantity: They have opened four new offices this year.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: I have been sending the file yesterday (continuous for a completed action with a past time)

✅ Right: I have sent the file

❌ Wrong: She has been writing three reports (continuous with a quantity)

✅ Right: She has written three reports
