164 Question Tags

Tags

Which tag completes the sentence? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The file arrived,
    gapdidn't it
    ?
  2. You haven't signed,
    gaphave you
    ?
  3. Nobody called,
    gapdid they
    ?
  4. Let's start,
    gapshall we
    ?
STATEMENT→+ opposite-polarity tag with the same auxiliary
Level B1 Grammar

Question Tags

Add a short question to check or invite agreement.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can build question tags that match the auxiliary, the polarity and the subject.
Examples in context
  • The file arrived, didn't it? Positive statement, negative tag. — Did carries the tense.
  • You haven't signed, have you? Negative statement, positive tag. — Have repeats the auxiliary.
  • Nobody called, did they? Negative meaning, positive tag, they for nobody. — Nobody takes they.

👀 What do you observe?

A question tag repeats the auxiliary of the statement with the opposite polarity: the file arrived, didn't it? A positive statement takes a negative tag, a negative statement a positive one. If the statement has no auxiliary, the tag uses do, does or did. The tag takes the subject pronoun, never a noun, and nobody, nothing and never count as negative, so the tag is positive.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What polarity does a positive statement take?
The file arrived, didn't it?
2. Which pronoun replaces nobody in a tag?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
positive statement negative tag the file arrived, didn't it?
negative statement positive tag you haven't signed, have you?
no auxiliary do / does / did in the tag she works here, doesn't she?
nobody / nothing / never positive tag with they / it nothing happened, did it?
let's shall we let's start, shall we?
imperative will you / won't you close the door, will you?

Formula / rule: Copy the auxiliary, flip the polarity, and use a pronoun. If there is no auxiliary, the tag brings do, does or did. Then check the negative words, because nobody, never and hardly make the statement negative and the tag positive.

★ Why it matters

Tags carry the social move rather than the information: a falling tag invites agreement (it's cold, isn't it?), a rising tag asks a real question. In British English they are constant and in American English less so, and using the wrong polarity turns a friendly check into a challenge.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use tags to open conversation (nice day, isn't it?) and to close an argument (I told you, didn't I?). In Indian and Singapore English, isn't it? works as a general tag, which is non-standard in British usage.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

A falling tag on a long vowel invites agreement; a rising tag asks. In speech the tag is unstressed when the speaker expects agreement: the file arrived, DIDn't it.

Additional example bank
  • Check: You're joining us, aren't you?
  • Invite agreement: The numbers are clear, aren't they?
  • Imperative: Pass the file, will you?
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The file arrived, isn't it? (tag auxiliary taken from the wrong verb)

✅ Right: The file arrived, didn't it?

❌ Wrong: Nobody called, didn't they? (double negative: nobody plus a negative tag)

✅ Right: Nobody called, did they?

165 Reflexive Pronouns

Reflexives

Is the object the same as the subject? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. She taught
    gapherself
    to negotiate.
  2. They blamed
    gapthemselves
    for the delay.
  3. The board
    gapitself
    approved the change.
  4. He hurt
    gaphimself
    lifting the crate.
SUBJECT = OBJECT→→ myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves
Level B1 Grammar

Reflexive Pronouns

Use myself, yourself and themselves where they belong.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use reflexive pronouns for a shared subject and for emphasis.
Examples in context
  • She taught herself to negotiate. Same person acts and receives. — Reflexive object.
  • The board itself approved the change. Emphasis on the subject. — Emphatic reflexive.
  • The system restarted by itself. Fixed phrase: alone, unaided. — By + reflexive.

👀 What do you observe?

A reflexive pronoun is used when the subject and the object are the same: she taught herself, they blamed themselves. It also marks emphasis, placed after the noun or at the end of the clause: the board itself approved it, the board approved it itself. Fixed phrases include by myself (alone), in itself (considered alone) and help yourself (serve yourself). It is not used after verbs that take no object.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

2. What does 'by itself' mean?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
reflexive object subject and object are the same she taught herself to negotiate
emphatic reflexive emphasis, not a new object the board itself approved the change
by + reflexive alone, unaided the system restarted by itself
in + reflexive considered alone the delay is not a problem in itself
help / behave yourself fixed imperative phrases help yourself to the file
not after intransitive verbs no object to reflect he sat down, not he sat himself down

Formula / rule: Ask whether the object is the same person or thing as the subject. If yes, use a reflexive; if the sentence only needs emphasis, place the reflexive after the noun. Then check the verb: verbs with no object take no reflexive.

★ Why it matters

Reflexives carry responsibility. The departments blamed themselves and the departments blamed the consultants are different findings in a review, and the reflexive is what makes the difference visible in one word.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use reflexives less than learners expect, especially after verbs of movement and rest: sit down, wake up, feel better. Overusing them is one of the clearest signs of translated English.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The -self part is stressed when the emphasis matters: the board itSELF approved it.

Additional example bank
  • Shared subject: The team organised itself into three groups.
  • Emphasis: The chair herself signed the minutes.
  • Fixed phrase: The decision is defensible in itself.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: He sat himself down at the table (reflexive with an intransitive verb)

✅ Right: He sat down at the table

❌ Wrong: The board approved itself the change (reflexive where emphasis is meant)

✅ Right: The board itself approved the change

166 Reported Questions and Commands

Reported speech

Question or command? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. She asked
    gapwhere the file was
    .
  2. He asked
    gapif we had signed
    .
  3. They told us
    gapto wait
    .
  4. The chair asked us
    gapnot to record

ASKED + question word + SUBJECT + VERB→→ TOLD + object + TO + verb
Level B1 Grammar

Reported Questions and Commands

Report what was asked or ordered, without the question form.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can report questions with statement order and commands with the infinitive.
Examples in context
  • She asked where the file was. Reported question, statement order. — No inversion, no question mark.
  • He asked if we had signed. Yes/no question with if. — If introduces the clause.
  • They told us to wait. Reported command. — Tell + object + infinitive.

👀 What do you observe?

Reported questions keep the question word but lose the inversion and the question mark: where is the file becomes she asked where the file was. Yes/no questions take if or whether. Reported commands use tell or ask plus an object plus the infinitive, and negatives put not before the infinitive. Say cannot take an object, so commands need tell, ask, order or advise.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

Element / structure Role in English Application example
reported wh-question statement order she asked where the file was
reported yes/no question if or whether he asked if we had signed
reported command tell + object + infinitive they told us to wait
reported negative command not before the infinitive asked us not to record
ask versus tell tell needs an object she asked me / she told me
tense backshift one step back after a past verb asked where the file was

Formula / rule: Decide whether it was a question or an order. A question keeps its question word, takes statement order and gets if when there is no question word. An order takes tell or ask, an object, and the infinitive. Then backshift the tense if the reporting verb is past.

★ Why it matters

These two patterns are the grammar of minutes and instructions, and the errors are the ones that make a report ambiguous: asked us to wait and asked if we would wait describe different events, and only the second leaves the decision open.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers keep the inversion in very informal reported questions (she asked where's the file), and they use ask for both questions and requests, relying on the pattern to disambiguate.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The reporting verb is unstressed and the reported clause carries the information stress: she asked where the FILE was.

Additional example bank
  • Wh-question: He asked when the panel would report.
  • Yes/no: They asked whether the deadline had moved.
  • Command: The auditor told the team to keep the drafts.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: She asked where was the file (inversion kept)

✅ Right: She asked where the file was

❌ Wrong: They said us to wait (say with an object)

✅ Right: They told us to wait

167 Reported Speech: Statements

Reported statements

How does the tense shift? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapwas
    working on it.

    gaphad
    already left.
  3. They said they
    gapwould
    send the file.

    gapcould
    not attend.
SAID / TOLD→→ one step back in time
Level B1 Grammar

Reported Speech: Statements

Report what someone said and shift the tense back.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can report a statement with the tense, pronouns and time words adjusted.
Examples in context
  • I am busy → He said he was busy. Present to past. — Am becomes was.
  • I have finished → She said she had finished. Perfect to past perfect. — Have becomes had.
  • I will call → He said he would call. Will becomes would. — Future to conditional.

👀 What do you observe?

Reported statements shift the tense one step back: present simple to past simple, present continuous to past continuous, present perfect to past perfect, will to would, can to could, must to had to. Pronouns and time words shift too: now becomes then, today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day. Say takes no object, tell takes a person: he said that, he told me that.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which verb takes a person as its object?

2. What does will become in reported speech?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
present → past tense shift I am busy → he said he was busy
present perfect → past perfect earlier action I have finished → she had finished
will → would future to conditional I will call → he would call
can → could, must → had to modal shift I can't come → he couldn't come
say vs tell tell takes a person he said that / he told me that
time and place words shift too now → then, here → there, tomorrow → the next day

Formula / rule: Move every tense back one step, move the pronouns to the reporter's point of view, and move the time words with them. Keep the tense if the statement is still true and the reporting verb is in the present: she says she is busy.

★ Why it matters

Reported speech is the grammar of minutes, journalism and summaries, and the tense shift is what keeps the timeline honest: a report that says he is busy has not reported anything, it has repeated it. The shift is also where pronouns go wrong, which is why a projected report must be checked for who said what.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers often skip the backshift in conversation when the fact is still true (she said she is coming). In writing, the shift is expected, and the time words are changed consistently or not at all.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The reporting verb is unstressed (he said that /hi ˈsed ðət/) and the reported clause carries the information stress.

Additional example bank
  • Simple: I am reviewing the file → She said she was reviewing the file.
  • Perfect: We have signed → They said they had signed.
  • Modal: I must leave → He said he had to leave.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: He said me that he was busy (say with a person object)

✅ Right: He told me that he was busy

❌ Wrong: She said she will send it (future not shifted)

✅ Right: She said she would send it

168 Reporting Verbs

Reporting verbs

Which pattern does the verb need? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. She
    gapadmitted
    taking the file.
  2. They
    gapdenied
    having seen it.
  3. He
    gapwarned
    us not to sign.
  4. The chair
    gapinsisted

VERB→→ + -ing / + to-infinitive / + that-clause
Level B1 Grammar

Reporting Verbs

Report what was said with a verb that carries the attitude.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use reporting verbs with their own patterns, from admit and deny to warn and insist.
Examples in context
  • She admitted taking the file. Verb + -ing. — Admit, deny, suggest, recommend.
  • He warned us not to sign. Verb + object + to-infinitive. — Warn, persuade, remind, urge.
  • The chair insisted on a written reply. Verb + preposition + noun or -ing. — Insist on, apologise for, object to.

👀 What do you observe?

Reporting verbs carry the speaker's attitude and each has its own pattern. Admit, deny, suggest, recommend and regret take the -ing form. Agree, refuse, offer, promise and threaten take the to-infinitive. Warn, persuade, remind and urge take an object plus the to-infinitive. Insist on, object to, apologise for and accuse of take a preposition. Many also accept a that-clause, which is the safest option when the pattern is uncertain.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
verb + -ing admit, deny, suggest, recommend she admitted taking the file
verb + to-infinitive agree, refuse, offer, promise they refused to sign
verb + object + to-infinitive warn, persuade, remind, urge he warned us not to sign
verb + preposition + -ing insist on, object to, apologise for insisted on a written reply
verb + that-clause safe option for most verbs she admitted that she had taken the file
verb + object + of accuse, suspect they accused him of leaking the file

Formula / rule: Choose the verb for the attitude first, then follow its pattern. If you are unsure of the pattern, use the that-clause, which nearly all reporting verbs accept. Keep the negative before the infinitive: warned us not to sign.

★ Why it matters

Reporting verbs are where a summary becomes an interpretation. Said is neutral; admitted, claimed, conceded and insisted each carry a judgement about the speaker's credibility, which is why they are the vocabulary of journalism and minutes.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use said and told for most reporting and reach for the attitude verbs in writing, where the choice of verb is doing the analysis. Claim in particular implies doubt, which is why lawyers avoid it for their own clients.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The reporting verb is usually unstressed before its clause, and the attitude verbs carry stress when the judgement is the point: she ADmitted it.

Additional example bank
  • Admission: The supplier admitted shipping the wrong batch.
  • Denial: The board denied authorising the payment.
  • Warning: The auditors warned the team against early sign-off.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: They denied to have seen it (infinitive after deny)

✅ Right: They denied having seen it

❌ Wrong: He warned us to not sign (split negative in the wrong place)

✅ Right: He warned us not to sign

169 Second Conditional

Hypotheses

Real or unreal? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. If I had
    gapmore time
    , I would take the course.
  2. If the office were
    gapcloser
    , we would walk.
  3. If we cut
    gapthe budget
    , what would happen?
  4. I would tell you
    gapif I knew

IF + PAST SIMPLE→→ would + base verb
Level B1 Grammar

Second Conditional

Talk about an unreal present or an unlikely future.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use if + past simple with would to describe hypotheses.
Examples in context
  • If I had more time, I would take the course. Unreal present. — Past form, present meaning.
  • If the office were closer, we would walk. Were for an unreal state. — Were for all persons in formal use.
  • What would you do if you lost the contract? Unlikely future. — Hypothetical question.

👀 What do you observe?

The second conditional describes something untrue now or unlikely in the future: if plus the past simple, then would plus the base verb. The past form does not refer to past time; it marks distance from reality. With be, were is used for all persons in careful English, and the if-clause can come second: I would take the course if I had more time.

💡 Check your understanding

Element / structure Role in English Application example
if + past simple unreal present if I had more time
would + base the unreal result I would take the course
were for all persons formal unreal be if she were here
if-clause second result first I would tell you if I knew
unlikely future hypothetical event if you lost the contract
would in the result only never in the if-clause if I knew, I would say

Formula / rule: Decide whether the situation is real or unreal. Real present or future takes the first conditional (if + present, will). Unreal present or unlikely future takes the second (if + past, would). Put the past form in the if-clause and would in the result, never the other way round.

★ Why it matters

The second conditional is the grammar of advice, negotiation and imagination: it lets a speaker propose something without committing to it. That is why it appears in every polite suggestion (would you consider...), and why learners who avoid it sound blunt.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use were in careful speech and was in casual speech without noticing, and they often reduce would to /d/ (I'd take it). The past form in the if-clause is never stressed unless the contrast is the point.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The stress falls on the hypothetical element: if I HAD more time, I would TAKE the course; the modal is weak.

Additional example bank
  • Unreal present: If the team were larger, we could take both clients.
  • Unlikely future: If the deadline moved, would you still bid?
  • Advice: If I were you, I would ask for the minutes.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: If I would have more time, I would take the course (would in the if-clause)

✅ Right: If I had more time, I would take the course

❌ Wrong: If she was here, she would know (indicative for an unreal present in careful writing)

✅ Right: If she were here, she would know

170 So, Such, So Much, So Many

Intensifiers

Which intensifier fits? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The report was
    gapso
    late that we missed the deadline.
  2. It was
    gapsuch
    a long meeting that we left early.
  3. There was
    gapso much
    noise that nobody heard the call.
  4. There were
    gapso many
    errors that we restarted.
SO + ADJECTIVE→→ such + (a/an) + adjective + noun
Level B1 Grammar

So, Such, So Much, So Many

Intensify an adjective, a noun or a quantity.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use so, such, so much and so many in the right pattern.
Examples in context
  • The report was so late. So before an adjective alone. — So + adjective.
  • It was such a long meeting. Such with a noun phrase. — Such + a + adjective + noun.
  • There were so many errors. So many with countable plurals. — So many + plural noun.

👀 What do you observe?

So intensifies an adjective or adverb alone: so late, so quickly. Such intensifies a noun phrase: such a long meeting, such errors. With quantities, so much goes with uncountable nouns and so many with countable plurals. The so ... that and such ... that patterns introduce a consequence. So is never used before a noun, and such never before an adjective alone.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

2. Which goes with an uncountable noun?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
so + adjective intensifies an adjective the report was so late
such + a + adjective + noun intensifies a noun phrase such a long meeting
so much + uncountable quantity, uncountable so much noise
so many + plural quantity, countable so many errors
so / such ... that consequence so late that we missed the deadline
such + plural or uncountable no article such errors, such noise

Formula / rule: Look at what follows. An adjective or adverb on its own takes so. A noun phrase takes such, with a or an if the noun is singular countable. A quantity takes so much or so many according to countability. Then add that plus the consequence if the sentence needs one.

★ Why it matters

These four are the most reliable intensifier errors at B1, because the wrong one is still understandable and therefore never corrected by the listener. In writing they also do argumentative work: so many errors that we restarted states the consequence and the judgement in one clause.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use so in speech for emphasis without a that-clause (it was so late), and such alone as a reaction (such a mess!). Both are informal and frequent.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

So and such are stressed when they carry the intensity: it was SO late; SUCH a long meeting.

Additional example bank
  • Adjective: The queue was so slow that we left.
  • Noun phrase: It was such a short notice period that nobody applied.
  • Quantity: So much paperwork, so little time.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: It was so long meeting that we left (so before a noun phrase)

✅ Right: It was such a long meeting that we left

❌ Wrong: There were so much errors (much with a countable plural)

✅ Right: There were so many errors

171 Third Conditional

Unreal past

What would have been different? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapthe file
    , we would have found the error.
  2. If she had known
    gap

    gapthe memo

IF + PAST PERFECT→→ would have + past participle
Level B1 Grammar

Third Conditional

Talk about a past that did not happen.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use if + past perfect with would have for unreal past situations.
Examples in context
  • If we had checked the file, we would have found the error. Unreal past. — Had checked, would have found.
  • She would have called if she had known. If-clause second. — Same pair, reversed order.
  • Had I seen it, I would have objected. Inverted, formal. — Had replaces if.

👀 What do you observe?

The third conditional describes an unreal past: something did not happen, and we imagine the consequence. It takes if plus the past perfect in the condition and would have plus the past participle in the result. Would never appears in the if-clause, and the inverted form Had I seen replaces if I had seen in formal writing.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
if + past perfect the unreal condition if we had checked the file
would have + participle the unreal result we would have found the error
if-clause second result first she would have called if she had known
inverted form Had + subject, formal had I seen it, I would have objected
negative wouldn't have + participle we wouldn't have lost the client
never would in the if-clause the commonest error if I had known, not if I would have known

Formula / rule: Decide that the situation is past and unreal, then put the past perfect in the condition and would have plus the participle in the result. If the register is formal, invert had and drop if.

★ Why it matters

The third conditional is the grammar of accountability and hindsight: if the file had been checked, the error would have been found is how a review states causation without stating blame. It is also the structure of every post-mortem, which is why it appears in every report of a failure.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use it constantly in speech, usually contracted (we'd have found it), and many replace would have with would of in writing by mistake. The inverted form is reserved for formal speech and writing.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The contraction carries the pattern: we'd have /wiːd əv/, often reduced to woulda in fast speech. The participle is stressed: we would have FOUND it.

Additional example bank
  • Unreal past: If the alarm had worked, the fire would have been contained.
  • Result first: They would have signed if the terms had been clearer.
  • Inverted: Had the audit been earlier, the loss would have been smaller.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: If I would have known, I would have called (would in the if-clause)

✅ Right: If I had known, I would have called

❌ Wrong: If we had checked, we would found the error (missing have)

✅ Right: If we had checked, we would have found the error

Verb pairs

    gapfor

VERB→+ fixed preposition (+ -ing)
Level B1 Grammar

Verb + Preposition

Keep the preposition that belongs to the verb.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use the fixed preposition after common verbs and the gerund that follows it.
Examples in context
  • We depend on the supplier. Verb + on + noun. — Depend on, rely on, insist on.
  • She apologised for the delay. Verb + for + noun. — Apologise for, thank for, blame for.
  • He insisted on a written reply. Verb + on + noun or -ing. — Insisted on replying.

👀 What do you observe?

Verbs take prepositions by convention and the pair is the unit: depend on, rely on, insist on, apologise for, agree to (a proposal) or agree with (a person), apply for (a job) or apply to (an institution), look after, refer to, deal with. When a verb or adjective plus preposition is followed by an action, the gerund follows: insisted on replying, apologised for being late.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
on depend, rely, insist, concentrate we depend on the supplier
for apologise, thank, blame, apply she apologised for the delay
to agree, refer, object, listen they agreed to the terms
with agree with a person, deal with a problem we dealt with the complaint
of accuse of, approve of, think of they accused him of leaking
preposition + -ing the gerund after the preposition insisted on replying

Formula / rule: Learn the verb with its preposition and with the gerund that follows. Where a verb takes different prepositions, the meaning decides: agree to a proposal, agree with a person, agree on a price.

★ Why it matters

These pairs decide meaning in exactly the cases that matter: apply for a job and apply to a company are both correct and not interchangeable, and accuse of is not the same as blame for. A wrong preposition turns a precise claim into a vague one.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers vary in a few pairs (different from, different to) and are fixed in the rest. The gerund after a preposition is automatic for a native and a common gap for a learner.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The preposition is unstressed and leans on the verb: dePEND on, aPOlogise for, inSIST on.

Additional example bank
  • Depend: The timetable depends on the audit.
  • Apply: She applied for the post and applied to the board.
  • Preposition plus gerund: They insisted on seeing the file.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: We depend of the supplier (wrong preposition)

✅ Right: We depend on the supplier

❌ Wrong: He insisted to see the file (infinitive after a preposition)

✅ Right: He insisted on seeing the file

173 Verbs of the Senses

Senses

Complete or in progress? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapleave
    the building.

    gapleaving
    the building.
  3. The room
    gapfelt

SEE / HEAR + object + bare infinitive→→ the whole action · + -ing → in progress
Level B1 Grammar

Verbs of the Senses

Describe what you see, hear and feel precisely.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use sense verbs with a bare infinitive, an -ing form or an adjective.
Examples in context
  • I saw him leave. The whole action, start to finish. — Bare infinitive.
  • I saw him leaving. An action already under way. — The -ing form.
  • The room felt cold. Sense verb plus adjective. — Feel + adjective describes.

👀 What do you observe?

Verbs of the senses take an object plus either a bare infinitive or an -ing form. The bare infinitive reports a complete action: I saw him leave. The -ing form reports an action in progress: I saw him leaving. Feel, look, sound, smell and taste also take adjectives to describe the impression: the room felt cold, the plan sounds risky.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
see / hear + object + bare infinitive complete action I saw him leave
see / hear + object + -ing action in progress I saw him leaving
feel / look / sound / smell / taste + adjective impression the plan sounds risky
feel like + -ing inclination I feel like leaving early
passive be seen to + infinitive he was seen to leave
watch / notice / observe same pattern as see we watched them work

Formula / rule: Decide whether the action was complete or in progress, then choose the bare infinitive or the -ing form. For impressions, use an adjective after the sense verb, not an adverb.

★ Why it matters

The difference between saw him leave and saw him leaving is evidential: the first reports the whole event, the second catches it mid-way. In a witness statement or an incident report, that distinction is the finding.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use the -ing form far more in speech, because most things we notice are already in progress when we notice them. The bare infinitive appears mainly after see and hear with a completed action.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The -ing form carries the stress when the progress is the point: I saw him LEAVing.

Additional example bank
  • Complete: We saw the panel sign the minutes.
  • In progress: We saw the panel arguing in the corridor.
  • Impression: The proposal sounds expensive.

❌ Wrong: I saw him to leave (to-infinitive after see)

✅ Right: I saw him leave

❌ Wrong: The room felt coldly (adverb where an adjective is needed)

✅ Right: The room felt cold

Past questions

Which auxiliary? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapdid

    gapdid
    the audit start?

WH-WORD→+ did + subject + base verb
Level B1 Grammar

Wh-Questions in the Past

Ask about the past with the right auxiliary.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can form past wh-questions with did and with be.
Examples in context
  • Where did you put the file? Wh-word, did, subject, base verb. — Did carries the past.
  • Why was the meeting cancelled? Be takes no did. — Was plus subject.
  • Who told the client? Who as subject takes no auxiliary. — Who + past verb.

👀 What do you observe?

Past wh-questions use did plus the base verb, and the past is carried by did alone: where did you put it, not where did you putted it. With be, the past form moves to the front and no did is used: why was the meeting cancelled. When who or what is the subject of the question, there is no auxiliary and the verb stays in the past: who told the client.

Formula / rule: Decide whether the question is about an action or a state. An action takes did plus the base verb. A state with be takes was or were plus the subject. If who or what is the subject, drop the auxiliary and keep the past verb.

★ Why it matters

Past question forms are where learners leave the tense twice: what did you did is the classic error, because the past is already carried by did. Getting it right also matters for reported questions, where the auxiliary disappears entirely.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use who did you tell and who told you side by side without confusion, because the subject role decides. In informal speech, did reduces to /dɪd/ or nearly vanishes.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Did carries the stress in a real question: WHERE did you PUT it? In a follow-up, the wh-word is stressed instead.

  • Action: When did the panel publish the minutes?
  • State: Where were the files before the audit?
  • Subject: Who signed the contract?

175 Wish and If Only

Regret

Which time does the regret refer to? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. I wish I
    gaphad
    more time.
  2. I wish I
    gaphad taken
    the job.

    gapwould

WISH / IF ONLY→→ one step back in tense
Level B1 Grammar

Wish and If Only

Express regret about the present, the past and other people.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use wish and if only for three different times.
Examples in context
  • I wish I had more time. Regret about the present. — Past simple after wish.
  • I wish I had taken the job. Regret about the past. — Past perfect after wish.
  • I wish they would answer. Wish for a change in others. — Would after wish.

👀 What do you observe?

Wish and if only take the same tense pattern, and if only is the stronger form. Regret about the present takes the past simple: I wish I had more time. Regret about the past takes the past perfect: I wish I had taken the job. A wish for someone else to change takes would: I wish they would answer. Wish plus the infinitive (I wish to complain) is a formal request, not a regret.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

2. Which form asks someone else to change?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
wish + past simple regret about the present I wish I had more time
wish + past perfect regret about the past I wish I had taken the job
wish + would wish for change in others I wish they would answer
if only + past perfect stronger regret about the past if only we had known
wish + to-infinitive formal request I wish to complain
wish + could regret about ability I wish I could help

Formula / rule: Decide the time of the regret, then move one step back: present regret takes the past simple, past regret takes the past perfect, and a wish about someone else's behaviour takes would. If only does the same work with more force and can stand alone as an exclamation.

★ Why it matters

Wish is how English expresses regret without naming a mistake, which makes it the polite form of criticism: I wish the file had been checked says the same as the file was not checked, without an accusation. If only adds the sense that it is now too late.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use I wish I had in speech constantly, often reduced to I wish I'd, and they use if only mostly in writing or in exclamations. Wish plus would can sound irritated, which is why it is avoided in formal correspondence.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The contracted had is weak (I wish I'd known), and the stress falls on the regret: I wish I HAD more time; if ONly we had known.

Additional example bank
  • Present: I wish the office were closer to the station.
  • Past: If only we had kept the original file.
  • Other people: I wish the panel would publish its reasons.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: I wish I would have taken the job (would in a past regret)

✅ Right: I wish I had taken the job

❌ Wrong: I wish I have more time (present tense after wish)

✅ Right: I wish I had more time

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Second conditional · Would rather, would sooner

176 Would Rather and Would Sooner

Preferences

Who is choosing? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. I
    gapwould rather
    wait.
  2. I'd rather
    gapyou waited
    outside.
  3. She
    gapwould sooner
    resign than move.
  4. We'd rather
    gapnot discuss
    it now.
WOULD RATHER + base→→ same subject · + subject + past → different subject
Level B1 Grammar

Would Rather and Would Sooner

Express a preference, with one subject or two.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use would rather and would sooner with the base verb and with a past form for another subject.
Examples in context
  • I would rather wait. Same subject, base verb. — I'd rather wait.
  • I'd rather you waited. Different subject, past form. — Unreal past for politeness.
  • She would sooner resign than move. Comparison with than. — Rather ... than.

👀 What do you observe?

Would rather and would sooner express preference. With the same subject, the base verb follows: I would rather wait. With a different subject, the past form follows: I would rather you waited, which is not about the past but about distance and politeness. Comparison takes than plus the base verb: rather resign than move. The negative puts not first: I'd rather not go.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
would rather + base same subject I would rather wait
would rather + subject + past different subject I'd rather you waited
would rather ... than comparison, base verbs rather resign than move
negative not before the base verb I'd rather not discuss it
would sooner same patterns, slightly more formal she would sooner resign
would prefer same meaning, to-infinitive I would prefer to wait

Formula / rule: Decide who is choosing. Same subject: base verb after would rather. Different subject: past form. Comparison: than plus the base verb. Negative: not plus the base verb.

★ Why it matters

Would rather is how English states a preference without demanding it, and the past form with another subject is the politest way to say what you want someone else to do. That is why it fills negotiation and correspondence.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers contract it constantly (I'd rather) and use it more than would prefer in speech. The past form after another subject is not a past meaning and natives never read it as one.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Rather carries the stress: I'd RATHER wait; the contraction I'd is barely audible.

Additional example bank
  • Preference: I'd rather keep the current supplier.
  • Other subject: We'd rather the panel decided first.
  • Comparison: They would sooner delay than sign a weak contract.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: I'd rather you wait outside with a different subject (base verb where the past form is expected)

✅ Right: I'd rather you waited outside

❌ Wrong: I'd rather to wait (infinitive after would rather)

✅ Right: I'd rather wait

177 Adverbs: Types and Position

Adverb position

Where does the adverb go? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. She
    gaprarely
    misses a deadline.
  2. He spoke
    gapquietly
    and left.
  3. gapFortunately
    , the audit found nothing.
  4. We have
    gapalready
    sent the file.
MID-POSITION→→ before the main verb, after the auxiliary
Level B2 Grammar

Adverbs: Types and Position

Place the adverb where the sentence expects it.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can place adverbs of manner, frequency, time and comment in the right slot.
Examples in context
  • She rarely misses a deadline. Frequency before the main verb. — Mid-position.
  • He spoke quietly and left. Manner after the verb. — End position.
  • Fortunately, the audit found nothing. Comment on the whole clause. — Front position.

👀 What do you observe?

Adverbs fall into types that prefer different positions. Manner adverbs go at the end (she spoke quietly) or after the object. Frequency adverbs take mid-position, before the main verb and after the auxiliary (she rarely misses, she has rarely missed). Time adverbs go at the end or the front. Comment adverbs, which judge the whole sentence, take the front position with a comma (fortunately, admittedly).

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

2. What position does a comment adverb take?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
manner end, after the verb or object he spoke quietly
frequency mid-position she rarely misses a deadline
time end or front we met yesterday / yesterday we met
comment front with a comma fortunately, the audit found nothing
degree before the adjective or adverb the results were surprisingly strong
linking adverb front with a comma however, the data was incomplete

Formula / rule: Decide the type first, then the position: manner at the end, frequency in the middle, time at either end, comment at the front with a comma. Never put an adverb between the verb and its object: she speaks English well, not she speaks well English.

★ Why it matters

Adverb position is where word order carries meaning: only rarely does the difference between often and rarely depend on where they sit. A misplaced frequency adverb also changes emphasis, which is why he rarely is late and he is rarely late are both possible but not equivalent in rhythm.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers vary the position for emphasis: mid-position is neutral, front position emphasises, and end position is the default in speech. In academic writing, front-position comment adverbs are frequent and mid-position hedges are frequent.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The adverb carries the stress when it is fronted: FORTUNATELY, the audit found nothing. In mid-position it is usually unstressed.

Additional example bank
  • Manner after the object: She answered the question calmly.
  • Frequency mid-position: The board has never rejected a proposal.
  • Comment: Admittedly, the timetable was optimistic.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: She speaks well English (adverb between the verb and its object)

✅ Right: She speaks English well

❌ Wrong: Rarely she misses a deadline (frequency adverb before the subject, no inversion)

✅ Right: She rarely misses a deadline

178 Alternatives to If

Conditions

Which conditional linker fits? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. Unless
    gapthe funding arrives
    , the pilot stops in June.
  2. Provided that
    gapthe data is complete
    , we can publish.
  3. Take an umbrella
    gapin case
    it rains.
  4. Had
    gapwe known
    , we would have acted.
CONDITION LINKER→→ meaning and register
Level B2 Grammar

Alternatives to If

Make a condition sound formal, tentative or hypothetical.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can build conditionals with unless, provided that, in case, otherwise and inversion.
Examples in context
  • Unless the audit clears, the launch slips. If the audit does not clear. — Unless = if not.
  • Provided that the terms hold, we sign. Only on that condition. — A stated condition.
  • In case the line fails, we keep a backup. Precaution, not condition. — Different meaning from if.

👀 What do you observe?

Alternatives to if each carry their own logic. Unless means if not, and it cannot take a second negative. Provided that, as long as and on condition that state an explicit requirement. In case means as a precaution, so it describes an action taken before a possible event, not a condition on a result. Otherwise states the consequence of not meeting the condition. Inversion (Had we known, Should the offer fail, Were the data complete) raises the register and removes if altogether.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

2. Can unless be followed by another negative?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
unless if not unless the funding arrives, the pilot stops
provided that / as long as explicit requirement provided that the data is complete
on condition that formal requirement on condition that the fee is paid
in case precaution take an umbrella in case it rains
otherwise consequence of not complying sign by Friday; otherwise the offer lapses
Had / Should / Were + inversion formal conditional without if had we known, we would have acted

Formula / rule: Choose by logic, not by style: unless for a negative condition, provided that for a requirement, in case for a precaution, otherwise for the alternative consequence. Then, if the register needs lifting, invert instead of using if: Had we known, Were the data complete, Should the offer fail.

★ Why it matters

These linkers are where legal and technical English lives, because they narrow a condition exactly: provided that the fee is paid is stricter than if the fee is paid. In case is the one learners misuse most, since it looks like if and means the opposite kind of thing.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use unless freely in speech and invert only in writing or prepared remarks. In case is common in speech as a precaution marker, and its negative form (in case it doesn't rain) is rarer than it looks.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Inversion carries a stress on the auxiliary: HAD we known; SHOULD the offer fail. Unstressed, the inverted form can be misheard as a statement.

Additional example bank
  • Condition: As long as the sample holds, the result stands.
  • Precaution: Keep the receipt in case the refund is refused.
  • Consequence: Submit the form by Friday; otherwise the application lapses.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: Unless you don't submit by Friday, the offer lapses (double negative)

✅ Right: Unless you submit by Friday, the offer lapses

❌ Wrong: We keep a backup if the line fails (precaution written as a condition)

✅ Right: We keep a backup in case the line fails

179 Clauses of Contrast, Purpose, Reason and Result

Linking ideas

Which relation is it? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. Although
    gapthe costs rose
    , the project continued.
  2. The team met early
    gapso that
    the launch could go ahead.
  3. The delay happened
    gapbecause
    the supplier failed an audit.
  4. The backlog grew
    gapso fast that
    the system stalled.
RELATION→→ connector + clause
Level B2 Grammar

Clauses of Contrast, Purpose, Reason and Result

Link two ideas with the relation the argument needs.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can signal contrast, purpose, cause and consequence with the right connector.
Examples in context
  • Contrast: Even though the data was thin, the board approved the pilot. — Concession.
  • Purpose: They doubled the checks in order to catch the errors earlier. — Intention.
  • Reason: Since the audit failed, the launch was postponed. — Cause.
  • Result: Sales fell so sharply that the target was abandoned. — Consequence.

👀 What do you observe?

Four relations, each with its own connectors. Contrast: although, even though, though, while, whereas, despite + noun or -ing. Purpose: so that + clause, in order to / so as to + infinitive, for + noun. Reason: because, since, as, given that. Result: so ... that, such ... that, consequently, as a result. The relation decides both the connector and the grammar that follows it.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which connector takes a noun or an -ing form rather than a clause?
Despite the delay / despite being late, but although the train was late.
2. Which pair expresses purpose?
So that and in order to answer why; so ... that answers what happened.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
although / even though concession with a clause although the costs rose, the project continued
despite / in spite of concession with a noun or -ing despite the rising costs
while / whereas direct contrast between two facts while exports grew, domestic sales fell
so that / in order to purpose so that the launch could go ahead
because / since / as reason because the supplier failed an audit
so ... that / such ... that result so fast that the system stalled

Formula / rule: Pick the relation first, then the connector, then the grammar: concession with a clause needs although; concession with a noun needs despite; purpose with a subject of its own needs so that; purpose with the same subject needs in order to. Reason and result look similar but answer different questions: because answers why, so ... that answers what came of it.

★ Why it matters

These connectors are the joints of an argument, and a wrong joint is the most common reason a B2 text reads as a list rather than a case. The register matters too: since and as are more formal than because, and thereby or consequently belong in writing, not in speech.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers front concession (Although the costs rose) and postpone result (so fast that the system stalled). Fronted concession signals a balanced view; a result clause at the end lands the consequence where the reader expects the conclusion.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Although is stressed on the second syllable /ɔːlˈðəʊ/; the clause after it carries a fall-rise, and the main clause falls, which is how a listener hears where the concession ends.

Additional example bank
  • Concession with a noun: Despite the warning, the launch went ahead.
  • Purpose with a change of subject: They added a review step so that errors would surface earlier.
  • Result: Such was the backlog that the system stalled.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: Although the costs rose, but the project continued (double connector)

✅ Right: Although the costs rose, the project continued

❌ Wrong: Despite the costs rose (noun form after despite with a full clause)

✅ Right: Despite the rise in costs, the project continued

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Alternatives to if · Discourse markers

180 Cleft Sentences and Emphasis

Emphasis

Which element does the cleft highlight? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. It was
    gapthe delay
    that cost us the contract.
  2. What we need
    gapis
    a clear owner.
  3. It is
    gapnot the cost
    that worries me.
  4. All I asked for
    gapwas
    a decision.
IT / WHAT→→ highlighted element + rest
Level B2 Grammar

Cleft Sentences and Emphasis

Put the important element in its own clause.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use it-clefts and what-clefts to make one part of a sentence carry the emphasis.
Examples in context
  • It was the board that rejected the plan. The board rejected the plan. — It-cleft: highlights the board.
  • What the board rejected was the plan. The board rejected the plan. — What-cleft: highlights the plan.
  • It was in June that the policy changed. The policy changed in June. — Highlights a time.

👀 What do you observe?

A cleft splits one sentence into two clauses so that the highlighted element sits in its own slot. The it-cleft opens with it was and places the focus after it: it was the delay that cost us the contract. The what-cleft opens with what and places the focus at the end: what cost us the contract was the delay. Both keep the original meaning and change only the emphasis.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which cleft puts the focus at the end of the sentence?

2. Does a cleft change the meaning of a sentence?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
it-cleft focus after it was it was the delay that cost us the contract
what-cleft focus at the end what cost us the contract was the delay
negative cleft focus on what is not the cause it is not the cost that worries me
all-cleft focus on the only thing all I asked for was a decision
there-cleft presents an entity there was a delay that cost us the contract
cleft with a time or place highlights an adverbial it was in June that the policy changed

Formula / rule: Pick the element the reader must remember, then put it in the focus slot: after it was for the it-cleft, at the end for the what-cleft. Watch the agreement in the what-cleft, where what is singular even when the complement is plural.

★ Why it matters

Clefts are how English marks contrast without raising the voice in writing. A report that says it was the approval process that delayed the launch has already told you where to look for the fix, which a plain sentence does not.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, the cleft is carried by stress rather than by syntax: a speaker may simply stress the delay. Clefts become frequent in speech when correcting an assumption: it wasn't the cost, it was the timing.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The cleft marker carries the stress if the correction is the point: it WAS the delay; what we NEED is an owner.

Additional example bank
  • Correction: It wasn't the price that lost the deal, it was the delivery date.
  • Narrowing: All the board asked for was a timetable.
  • Focus on time: It was in March that the first warning appeared.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: What we need are a clear owner (agreement with a plural complement)

✅ Right: What we need is a clear owner

❌ Wrong: It was the delay what cost us the contract (what after an it-cleft)

✅ Right: It was the delay that cost us the contract

Fronting for focus · Rhetorical questions and parallelism

181 Compound Nouns

Compound nouns

How is the compound written? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The
    gapboard meeting
    was moved to Thursday.
  2. We need a
    gaprisk assessment
    before launch.
  3. She wrote a
    gaptwo-page brief
    .
  4. The
    gapcheck-in desk
    closes at nine.
MODIFIER→+ HEAD NOUN → one idea, first element stressed
Level B2 Grammar

Compound Nouns

Join two words into the noun the language has settled on.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can build and stress compound nouns, and know when to hyphenate.
Examples in context
  • a board meeting board modifies meeting — The head noun comes last.
  • a risk assessment risk modifies assessment — Two nouns, no hyphen.
  • a two-page brief number + noun, hyphenated — Hyphen when the compound precedes the noun.

👀 What do you observe?

A compound noun puts the modifier first and the head last, and the head decides number and meaning: a board meeting is a meeting, a meeting board is a board. Most compounds are written as two words (risk assessment), some close up (notebook, database), and compounds with a number or a participle are hyphenated when they come before the noun (a two-page brief, a well-known author). Stress falls on the first element, which is how listeners tell a compound from a phrase.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

2. Where does the stress fall in a compound?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
noun + noun modifier before head risk assessment, board meeting
head decides number plural on the final noun board meetings, risk assessments
closed form written as one word notebook, database, website
hyphen before the noun compound used as a modifier a two-page brief, a well-known author
no hyphen after the noun predicate position the brief was two pages long
stress on the first element distinguishes compound from phrase a GREENhouse and a green HOUSE

Formula / rule: Decide the head noun first, then the modifier, then the spelling: two words by default, one word if the language has closed it, hyphens only when the compound modifies another noun and would otherwise be misread. Keep the plural on the head.

★ Why it matters

Compounds are where vocabulary and grammar meet, and where a wrong head produces a different object: a training manager manages training, a manager training trains managers. In technical and business English, compounds carry most of the terminology, so the head noun is the word the reader is actually looking for.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers stress the first element so reliably that the stress pattern is the real marker: a blackBIRD is a species, a black BIRD is a bird that is black. Learners who stress the last element sound as if they are describing rather than naming.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The first element is stressed and slightly longer, and the second is weaker: BOARD meeting, RISK assessment. In hyphenated modifiers each element keeps a light stress: a TWO-page BRIEF.

Additional example bank
  • Business: The quarterly risk review is on Friday.
  • Technical: The check-in system failed twice.
  • Predicate: The brief is two pages long.

❌ Wrong: a two-pages brief (plural inside a hyphenated modifier)

✅ Right: a two-page brief

❌ Wrong: meetings board (head and modifier reversed)

✅ Right: board meetings

182 Conditional Inversion

Formal conditions

Which auxiliary opens the clause? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. Had
    gapwe known
    , we would have acted.
  2. Should
    gapthe offer fail
    , we will renegotiate.
  3. Were
    gapthe data complete
    , we could publish.
  4. Had
    gapit not been
    for the audit, we would have launched.
HAD / SHOULD / WERE→+ subject + rest (no if)
Level B2 Grammar

Conditional Inversion

Drop if and invert the auxiliary.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can write Had I known, Should the offer fail and Were the data complete.
Examples in context
  • Had we known, we would have acted. Third conditional, inverted. — Had + subject + participle.
  • Should the offer fail, we will renegotiate. First conditional, tentative. — Should + subject + base.
  • Were the data complete, we could publish. Second conditional with be. — Were + subject.

👀 What do you observe?

Inversion replaces if in three conditionals. Third: had + subject + past participle. First, with a tentative tone: should + subject + base verb. Second with be: were + subject. The meaning is identical to the if-form and the register is higher, which is why the inverted forms appear in contracts, minutes and formal correspondence but rarely in speech.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which conditional is inverted as 'Should the offer fail'?

2. Can were be used for all persons in an inverted second conditional?
Were is the inverted form for all persons.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
had + subject + participle third conditional had we known, we would have acted
should + subject + base first conditional, tentative should the offer fail, we will renegotiate
were + subject second conditional with be were the data complete, we could publish
negative with not not follows the subject had it not been for the audit
no if the inversion replaces it had we known, not if we had known
register formal, written used in contracts and minutes

Formula / rule: Choose the conditional, then invert: past condition becomes had + subject + participle; hypothetical present with be becomes were + subject; tentative future becomes should + subject + base. Never keep if and invert at the same time, and keep not after the subject.

★ Why it matters

Inversion is how a formal document makes a condition sound considered rather than conversational, and it is the standard way to open a contract clause or a minute. It also saves words: had we known does the work of if we had known in one syllable fewer, which matters in a document read aloud.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, the inverted forms sound formal or theatrical, and speakers usually keep if. The one exception is were I you, which survives as a set phrase.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The auxiliary is stressed: HAD we known; SHOULD the offer fail; WERE the data complete. The stress is what signals that the sentence is conditional at all.

Additional example bank
  • Third: Had the warning been heeded, the loss would have been smaller.
  • First: Should the deadline slip, we will publish a revised plan.
  • Set phrase: Were I you, I would ask for the minutes.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: If had we known, we would have acted (if kept with an inverted clause)

✅ Right: Had we known, we would have acted

❌ Wrong: Had not it been for the audit (not in the wrong position)

✅ Right: Had it not been for the audit

PAIR→→ one difference of meaning or form
Level B2 Grammar

Confusing Grammar: Pairs that Look Alike

Separate the structures learners mix up most at B2.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can tell apart the pairs that produce the most persistent B2 errors.
Examples in context
  • used to work / am used to working Past habit versus present familiarity. — The -ing marks familiarity.
  • It's time we left / it's time to leave Same meaning, different subject frame. — Past form after we.
  • stop to check / stop checking Pause in order to check versus no longer check. — The complement decides.

👀 What do you observe?

The pairs that trouble B2 learners share a shape and differ in one point. Used to plus the base verb is a past habit; be used to plus the -ing form is present familiarity. It's time plus the past form looks at a shared deadline; it's time plus the infinitive states the action. Stop, remember and try change meaning with the complement. So do look forward to (verb, not preposition) and be used to.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which pair differs in meaning, not only in form?
The first changes the sense; the second changes the framing.
2. What follows be used to?
I am used to working nights.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
used to / be used to past habit versus familiarity used to work / am used to working
it's time we + past / it's time to + base deadline framing it's time we left / it's time to leave
stop to / stop -ing pause versus cease stop to check / stop checking
remember to / remember -ing duty versus memory remember to lock / remember locking
look forward to + -ing to is a preposition here look forward to hearing from you
would rather / had better preference versus advice I'd rather wait / you'd better wait

Formula / rule: For each pair, learn the single point that separates them, then test the sentence against that point: is the meaning past or present, duty or memory, preference or warning? The form follows the meaning, and the pairs only stay confusing while they are learned as shapes rather than as meanings.

★ Why it matters

These pairs are the difference between a B2 script that reads as controlled and one that reads as translated. Examiners recognise them immediately because they are the errors that persist after everything else has been fixed, and each one has a clean explanation.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers rarely confuse the pairs, but they do overuse used to in nostalgic talk and had better in warnings; the choice between would rather and prefer is a register choice as much as a meaning one.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The pairs are distinguished by weak forms in speech: used to /ˈjuːstə/ and be used to /biː ˈjuːst tə/ are distinct, and the /tə/ of the infinitive is weaker than the /tə/ of a preposition followed by -ing.

Additional example bank
  • Duty versus memory: I remembered to lock the door, and I remember locking it.
  • Preference versus advice: I'd rather wait; you'd better tell them.
  • Preposition plus gerund: We look forward to seeing the draft.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: I am used to work nights (base verb after be used to)

✅ Right: I am used to working nights

❌ Wrong: I look forward to hear from you (infinitive after a preposition)

✅ Right: I look forward to hearing from you

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Used to, would and be used to · It's time, would rather, had better

Prepositions

Which preposition does the word require? tap the line.write it on the line.

WORD→+ fixed preposition
Level B2 Grammar

Dependent Prepositions

Keep the preposition the noun or adjective requires.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use the preposition that belongs to a noun, an adjective or a verb.
Examples in context
  • an increase in demand noun + in — an increase in demand, a rise in costs
  • responsible for adjective + for — responsible for the budget
  • depend on verb + on — we depend on one supplier

👀 What do you observe?

Prepositions are attached to words, not chosen by logic: an increase in, a decrease in, a demand for, a solution to, evidence for, responsibility for, dependent on, similar to, interested in. The same preposition can be right with one word and wrong with its near-synonym, so the word and the preposition have to be learned as a unit.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

Score : 0 / 2

2. Which preposition follows responsible?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
noun + in increase, decrease, rise, fall an increase in demand
noun + for demand, evidence, responsibility, reason the reason for the delay
noun + to solution, answer, access, approach a solution to the problem
adjective + of aware, capable, afraid aware of the risk
adjective + to similar, due, committed, opposed similar to last year
verb + on / for depend on, account for we depend on one supplier

Formula / rule: Learn the pair, then check the pattern: a noun takes in, for, to or of by convention; an adjective takes of, to, for or with; a verb takes its own preposition. Where the preposition carries meaning (responsible for a task, responsible to a manager), the meaning decides, and both are correct.

★ Why it matters

Dependent prepositions are the clearest sign of a text written by someone translating: the meaning survives and the preposition does not. Because the pairs are arbitrary, they have to be learned with the word, and because they are frequent, a wrong one appears in almost every paragraph.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers sometimes differ: different from is standard British, different to is common in British speech, different than is American. In an exam, follow the variety you have been taught and stay with it.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The preposition is unstressed and joins the word before it: reSPONsible for, dePENdent on, an INcrease in.

Additional example bank
  • Noun: There is no evidence for the claim.
  • Adjective: The result is similar to last year's.
  • Verb: The delay accounts for most of the loss.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: an increase of demand (wrong preposition for an uncountable rise)

✅ Right: an increase in demand

❌ Wrong: dependent of one supplier (preposition taken from another adjective)

✅ Right: dependent on one supplier

185 Discourse Markers

Cohesion

Which marker does the relation need? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The data is thin.
    gapMoreover
    , it was collected under pressure.
  2. The plans were ambitious.
    gapHowever
    , the funding never appeared.
  3. The results improved.
    gapConsequently
    , the pilot was extended.
  4. In light of
    gapthe audit
    , the launch has been deferred.
RELATION→→ marker + sentence
Level B2 Grammar

Discourse Markers

Show the reader how each sentence relates to the last.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can mark addition, contrast, concession, sequence and conclusion in formal prose.
Examples in context
  • Addition: Moreover, the sample was too small to generalise. — Adds a second point.
  • Concession: Admittedly, the cost is high; nevertheless, the case is sound. — Concedes, then holds.
  • Conclusion: In conclusion, the policy needs an owner. — Signals the end.
  • Reframing: As far as staffing is concerned, the picture is different. — Limits the topic.

👀 What do you observe?

A discourse marker names the relation between two sentences: addition (furthermore, moreover, in addition), contrast (however, nevertheless, in contrast), concession (admittedly, granted that, even so), sequence (first, subsequently, finally), result (consequently, as a result), and stance (arguably, in fact, roughly speaking). Most take a comma, and fronted ones usually take a comma after them.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which marker concedes a point and then continues to argue?
Admittedly concedes; moreover adds.
2. Which order is right for however?
Fronted however takes a comma after it.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
addition adds a supporting point furthermore, moreover, in addition
contrast sets two points against each other however, in contrast, by comparison
concession admits a point, keeps the case admittedly, granted that, even so
sequence orders the parts first, subsequently, finally
result states the consequence consequently, as a result, therefore
stance marks the writer's position arguably, in fact, on the contrary

Formula / rule: Choose the marker by the relation, then check the punctuation and the register. However and in contrast start a new sentence with a comma after them; although and whereas join clauses inside one sentence. On the contrary contradicts a previous statement, while on the other hand balances two sides, and confusing the two is the most common marker error at this level.

★ Why it matters

Markers are how a reader knows whether a sentence adds, contradicts or concludes, and a missing marker forces the reader to guess the relationship, which is where arguments lose their shape. They are also a register signal: moreover and consequently belong in reports, while plus and also belong in speech.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers overuse actually and basically in speech, and underuse moreover in speech; in writing they rely on however, therefore and by contrast. Note that In fact introduces a correction of an impression, not an addition.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Most markers of two syllables or more are unstressed except the one that carries the contrast, so however /haʊˈev.ə/ keeps the stress on the second syllable while moreover /mɔːrˈəʊ.və/ keeps it on the second as well.

Additional example bank
  • Contrast: Exports rose; in contrast, domestic demand fell.
  • Concession: Granted that the sample is small, the pattern is consistent.
  • Stance: On the contrary, the evidence points the other way.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The plans were ambitious, however the funding never appeared (comma splice before however)

✅ Right: The plans were ambitious. However, the funding never appeared

❌ Wrong: On the other hand, the report says the opposite (opposition instead of contradiction)

✅ Right: On the contrary, the report says the opposite

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Clauses of contrast, purpose, reason and result · Ellipsis and substitution

Contrast between the evidence and the conclusion.

186 Distancing Passive Reporting

In the news

Who said it? Complete the report. tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. It is
    gapalleged
    that the firm hid the losses.
  2. The firm is said
    gapto have
    hidden the losses.
  3. Three officials are
    gapbelieved
    to be under investigation.
  4. The report is
    gapunderstood
    to recommend a merger.
IT IS SAID / X IS SAID→+ to + infinitive (perfect infinitive for the past)
Level B2 Grammar

Distancing Passive Reporting

Report a claim without naming who made it.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can report an allegation, a belief or a rumour while keeping the source out of the sentence.
Examples in context
  • It is reported that the talks collapsed. The talks are reported to have collapsed. — Source removed, claim kept.
  • It is believed that she resigned. She is believed to have resigned. — Perfect infinitive for a past event.
  • Officials think the delay will grow. The delay is expected to grow. — Expectation reported, not predicted.

👀 What do you observe?

Two shapes carry the same claim. The impersonal shape opens with it is plus a reporting verb and a that-clause: it is said that he left. The personal shape moves the subject forward and uses the infinitive: he is said to have left. For a past event the infinitive is perfect (to have left); for a simultaneous state it is simple (he is said to be abroad).

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which shape needs a perfect infinitive?
He is said to have left: the leaving is earlier than the report.
2. What does the passive do to the source?
That is the point: the claim travels, the source does not.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
It is said that + clause impersonal report it is said that the plan failed
X is said to + infinitive report about a present state the plan is said to be unworkable
X is said to have + participle report about the past the plan is said to have failed
It is alleged / reported / understood claim without commitment it is alleged that funds were moved
X is believed / thought / expected to belief or expectation the talks are expected to resume
X is understood to quiet official confirmation the board is understood to have voted

Formula / rule: Use the impersonal form when the claim itself is the topic: It is alleged that funds were moved. Use the personal form when the person is the topic and the claim is background: He is alleged to have moved the funds. The reporting verb decides the strength: alleged signals dispute, understood signals a briefing, reported signals the press.

★ Why it matters

This is the structure of institutional caution. A ministry that says the contract is understood to have been awarded reports what it has heard without committing to it, and a newspaper that writes it is alleged avoids being sued. Reading these verbs tells you how much the writer trusts the claim, which is often the most important information in the sentence.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers treat these as fixed collocations and rarely invent new ones: is said to, is believed to, is understood to, is expected to, is alleged to. Is thought to is slightly more tentative than is believed to, and is reported to suggests a source the writer has not checked.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The weak forms carry the structure: /ɪt ɪz əˈledʒd/ with the stress on the reporting verb, and in the personal form the stress falls on the infinitive: he is said to have LEFT.

Additional example bank
  • Impersonal: It is understood that the deal was signed in June.
  • Personal: The deal is understood to have been signed in June.
  • Expected: The results are expected to be published on Friday.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: It is said that he left yesterday, he is said to leave yesterday (present infinitive for a past event)

✅ Right: He is said to have left yesterday

❌ Wrong: It is believed that she is resigning, she is believed resigning (no infinitive after the reporting verb)

✅ Right: She is believed to be resigning

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Passive verbs with two objects · Reporting verbs with prepositions

187 Ellipsis & Substitution

Ellipsis

Recover the missing words. What remains? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. Some members accepted the terms; others
    gapdid not
    .
  2. I expected the review by Friday, but it
    gapwasn't
    .
  3. The first proposal was rejected, and the second
    gapone
    was withdrawn.
  4. He said he would resign, and he
    gapdid
    .
REPEATED CLAUSE→→ do so · one/ones · so · not
Level B2 Grammar

Ellipsis & Substitution

Leave out what the reader can recover, and replace what cannot be dropped.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can shorten a repeated clause without losing the meaning.
Examples in context
  • Noun: Some members accepted the terms; others did not. — The auxiliary survives, the verb goes.
  • Substitution: The first draft was rejected and the second one never reached the board. — One replaces a countable noun.
  • Clause: It may rain; if so, we meet online. — So replaces a whole clause.

👀 What do you observe?

Ellipsis deletes words that the context restores: others did not [accept the terms]. Substitution replaces them with a pro-form when deletion would be ambiguous: the second one stands for the second proposal, do so stands for a repeated verb phrase, so stands for a whole clause. Auxiliaries usually survive ellipsis, which is why did not remains after the main verb disappears.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What does 'the second one' replace?
One substitutes for a countable noun already mentioned.
2. Which part typically survives ellipsis?
Others did not; the main verb is recoverable, the auxiliary is kept.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
auxiliary stranded keeps tense and polarity visible others did not / he has
do so / do it substitutes a verb phrase they promised a review and did so
one / ones substitutes a countable noun the second one, the cheaper ones
so / not substitutes a whole clause if so, I think not
former / latter orders two named items the former, the latter
to (infinitive ellipsis) avoids repeating the verb I meant to, but I didn't

Formula / rule: Delete what a reader can restore without a second reading, and substitute when the deletion would leave two possible readings. Keep the auxiliary, the negative and any contrasting element: they carry the meaning the deletion would otherwise lose.

★ Why it matters

Ellipsis is a test of control: a writer who keeps the auxiliary and drops the verb sounds fluent, while a writer who drops the auxiliary leaves a sentence that has to be re-read. Substitution with one and do so is also how formal English avoids repeating a noun three times in a paragraph.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, ellipsis goes much further than in writing, because intonation replaces the missing words: 'Want some?' 'Later.' In writing, keep at least the auxiliary and never delete an element the reader would have to guess.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The stranded auxiliary takes the weak form: did not /ˈdɪd nɒt/ in careful speech, /ˈdɪdn̩t/ in normal speech; do so is stressed on do when it carries the contrast.

Additional example bank
  • Substitution: The first draft was rejected and the second one never reached the board.
  • Ellipsis: Some accepted the terms; most did not.
  • Whole clause: It may rain; if so, we meet online.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: Others did not accepted the terms (auxiliary and verb both half-kept)

✅ Right: Others did not accept the terms

❌ Wrong: They promised a review and they delivered (verb repeated, object dropped)

✅ Right: They promised a review and they delivered one

🔗 Connects to what you already know
