188 Formal and Informal Register

Register

Formal or informal? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. We
    gapregret
    to inform you that the application was unsuccessful.
  2. Sorry,
    gapwe can't
    make Friday.
  3. I would be grateful
    gapif you could
    confirm receipt.
  4. Can you
    gapsend it over
    today?
AUDIENCE→→ wording, length and distance
Level B2 Grammar

Formal and Informal Register

Choose the wording the situation expects.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can move a message between conversational and formal English without losing it.
Examples in context
  • Informal: We'll sort it out next week. — Contracted, phrasal, short.
  • Formal: We will resolve the matter next week. — No contraction, Latinate verb.
  • Informal: Can you check this? — Direct question.
  • Formal: I would be grateful if you could check this. — Indirect, softened.

👀 What do you observe?

Register shifts on four axes: vocabulary (get / obtain, help / assist), grammar (contractions, phrasal verbs, question forms), distance (I want / I would like; direct order / indirect request) and length (one clause or a nominalised phrase). Formal English avoids contractions, prefers single Latinate verbs to phrasal verbs, and puts requests in the conditional.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which is more formal?
Conditional plus Latinate verb.
2. Are contractions always wrong in formal writing?
Avoid them by default, but many style guides allow them in reports.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
lexis Latinate verb instead of phrasal obtain, not get; resolve, not sort out
grammar no contractions, full forms we will, not we'll
requests conditional and indirect I would be grateful if you could…
distance impersonal subject the report indicates, not I think
density nominalisation the implementation of the policy
hedging softened claims this would appear to be the case

Formula / rule: Decide the audience, then adjust all four axes at once. Formalising only the vocabulary and leaving contractions produces a letter that reads as uncertain, and formalising only the grammar leaves phrasal verbs that sound out of place.

★ Why it matters

Register is not politeness, it is the signal that a writer knows which genre they are in. A complaint written in casual register is read as unserious; an internal note written in legal register is read as evasive. B2 is where learners are expected to move along the scale rather than fix at one point.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers rarely formalise a whole message; they formalise the opening and the request, and keep the middle plain. Very formal English in the wrong place (an email to a close colleague) reads as coldness or sarcasm.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Contractions reduce the vowels (we'll, can't), and formal speech restores them, which is one reason a formal statement sounds slower and more measured than the same content in conversation.

Additional example bank
  • Formal request: I would be grateful if you could confirm receipt by Friday.
  • Formal refusal: Unfortunately, we are unable to attend on that date.
  • Informal equivalent: Sorry, we can't make it on the 12th.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: I want that you send the file (formal vocabulary, ungrammatical pattern)

✅ Right: I would like you to send the file

❌ Wrong: We regret to inform you that we can't come (mixed register within one sentence)

✅ Right: We regret to inform you that we are unable to attend

🔗 Connects to what you already know

189 Fronting for Focus

Fronting

Which element belongs at the front? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. In the third quarter
    gapof last year
    , the deficit doubled.
  2. Rarely
    gaphas the board
    seen such a divided vote.
  3. That the plan was rushed
    gapthe auditors
    never denied.
  4. Out of the negotiation
    gapwalked
    the smaller delegation.
FRONTED ELEMENT→→ subject + verb (invert after a negative adverb)
Level B2 Grammar

Fronting for Focus

Move an element to the front when the reader needs it first.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can open a sentence with the information that carries the argument.
Examples in context
  • Time: In the third quarter of last year, the deficit doubled. — A fronted adverbial sets the frame.
  • Negative: Rarely has the board seen such a divided vote. — A negative front triggers inversion.
  • Object: That the plan was rushed, the auditors never denied. — A fronted object is topicalised, not inverted.
  • Particle: Out of the negotiation walked the smaller delegation. — Inversion after a particle.

👀 What do you observe?

Fronting moves an element out of its neutral position to the start of the clause, which makes it the frame for everything that follows. When the fronted element is negative or limiting (never, rarely, not until, under no circumstances), the subject and operator invert. When it is a plain adverbial or object, the order of subject and verb does not change.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Does 'In June the report appeared' need inversion?
Inversion follows negative or limiting fronting only.
2. Why front a phrase?
Fronting is about information order, not length.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
fronted adverbial sets time, place or condition In the third quarter, the deficit doubled
negative fronting inverts subject and operator Rarely has the board seen such a vote
not until / only when inverts, often with a delay Only when the audit ended did the scale emerge
fronted object topicalises the object That the plan was rushed, the auditors never denied
fronted complement inversion with be Such was the outcry that the plan was withdrawn
fronted particle inversion in narrative Out of the negotiation walked the smaller delegation

Formula / rule: Front an element when the rest of the sentence depends on it. Keep the neutral order when nothing is at stake, because heavy fronting reads as rhetoric. With negative or limiting fronting, invert: Rarely has the board, Not until June did the ministry, Under no circumstances will we.

★ Why it matters

Fronting is how English says 'pay attention to this part first' without adding words. In reports and briefings it carries the argument: the same facts, ordered so that the conclusion arrives at the end. Overuse turns a briefing into a speech, so front one element per paragraph at most.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, fronting is often marked by a pause and a raised pitch on the fronted phrase, and the inversion after negatives is rarer than in writing. A spoken 'Rarely have I seen' sounds formal; 'I've rarely seen' is the neutral choice.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Inversion after a negative adverb carries stress on the auxiliary: Rarely HAS the board; Not until June DID the ministry. The fronted phrase itself is usually unstressed.

Additional example bank
  • Conditional: Should the offer be withdrawn, we will renegotiate.
  • Limiting: Only after the vote did the scale of the split appear.
  • Topicalised object: This point the minister did not address.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: Rarely the board has seen such a vote (no inversion after a negative adverb)

✅ Right: Rarely has the board seen such a vote

❌ Wrong: In the third quarter, doubled the deficit (verb before subject after a plain adverbial)

✅ Right: In the third quarter, the deficit doubled

EVIDENCE / PLAN / TIMETABLE→→ going to / be -ing / present simple
Level B2 Grammar

Future Forms

Pick the future form by what the speaker knows, not by the clock.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can choose between will, going to, the present continuous, the present simple and the future perfect.
Examples in context
  • Arrangement: I am seeing the minister on Tuesday. — Fixed in a diary.
  • Prediction from evidence: Costs are going to rise. — Visible now.
  • Decision made now: I will send it today. — Announced at the moment of speaking.
  • Deadline: By Friday we will have sent the file. — Completed before a future point.

👀 What do you observe?

The form follows the evidence. Present simple for timetables and programmes. Present continuous for arrangements already made with other people. Going to for intentions and for predictions with present evidence. Will for decisions taken at the moment of speaking, offers and promises. Will be + -ing for an activity in progress at a future time, and will have + participle for what is complete before a future point.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form fits a train timetable?

2. What does 'I'll send it today' usually signal?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
present simple timetable, programme, schedule the train leaves at 07:40
present continuous arrangement with a time and a person we are meeting the board on Thursday
going to intention or evidence-based prediction it is going to rain
will decision now, offer, promise I will send it today
will be + -ing activity in progress at a future time at ten we will be presenting
will have + participle completed before a future point by June we will have finished

Formula / rule: Ask three questions: is the future fixed by a schedule, agreed with someone, or decided as I speak? Is my prediction based on evidence I can see, or on opinion? Will the action be in progress, or complete, at the reference time? Each answer picks a different form, and mixing them changes what the listener understands about how firm the plan is.

★ Why it matters

Getting future forms right is mostly about commitment. Are you going to do it means the decision is made; I will do it can announce a decision or offer help; I am doing it means someone else is expecting you. In professional English these three carry very different weight, which is why contracts are not written in will.

💭 Think like a native speaker

With go and come, native speakers prefer the present continuous for arrangements even in the far future (we are going to Lisbon in July), and the present simple for departure times. Going to is the most frequent form in speech for predictions about the visible world.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Will contracts to /əl/ or /l/ in fast speech (we'll, I'll), and going to reduces to gonna. The reduced form is normal in speech and wrong in writing except in dialogue.

Additional example bank
  • Schedule: The hearing starts at nine and ends at noon.
  • Arrangement: We are signing the contract on Friday.
  • Deadline: By the end of March we will have trained every team.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: We will meet the board on Thursday (will for an arrangement already made)

✅ Right: We are meeting the board on Thursday

❌ Wrong: By June we will finish the audit (will + base for a completed action before a deadline)

✅ Right: By June we will have finished the audit

191 Future in the Past

Future in the past

What was still ahead at that moment? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. He said he
    gapwould
    call on Friday.
  2. We
    gapwere going to
    launch in March, but the audit intervened.
  3. She
    gapwas about to
    sign when the call came.
  4. The board
    gapwas to
    meet the next morning.
WOULD / WAS GOING TO / WAS ABOUT TO→→ future seen from the past
Level B2 Grammar

Future in the Past

Describe a future that was still ahead at a past moment.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use would, was going to and was about to to report past intentions and predictions.
Examples in context
  • They would announce the result at noon. Future from a past viewpoint. — Would + base.
  • We were going to publish in March. Intention, often unfulfilled. — Was going to + base.
  • She was about to sign. Immediate future, interrupted. — Was about to + base.

👀 What do you observe?

Future in the past reports a future that was still ahead when the story is set. Would plus the base verb is the neutral form in reported speech and narrative. Was going to marks an intention, and often implies that it was not carried out. Was about to marks the immediate future, usually interrupted. Was to marks an arrangement or a plan in formal narrative.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form often implies the plan did not happen?
We were going to launch in March, but...
2. What does was about to emphasise?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
would + base neutral future from the past he said he would call
was / were going to + base intention, often unfulfilled we were going to launch in March
was / were about to + base immediate future, interrupted she was about to sign
was / were to + base formal arrangement or destiny the board was to meet the next morning
was / were due to + base scheduled future the report was due to appear in June
past perfect of be going to earlier intention in reported speech he had been going to resign

Formula / rule: Anchor the story in the past, then choose the shade of future: would for neutral reporting, was going to for intention, was about to for the next moment, was to for a formal plan. In reported speech the future shifts back one step, which is why will becomes would.

★ Why it matters

This structure is how a report explains that a plan existed before the outcome was known, and it is the only way to write a sequence without breaking the past tense. It also carries judgement: was going to signals that the intention lapsed, which is often the point of the sentence.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use was going to constantly in speech, and often reduce it to was gonna. Would in reported speech is neutral, and was to is reserved for written narrative and obituaries.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Would reduces to /d/ after a pronoun (he'd call), and was going to reduces to was gonna, which is normal in speech and absent from formal writing.

Additional example bank
  • Reported: They said the review would start in May.
  • Unfulfilled: We were going to expand, but the funding was withdrawn.
  • Interrupted: He was about to speak when the chair closed the meeting.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: He said he will call on Friday (future not shifted in reported speech)

✅ Right: He said he would call on Friday

❌ Wrong: She was about signing when the call came (missing to after about)

✅ Right: She was about to sign when the call came

192 Generic and Common-Gender Pronouns

Reference

Which pronoun keeps the sentence neutral? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. If a candidate is late,
    gapthey
    must inform the panel.
  2. One should check
    gapone's
    sources before publishing.
  3. Everyone submitted
    gaptheir
    form on time.
  4. The chair asked
    gapus
    to wait.
SUBJECT→→ they / one / you
Level B2 Grammar

Generic and Common-Gender Pronouns

Refer to people without guessing their gender.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use they, one and the singular they in formal and neutral writing.
Examples in context
  • Everyone submitted their form. Singular they. — Agreement with a singular antecedent.
  • One should check one's sources. Formal generic one. — Impersonal reference.
  • You should check your sources. Generic you. — Informal general reference.

👀 What do you observe?

English has three generic pronouns. They, with they, them and their, refers to a person of unknown or unspecified gender, and it is standard in modern usage even with a singular antecedent: everyone submitted their form. One, with one's, is impersonal and formal, and works best in rules. You is generic in speech and informal writing, where it means people in general.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Is 'everyone submitted their form' standard?

2. Which generic pronoun suits a formal rule?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
singular they unknown or unspecified gender if a candidate is late, they must inform the panel
their with everyone / anybody agreement with singular antecedent everyone submitted their form
one / one's formal impersonal one should check one's sources
generic you informal general reference you should check your sources
he or she avoided in modern usage use they unless the person is known
who for people relative reference the candidate who applied

Formula / rule: Choose by register and by knowledge: a known person takes he or she, an unknown person takes they, a rule takes one, and a conversation takes you. Keep the pronoun consistent through the paragraph, since switching from one to you in the same rule is a register error.

★ Why it matters

Singular they is the modern default in institutional writing precisely because it avoids both the clumsy he or she and the assumption that a role has a gender. A rulebook that uses one reads as formal and distant, which is sometimes the point and sometimes the problem.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use singular they constantly in speech without noticing, and generic you even in semi-formal writing. One is rare in speech outside Britain and can sound affected; in a report it is still normal.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Generic one is unstressed and often avoided in speech by using you or we instead; the singular they is always stressed when it is the subject of its clause.

Additional example bank
  • Singular they: Anyone who misses the deadline must explain themselves to the panel.
  • Formal one: One should not assume the figures are complete.
  • Generic you: You can't publish without a second reviewer.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: If a candidate is late, he must inform the panel (gendered pronoun for an unknown person)

✅ Right: If a candidate is late, they must inform the panel

❌ Wrong: One should check your sources (one and your mixed in one clause)

✅ Right: One should check one's sources

193 Gerunds and Infinitives

Verb forms

Gerund or infinitive, and which time? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. He denied
    gaphaving seen
    the memo.
  2. I remember
    gaplocking
    the door.
  3. We regret
    gapto inform
    you that the bid failed.
  4. The plan needs
    gapreviewing
    before launch.
GERUND→→ fact, experience, activity · INFINITIVE → purpose, potential
Level B2 Grammar

Gerunds and Infinitives

Choose the gerund, the infinitive or the perfect form by meaning.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use the -ing form, the to-infinitive and their perfect forms with the right meaning.
Examples in context
  • He denied having seen the memo. Perfect gerund: earlier action. — Deny + having + participle.
  • I remember locking the door. Gerund: the memory of an action. — Remember + -ing.
  • I remembered to lock the door. Infinitive: the duty performed. — Remember + to.

👀 What do you observe?

The gerund names an activity as a fact or an experience: I enjoy reading, he denied taking it. The infinitive names a purpose, a potential or a duty: I remembered to lock it, we agreed to wait. After deny, admit, regret (a past action), and after prepositions, the gerund is the only option, and the perfect gerund (having + participle) marks an action earlier than the main verb.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which sentence says the action was done and remembered?

2. What does the perfect gerund mark?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
verb + -ing activity or experience he denied taking the file
verb + to-infinitive purpose or duty we agreed to wait
having + participle earlier action he denied having taken the file
after a preposition always -ing before signing, read the terms
mean / try / stop sense changes with the form it means waiting / it means to help
need + -ing or to be + participle passive need the plan needs reviewing

Formula / rule: Ask what the verb is doing: naming an activity (gerund), pointing at a purpose or a duty (infinitive), or reaching back before the main verb (perfect gerund). After a preposition, only the gerund is possible.

★ Why it matters

The choice is a choice of meaning, not of style: regret to inform announces bad news, regret informing admits that you passed it on. In formal writing the perfect gerund is what lets you report an earlier action without a second clause.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers keep remember, forget and try apart by the form alone, and the difference is taught early, which is why the wrong choice stands out sharply to a listener.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The -ing ending is unstressed, while the to of the infinitive is weak /tə/ except when it introduces a purpose, where it carries a light stress.

Additional example bank
  • Admit: She admitted having received the figures early.
  • After a preposition: They left without telling the client.
  • Passive need: The contract needs renewing in June.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: He denied to have seen the memo (infinitive with a perfect form after deny)

✅ Right: He denied having seen the memo

❌ Wrong: I am used to work late (infinitive after a preposition)

✅ Right: I am used to working late

194 Get: Meanings and Patterns

Get

Which meaning is it here? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The situation
    gapgot
    worse.
  2. We
    gapgot
    the approval on Friday.
  3. He
    gapgot
    caught by the auditors.
  4. She
    gapgot
    the report rewritten.
GET→→ change · obtain · passive · causative
Level B2 Grammar

Get: Meanings and Patterns

Use get as a change, an obtainment, a passive and a causative.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can read and use the four main meanings of get without confusing them.
Examples in context
  • It got colder after lunch. Change of state. — Get + adjective.
  • We got the file at noon. Obtainment. — Get + object.
  • He got promoted. Passive with get. — Get + past participle.

👀 What do you observe?

Get is the workhorse verb of spoken English and carries four distinct patterns. Change: get plus adjective or comparative (get worse, get colder). Obtainment: get plus object (get the file, get approval). Passive: get plus past participle, usually for something unwanted or sudden (get caught, get fired). Causative: get plus object plus past participle, meaning to arrange for something to be done (get the report rewritten).

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which meaning is 'she got the car repaired'?
Get + object + participle is causative.
2. Which meaning is 'he got caught'?
Get + participle forms an informal passive.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
get + adjective change of state it got colder
get + object obtainment we got the approval
get + past participle informal passive, often unwanted he got caught
get + object + past participle causative she got the report rewritten
get + object + to-infinitive persuasion I got them to agree
get + -ing start or succeed we got moving at nine

Formula / rule: Identify the pattern, then read the meaning: adjective means change, noun object means obtainment, participle alone means passive, object plus participle means causative, object plus to-infinitive means persuasion. In formal writing, replace get with obtain, become, arrange or be plus participle.

★ Why it matters

Get is the verb learners avoid and native speakers cannot do without, which makes it both a comprehension gap and a register marker. Understanding the four patterns is what lets a learner follow ordinary conversation, and avoiding them in a report is what makes the report formal.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In British English, have got means possession (I've got the file) and have to means obligation; get is also the standard verb for arriving (what time do you get in?). Americans use gotten as the participle (he's gotten worse).

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Get is stressed in all four patterns, and the contracted have got reduces to /aɪv ɡɒt/ in British speech.

Additional example bank
  • Change: The market got quieter after the announcement.
  • Obtainment: We got three bids by Friday.
  • Causative: They got the contract translated before signing.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: She got the report rewrite (base verb where a participle is needed)

✅ Right: She got the report rewritten

❌ Wrong: It was got worse after lunch (passive with a change-of-state adjective)

✅ Right: It got worse after lunch

🔗 Connects to what you already know

195 Gradable and Extreme Adjectives

Intensifiers

Which intensifier fits the adjective? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapvery

    gapabsolutely
    disastrous.
  3. The room was
    gapfairly

    gaputterly

GRADABLE→→ very, fairly, slightly · EXTREME → absolutely, utterly
Level B2 Grammar

Gradable and Extreme Adjectives

Choose the intensifier the adjective allows.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can grade gradable adjectives and intensify extreme ones without breaking the collocation.
Examples in context
  • very good gradable: more or less good — The proposal is very good.
  • absolutely excellent extreme: no degrees — The proposal is absolutely excellent.
  • slightly late gradable, small degree — The train was slightly late.

👀 What do you observe?

Gradable adjectives admit degrees, so they take very, fairly, quite, slightly and rather, and they have comparatives: long, longer. Extreme adjectives already mean the top of the scale, so they take absolututes like absolutely, utterly, completely and totally, and normally have no comparative: disastrous, not more disastrous. Some adjectives sit in both groups depending on sense.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

2. Which adjective is gradable?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
gradable + very mid-scale adjectives very long, very useful
gradable + slightly / fairly small or moderate degree slightly late, fairly warm
extreme + absolutely / utterly top-of-scale adjectives absolutely disastrous, utterly worthless
extreme + completely / totally full extent completely exhausted, totally amazed
extreme, no comparative already at the limit disastrous, not more disastrous
both senses sense decides the group a very cold room, absolutely freezing

Formula / rule: Ask whether the adjective can be measured: if it can, grade it with very or slightly; if it already means the limit, intensify it with absolutely. Then check the collocation, because the intensifier and the adjective are learned together: absolutely delighted, utterly ridiculous, highly unlikely.

★ Why it matters

Wrong intensifiers are the most audible collocation error at B2, because native speakers hear very disastrous as a mistake rather than a style choice. The pairs are also a vocabulary test: knowing that exhausted is extreme tells you which intensifier belongs and which comparative does not.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use absolutely with extreme adjectives far more than very, and they often drop the intensifier altogether in speech: it was disastrous. Pretty is the spoken intensifier for gradable adjectives (pretty good), and it is informal.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Absolutely carries the main stress when it intensifies: it was ABSolutely disastrous; the adjective keeps a secondary stress.

Additional example bank
  • Extreme: The delay was absolutely catastrophic for the schedule.
  • Gradable: The reply was rather late.
  • Collocation: The figures are highly unlikely to change.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The failure was very disastrous (very with an extreme adjective)

✅ Right: The failure was absolutely disastrous

❌ Wrong: The evidence is absolutely weak (absolute intensifier with a gradable adjective)

✅ Right: The evidence is very weak

196 Hedging & Diplomatic Stance

Hedging

Soften the claim. Which word keeps the door open? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. It is
    gaparguably
    the most expensive option on the table.
  2. We would
    gapappear
    to have underestimated the timeline.
  3. To a
    gapcertain extent
    , the criticism is fair.
  4. The figures,
    gapadmittedly,
    are incomplete.
HEDGED CLAIM→admittedly · arguably · to a certain extent
Level B2 Grammar

Hedging & Diplomatic Stance

Say something contestable without picking a fight.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can soften a controversial claim so that it stays discussable.
Examples in context
  • Admittedly the rollout was rushed, and the results show it. — Concede first, then argue.
  • The proposal is arguably the safest of the three, though the cost is real. — Commit less, invite debate.
  • We would suggest that the deadline be revisited in June. — Recommendation without an order.

👀 What do you observe?

The claim still has content, but the speaker leaves room for the other side. Admittedly concedes a point before disagreeing; arguably marks a position as debatable; to a certain extent limits how far the speaker goes.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What does admittedly do at the start of a sentence?
Concession first, counter-argument second.
2. Which hedge limits the scope of an agreement?
Without any doubt removes the hedge altogether.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
arguably marks a claim as debatable arguably the safest option
admittedly concedes a point admittedly, the data is thin
to a certain extent limits the scope to a certain extent, you are right
it would appear that reports without asserting it would appear that the costs rose
we would suggest recommends without ordering we would suggest a later date
there may be a case for opens a possibility there may be a case for postponing

Formula / rule: Hedges sit at the edge of a claim: an adverb before the adjective (arguably the best), a reporting verb in the conditional (we would suggest), or a concessive opener (admittedly, to be fair). They do not remove the claim; they set its strength.

★ Why it matters

In academic and diplomatic English an unhedged claim invites attack, and the attack lands on the wording rather than the argument. Hedging is not weakness: it is what lets a minister say the policy failed without saying the government failed.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers hedge far more in speech than in writing, and they hedge with intonation as much as with words: a fall-rise on arguably signals 'I am not finished'. Writing the hedge without the intonation can read as sarcasm.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

arguably /ˈɑːɡ.ju.ə.bli/, admittedly /ədˈmɪt.ɪd.li/; both carry stress on the first syllable and a weak second.

Additional example bank
  • Concession: Admittedly, the schedule slipped twice.
  • Limit: To a certain extent, the criticism is fair.
  • Invitation: One might argue that the opposite is true.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The policy is a disaster (no hedge in a formal report)

✅ Right: The policy has arguably produced worse outcomes than intended

❌ Wrong: I think you are wrong (flat contradiction)

✅ Right: I would take a different view on that point

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Mandative subjunctive · Register: formal vs informal

197 Inversion after Negative Adverbials

Inversion

Which auxiliary completes the inverted clause? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. Never
    gaphave
    I seen such a rapid decline.
  2. Not only
    gapdid
    costs rise, but quality fell.
  3. Under no circumstances
    gapshould
    the data be shared.
  4. Hardly
    gaphad
    we started when the line stopped.
NEGATIVE ADVERBIAL→→ auxiliary + subject + verb
Level B2 Grammar

Inversion after Negative Adverbials

Front a negative adverbial, then invert the verb.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use never, rarely, not only and under no circumstances with correct inversion.
Examples in context
  • Rarely has the board been so divided. The board has rarely been so divided. — Fronted rare + inversion.
  • Not until June did the figures appear. The figures did not appear until June. — Not until + inversion.
  • No sooner had we signed than the price fell. We had no sooner signed than the price fell. — No sooner ... than.

👀 What do you observe?

When a negative or limiting adverbial opens the clause, the subject and auxiliary swap. The auxiliary is the one the sentence already needs: have for a perfect, did for a past simple, should or will for a modal. With no sooner and hardly, the second clause takes than or when, and it does not invert.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What moves in an inverted clause?
Never have I seen: have and I swap.
2. Which word follows 'no sooner' in the second clause?
No sooner had we signed than the price fell.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
never / rarely / seldom invert with the existing auxiliary rarely has the board been so divided
not only ... but also invert the first clause only not only did costs rise, but quality fell
not until / only when invert the main clause not until June did the figures appear
under no circumstances / on no account invert the modal under no circumstances should the data be shared
no sooner ... than invert the first clause, than in the second no sooner had we signed than the price fell
hardly ... when invert the first clause, when in the second hardly had we started when the line stopped

Formula / rule: Front the negative adverbial, find the auxiliary the sentence needs, then invert. If the clause has no auxiliary, add do, does or did and use the base verb. Keep no sooner ... than together, and never invert the second clause.

★ Why it matters

This structure is the written marker of emphasis and the exam marker of control: a report that opens with rarely has the board been so divided sounds authoritative, while the same sentence without inversion sounds like a translation. It also carries real weight in legal prohibitions: under no circumstances is not a stylistic choice.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, inversion after a negative front is rare except in set phrases (never have I seen, not only did they). Speakers usually keep the normal order and stress the negative: I've rarely seen.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The auxiliary is stressed in inversion: never HAVE I seen; under no circumstances SHOULD the data be shared.

Additional example bank
  • Time: Not until the audit closed did the scale of the loss emerge.
  • Condition: Only if the fee is paid will the application proceed.
  • Sequence: No sooner had the vote ended than the resignations began.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: Never I have seen such a decline (no inversion after a fronted negative)

✅ Right: Never have I seen such a decline

❌ Wrong: Not only costs rose, but quality fell (missing auxiliary in the first clause)

✅ Right: Not only did costs rise, but quality fell

198 It's Time, Would Rather, Had Better

Advice and preference

Which verb form follows? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. It's time
    gapwe left
    .

    gapnot discuss
    it here.
  3. You'd better
    gapcheck
    the figures.
  4. It's high time
    gapthe board acted
    .
IT'S TIME / I'D RATHER / YOU'D BETTER→→ past form or base verb
Level B2 Grammar

It's Time, Would Rather, Had Better

Give advice, express preference and set a deadline.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use it's time, would rather and had better with the right verb form.
Examples in context
  • It's time we left. Present or future meaning, past form. — Past subjunctive after it's time.
  • You'd better check the figures. Advice with a consequence. — Had better + base verb.
  • I'd rather you told her. Preference about someone else. — Would rather + subject + past form.

👀 What do you observe?

It's time (that) and it's high time take a past form with present meaning: it's time we left, meaning we should leave now. Had better takes the base verb and implies a consequence if the advice is ignored: you'd better check. Would rather takes the base verb when the subject is the same (I'd rather stay) and a past form when the subject changes (I'd rather you stayed).

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form follows it's time we ___?

2. What does had better add to advice?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
it's time + past form deadline, present meaning it's time we left
it's high time + past form stronger deadline, often critical it's high time the board acted
had better + base verb advice with a warning you'd better check the figures
would rather + base verb same subject I'd rather stay
would rather + subject + past different subject I'd rather you stayed
would rather + than comparison of options I'd rather wait than sign today

Formula / rule: Decide who is acting. Same subject with would rather: base verb. Different subject: past form. A deadline with it's time: past form. Advice with a consequence: had better plus the base verb, never to.

★ Why it matters

These three structures carry different pressures. It's time signals that something is overdue; had better signals that not doing it has a cost; would rather signals a preference the speaker is entitled to. Using them interchangeably makes advice sound either weak or rude.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use it's time we went and it's time to go with the same meaning, the first being slightly more personal. Had better is usually contracted to you'd better, and in speech it can sound like a threat.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Had better reduces to /ˈbetə/ with the auxiliary almost lost, and would rather to /aɪd ˈrɑːðə/, with the stress on rather.

Additional example bank
  • Deadline: It's high time the policy was reviewed.
  • Warning: You'd better tell the client before Friday.
  • Preference: I'd rather the team decided together.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: It's time we leave (base verb after it's time + subject)

✅ Right: It's time we left

❌ Wrong: You'd better to check the figures (to after had better)

✅ Right: You'd better check the figures

199 Mandative & Formulaic Subjunctive

Advice and demands

Which verb form? Complete the clause. tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The doctor suggested that he
    gaprest
    .
  2. It is essential that she
    gapbe
    on time.
  3. They demanded that he
    gapleave
    .
  4. I insist that you
    gapcome
    .
SUGGEST · DEMAND · INSIST THAT→+ subject + BASE verb
Level B2 Grammar

Mandative & Formulaic Subjunctive

Use the base verb after verbs of demand and adjectives of necessity.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can express formal demands, recommendations and fixed subjunctive expressions.
Examples in context
  • They demanded that he resign. Base verb after demand. — No -s, no tense change.
  • It is vital that the file be kept. Base be after an adjective of necessity. — Be, not is.
  • The board recommended that the plan be revised. Recommendation in formal register. — Same pattern after recommend.

👀 What do you observe?

The mandative subjunctive uses the base form of the verb after verbs of demand and suggestion (suggest, demand, insist, propose, recommend, request, urge) and after adjectives of necessity (essential, vital, crucial, imperative, necessary). The base form does not change with person or tense: it is essential that she be on time, they demanded that he leave, we insist that the report be published.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form follows 'It is essential that she ___'?

2. Does the subjunctive change in the past?
The base form stays the same.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
suggest / recommend that advice, formal the doctor suggested that he rest
demand / insist / request that pressure, formal they demanded that he leave
it is essential / vital that necessity it is essential that she be on time
it is imperative / crucial that urgency it is imperative that the file be kept
negative subjunctive not before the base verb we recommend that it not proceed
fixed formulas set expressions be that as it may, suffice it to say

Formula / rule: Use the base verb, never a tense form, after the that-clause: that he be, that she leave, that it not proceed. In British English the indicative is acceptable in informal writing (that she is on time), but the subjunctive is expected in formal and academic registers. Keep not before the base verb in the negative.

★ Why it matters

The subjunctive is the marker of formal obligation: a recommendation written with the subjunctive reads as binding, while the same sentence in the indicative reads as a description. This is why contracts, minutes and academic recommendations keep it, and why its absence is noticed.

💭 Think like a native speaker

American English uses the subjunctive far more consistently than British English, where the indicative is common in speech (I suggest that he goes). In writing, both varieties accept the subjunctive after demand-verbs, and examiners expect it.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The base verb after that is unstressed, and the stress falls on the adjective of necessity: it is esSENtial that she be on time.

Additional example bank
  • Recommendation: The panel recommends that the report be published in full.
  • Necessity: It is vital that the data be checked twice.
  • Negative: They insisted that the meeting not be recorded.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: It is essential that she is on time in a formal recommendation (indicative in a mandatory clause)

✅ Right: It is essential that she be on time

❌ Wrong: They demanded that he leaves (third person -s in the subjunctive)

✅ Right: They demanded that he leave

Review

Name the system, then the form. tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapbe
    submitted by Friday.

IDENTIFY→→ structure, form, then effect
Level B2 Grammar

B2 Master Review

The whole B2 system on one page, in the order the exam tests it.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can select, combine and correct the B2 structures under exam conditions.
Examples in context
  • Mandative subjunctive It is essential that he be informed. — Base verb after demand verbs.
  • Distancing passive The report is said to reflect a trend. — Agent removed, claim reported.
  • Inversion Rarely has the board seen such a split. — Negative fronting inverts.
  • Hedging The proposal is arguably the safest. — Claim marked as debatable.

👀 What do you observe?

The B2 system has four families. Verb forms: mandative subjunctive, mixed conditionals, distancing passives, reporting patterns. Information order: fronting, inversion, cleft sentences. Compression and register: nominalisation, ellipsis, substitution. Stance: hedging, concession, rhetorical structure. An exam task rarely tests one family alone: a reformulation task asks you to move a clause into a noun phrase, and a transformation task asks you to invert after a negative adverb.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
verb forms subjunctive, conditionals, passives It is essential that he be informed
information order fronting, inversion, clefts Rarely has the board seen such a split
compression nominalisation, ellipsis, substitution The implementation of the policy took two years
stance hedging, concession, rhetoric The proposal is arguably the safest
reformulation clause to noun phrase When we automate → the automation of
transformation same meaning, required structure Not only did costs rise...

Formula / rule: In an exam, read the instruction before the sentence: transformation tasks name the structure (begin with Not only, rewrite using a noun phrase), while reformulation tasks only fix the meaning. Then check three things in order - verb form, information order, stance - because that is the order markers are lost.

★ Why it matters

The final unit of the course is a review, not new grammar: it exists so that the structures learned separately appear together, which is the condition under which they are examined. Answer the transformation first, then check the auxiliary and the agreement, because those are where the marks go.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Examiners reward control over ambition. A correctly hedged, correctly nominalised plain sentence scores better than a broken inversion, and the empty structure that reads well aloud is usually the right answer in writing.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Read transformation answers aloud: the stress pattern tells you whether the auxiliary landed in the right place, since inversion and ellipsis both move the stressed element.

Additional example bank
  • Subjunctive: The committee demanded that the figures be released.
  • Inversion: Under no circumstances should the data be shared.
  • Compression: The refusal to publish delayed the audit.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: Not only the costs rose but quality fell (inversion missing)

✅ Right: Not only did the costs rise, but quality fell

❌ Wrong: It is essential that he is informed (indicative after a mandative verb)

✅ Right: It is essential that he be informed

201 Mixed Conditionals

Time and condition

Which time does each half refer to? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. If I had taken
    gapthe job
    , I would be in Berlin now.
  2. If she were
    gapmore careful
    , the error would not have happened.
  3. If he had left
    gapearlier
    , he would be at the meeting.
  4. If we knew
    gapthe answer
    , we would have told you.
PAST CONDITION→→ would + base (present result)
Level B2 Grammar

Mixed Conditionals

Match the condition's time to the result's time.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can talk about a past condition with a present result, or a present condition with a past result.
Examples in context
  • If I had studied medicine I would be a doctor now. — Past condition, present result.
  • If she were not so stubborn she would have accepted the offer. — Present condition, past result.
  • If they had invested in 2019 they would own the market today. — Same form, different decades.

👀 What do you observe?

A mixed conditional joins two time frames. Past condition with present result: if + past perfect, would + base verb (If I had taken the job, I would be in Berlin now). Present condition with past result: if + past simple, would have + participle (If she were more careful, the error would not have happened). The condition and the result do not have to share a time.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. In 'If I had taken the job, I would be in Berlin now', when is the result?
Would be, not would have been.
2. Which half is hypothetical in 'If she were more careful, the error would not have happened'?
Were marks an unreal present trait.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
past condition + present result if + past perfect, would + base if I had taken it, I would be there now
present condition + past result if + past simple, would have + participle if she were careful, it would not have happened
past condition + past result third conditional if I had known, I would have called
present condition + present result second conditional if I knew, I would tell you
unreal past trait were for all persons if he were here
inverted form Had / Were / Should + subject had I taken the job, I would be in Berlin

Formula / rule: Choose the tense of each half by the time it refers to, not by the other half. If the condition is past and the result is now: if + past perfect, would + base. If the condition is now and the result is past: if + past simple, would have + participle. Never put would in the if-clause.

★ Why it matters

Mixed conditionals are how English argues about consequences that outlive their causes. A policy decision in 2019 explains a present shortage, and the third conditional alone cannot say that. Getting the mix right is the difference between a history essay and an analysis.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers mix conditionals freely in speech and rarely notice the time shift; what they notice is would in the if-clause, which marks a learner. In writing, the mixed form signals that the writer has thought about which half belongs to which period.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The stress falls on the time marker, which is what makes the mix audible: I would BE there NOW; it would not HAVE happened.

Additional example bank
  • Past to present: If we had kept the factory, the town would still have work.
  • Present to past: If he were better organised, the deadline would have been met.
  • Inverted: Had the warning been heeded, we would not be in this position.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: If I would have taken the job, I would be in Berlin (would in the if-clause)

✅ Right: If I had taken the job, I would be in Berlin

❌ Wrong: If she was more careful, the error would not have happened (indicative for an unreal present)

✅ Right: If she were more careful, the error would not have happened

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Alternatives to if · Conditional inversion

202 Narrative Tenses

Narrative

Which tense orders the events? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. We
    gapwere waiting
    when the call came.
  2. She
    gaphad already left
    before I arrived.
  3. He
    gapwalked in
    , sat down and said nothing.
  4. They
    gapused to
    meet on Fridays.
BACKGROUND→→ past continuous · EVENT → past simple · EARLIER → past perfect
Level B2 Grammar

Narrative Tenses

Tell a story with the tenses that order it.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can move between past simple, past continuous, past perfect and used to when telling a story.
Examples in context
  • The rain was falling and the streets were empty. Background, past continuous. — Sets the scene.
  • Then the lights went out. Event, past simple. — Moves the story.
  • Someone had cut the cable. Earlier event, past perfect. — Explains what we found.

👀 What do you observe?

A narrative uses three layers. Past continuous for the scene and the action in progress; past simple for the events that move the story forward, in order; past perfect for what happened before the moment being told. Used to and would mark repeated past behaviour, and the past perfect continuous marks a state that had been going on before an event.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which tense moves the story forward?
The events in order are past simple.
2. What does the past perfect mark?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
past continuous scene and action in progress we were waiting when the call came
past simple events in sequence he walked in, sat down and said nothing
past perfect earlier event, explains the scene someone had cut the cable
past perfect continuous state continuing before an event they had been arguing for an hour
used to / would repeated past behaviour they used to meet on Fridays
when / while interruption or simultaneity while we were waiting, the line failed

Formula / rule: Set the scene in the past continuous, tell the events in the past simple in order, and reach back with the past perfect when the reader needs to know what came before. Use when for an interruption after a continuous clause, and while for two simultaneous actions.

★ Why it matters

Narrative tense control is what makes a story readable: a reader who cannot tell which event happened first stops following. Past perfect is the tool that lets a writer explain a consequence before revealing the cause, which is the basic move of report writing as well as fiction.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use the past perfect sparingly in speech and rely on before, after and then to order events; overusing it in writing sounds literary. Would for past habit is common in storytelling (we would sit for hours) but not for single events.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The past perfect is usually contracted in speech (she'd already left), which is why the auxiliary carries the stress when the order is the point: she HAD already left.

Additional example bank
  • Scene: The office was emptying and the phones had stopped ringing.
  • Sequence: He opened the file, read the first page and closed it again.
  • Earlier: By the time the auditors arrived, the records had disappeared.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: When I arrived, she already left (past simple for an earlier event)

✅ Right: When I arrived, she had already left

❌ Wrong: While we waited, the line failed (past simple where an action in progress is meant)

✅ Right: While we were waiting, the line failed

203 Nominalisation & Register

Nominalisation

Which noun phrase replaces the clause? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The
    gapimplementation
    of the policy took two years.
  2. Their
    gaprefusal
    to publish the data delayed the audit.
  3. A sharp
    gaprise
    in complaints followed the change.
  4. The
    gapintroduction
    of the levy provoked the strike.
CLAUSE→→ noun phrase (verb becomes head noun)
Level B2 Grammar

Nominalisation & Register

Turn a clause into a noun when the text has to sound formal.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can compress a clause into a noun phrase and keep the sentence readable.
Examples in context
  • When we automate the line, costs fall. The automation of the line reduces costs. — Clause becomes subject.
  • They refused to publish the data. Their refusal to publish the data delayed the audit. — Agent moves into a possessive.
  • Complaints rose sharply. There was a sharp rise in complaints. — Manner becomes an adjective.

👀 What do you observe?

Nominalisation turns a verb or adjective into the head of a noun phrase: implement → the implementation of, refuse → their refusal to, rise → a sharp rise in. The original subject either becomes a possessive (their refusal) or disappears (the implementation of the policy), and the original verb's object becomes an of-phrase.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·b

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What happens to the agent in 'the implementation of the policy'?
Nobody is named, which is often the point of the passive nominal.
2. Which is more formal?
Nominalisation raises the register and hides the agent.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
verb → noun names the action implement → implementation
adjective → noun names the quality refuse → refusal
of-phrase carries the original object the implementation of the policy
possessive keeps the agent visible their refusal to publish
there + noun presents a change there was a sharp rise in complaints
nominal + verb one main verb per clause the introduction of the levy provoked the strike

Formula / rule: Nominalise when the action, not the actor, is the topic: the implementation of the policy took two years. Keep the agent in a possessive when responsibility matters: their refusal delayed the audit. Limit yourself to one nominalisation per clause, and keep a verb in the sentence so it still moves.

★ Why it matters

Formal English compresses: a report says the introduction of the levy, not when the government introduced the levy. Compression raises the register but hides who did what, which is why the passive nominal is the favourite structure of anyone avoiding responsibility - and why an editor should ask for the agent back.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Nominalisations are heavy in speech and sound bureaucratic. Native speakers use them in writing and in prepared statements, and they lighten them in conversation: 'we introduced the levy' rather than 'the introduction of the levy'.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Nominalised forms shift the stress: implement /ˈɪm.plɪ.ment/ but implementation /ˌɪm.plɪ.menˈteɪ.ʃən/, with the main stress on the syllable before -tion.

Additional example bank

  • Agent kept: Their withdrawal of the offer ended the negotiation.
  • Presented: There was a marked decline in applications after the change.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The implement of the policy took two years (verb used as a noun)

✅ Right: The implementation of the policy took two years

❌ Wrong: The policy was implemented and it took two years and it was expensive (chain of clauses)

✅ Right: The implementation of the policy took two years and cost more than planned

Adjective order

Level B2 Grammar

Order of Adjectives

Put several adjectives in the order English expects.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can order two to four adjectives before a noun without sounding foreign.
Examples in context
  • A beautiful old wooden desk opinion, age, material — Three adjectives in order.
  • A small round glass table size, shape, material — No opinion, still ordered.
  • A long grey silk scarf size, colour, material — Colour before material.

👀 What do you observe?

Adjectives fall into slots: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. The order is fixed, and opinion always comes first even when it is the least important word. When two adjectives belong to the same slot, join them with and: a long and difficult year, not a long difficult year.

Element / structure Role in English Application example
opinion judgement lovely, awful, remarkable
size dimension small, vast, narrow
age how old old, new, ancient
shape form round, square, curved
colour hue grey, scarlet, pale
origin / material where from, what of Italian, wooden, silk

Formula / rule: Learn the slot order as a single string and place each adjective in its slot: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. Two or three adjectives are normal; four is the practical limit, and a fifth means the sentence should be rewritten.

★ Why it matters

Native speakers hear the wrong order immediately, even when they cannot name the rule, which is why adjective order is one of the clearest markers of non-native writing. Getting it right costs nothing and removes an accent from the page.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, the last adjective before the noun carries the stress, and that is usually the material or origin: a lovely old STONE cottage. A fronted opinion adjective is often followed by a slight pause.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Each adjective keeps its own stress, but the strongest falls on the last slot: a beautiful old WOODEN desk, with the material as the most informative item.

Additional example bank
  • Opinion and age: an ugly new building
  • Size, colour, origin: a large blue Japanese print
  • Same slot: a quiet and careful report
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: A wooden beautiful old desk (material before opinion and age)

✅ Right: a beautiful old wooden desk

❌ Wrong: A French remarkable clear report (origin before opinion)

✅ Right: a remarkably clear French report

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use be to, be about to, be due to and be on the point of.
Examples in context
  • The panel is to report by June. Formal plan or instruction. — Be to + base.
  • The train is about to leave. Immediate future. — Be about to + base.
  • The audit is due to start in April. Scheduled future. — Be due to + base.

👀 What do you observe?

Beyond will and going to, English has semi-modals that carry a plan, a schedule or an imminent event. Be to plus the base verb states a formal plan or an instruction (the panel is to report by June). Be about to and be on the point of state what will happen in the next moment. Be due to states what is scheduled. Be bound to states what is certain.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form marks an imminent event?
The train is about to leave.
2. Which form states a formal plan?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
be to + base formal plan or instruction the panel is to report by June
be about to + base immediate future the train is about to leave
be on the point of + -ing immediate future, formal we are on the point of signing
be due to + base scheduled future the audit is due to start in April
be bound to + base certain future the cost is bound to rise
be set to + base expected future in news the firm is set to announce cuts

Formula / rule: Pick by the kind of certainty: a plan in a document is be to, a timetable is be due to, the next moment is be about to or be on the point of, and a logical certainty is be bound to. All of them take the base verb except be on the point of, which takes the gerund.

★ Why it matters

These semi-modals are what make a written plan read as a plan: is to report sounds like a decision, will report sounds like a prediction, and is due to report sounds like a timetable. In news English, is set to has become the standard way to report an expected event without committing to it.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, be about to is the common form and be on the point of sounds literary. Be to survives mostly in official notices and in the negative (you are not to leave), which is a prohibition.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The stress falls on the semi-modal when the timing is the point: the train is ABOUT to leave; the panel IS to report by June.

Additional example bank
  • Instruction: Staff are to submit timesheets by Friday.
  • Schedule: The hearing is due to resume on Monday.
  • Certainty: The delay is bound to affect the launch.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: We are on the point to sign (infinitive after on the point of)

✅ Right: We are on the point of signing

❌ Wrong: The panel is to reporting by June (gerund after be to)

✅ Right: The panel is to report by June

206 Participle Clauses

Compression

Which participle completes the sentence? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. Having finished
    gapthe audit
    , the team filed the report.
  2. Written
    gapin 1904
    , the manual is still used.
  3. Walking
    gapto the office
    , she called the client.
  4. Faced
    gapwith a deadline
    , the unit reorganised.
SHARED SUBJECT→→ -ing (active) or -ed (passive) clause
Level B2 Grammar

Participle Clauses

Compress a second clause into a participle.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can replace a full clause with an -ing or -ed clause when the subject is shared.
Examples in context
  • Feeling unwell, he left early. He felt unwell and he left early. — Same subject, active.
  • Published in May, the report caused a stir. The report was published and caused a stir. — Passive relation.
  • Having signed the deal, they celebrated. They had signed, then they celebrated. — Earlier action.

👀 What do you observe?

A participle clause replaces a clause when both clauses share the same subject. The -ing participle is active and often simultaneous: walking to the office, she called. The -ed participle is passive: written in 1904, the manual is still used. Having + participle marks an action completed before the main one. A wrong subject is a dangling participle, the error this structure punishes hardest.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which participle marks an earlier action?

2. What is a dangling participle?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
-ing (active) same subject, simultaneous walking to the office, she called the client
-ed (passive) the subject receives the action written in 1904, the manual is still used
having + participle action completed first having finished the audit, the team filed
having been + participle passive action completed first having been warned, they checked again
reduced relative replaces who/which + verb the figures collected in March
with + noun + participle different subject allowed with the deadline moved, the plan changed

Formula / rule: Check that both clauses share a subject, then choose the participle by voice: active -ing, passive -ed, completed then having + participle. If the subjects differ, keep two clauses or use with + noun + participle: with the deadline moved, we replanned.

★ Why it matters

Participle clauses are how academic and journalistic English compresses: one sentence carries a cause, a condition or a sequence without a connector. They are also unforgiving, because a mismatched subject produces a sentence that says something absurd, and readers notice.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, participle clauses are rare outside fixed openers (speaking of which, given the time). In writing, they cluster at the start of sentences, where the shared subject is checked by the reader on the first pass.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The participle is unstressed in the middle of a clause and stressed when it opens one: HAVING finished the audit, the team filed. The comma marks the boundary and the fall in pitch.

Additional example bank
  • Cause: Having missed the deadline, the team lost the contract.
  • Passive: Submitted late, the application was rejected.
  • Different subject: With the vote taken, the meeting closed.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: Walking to the office, the phone rang (dangling participle: the phone was not walking)

✅ Right: Walking to the office, she took the call, or: as she walked to the office, the phone rang

❌ Wrong: Having finished the audit, the report was filed (subject of the participle is not the report's)

✅ Right: Having finished the audit, the team filed the report

207 Passive Verbs with Two Objects

Two objects

Which object is now the subject? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The board
    gapwas offered
    a revised timetable.
  2. She
    gapwas given
    two weeks to decide.
  3. The file
    gapwas sent
    to every member.
  4. We
    gapwere told

VERB + PERSON + THING→→ either object can be the subject
Level B2 Grammar

Passive Verbs with Two Objects

Decide which object becomes the subject.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can turn give, offer, send and tell into the passive with either object in front.
Examples in context
  • They offered the board a timetable. The board was offered a timetable. — Person becomes the subject.
  • They offered a timetable to the board. A timetable was offered to the board. — Thing becomes the subject, with to.
  • They told us nothing. We were told nothing. — Person first is the usual passive.

👀 What do you observe?

Verbs with two objects (give, offer, send, show, tell, pay, teach, promise, hand, owe) can form two passives. When the person becomes the subject, the thing stays as it is: the board was offered a timetable. When the thing becomes the subject, the person moves into a to- or for-phrase: a timetable was offered to the board. The person-first passive is far more frequent, because people are usually the topic.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which passive is more frequent?
People are usually the topic of the sentence.
2. Which preposition introduces the person in a thing-first passive?
A timetable was offered to the board.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
person-first usual passive with two objects the board was offered a timetable
thing-first with to the thing is the topic a timetable was offered to the board
thing-first with for buy, get, book, make a room was booked for the delegation
verbs that allow both give, offer, send, show, tell, pay we were told nothing / nothing was told to us
verbs that allow one explain, suggest, describe, announce the plan was explained to us
reporting with two objects tell, inform, notify we were informed of the delay

Formula / rule: Choose the subject by the topic: if the reader is following a person, put the person first; if the reader is following a document or a sum, put the thing first and use to. With explain, suggest and describe, only the thing-first passive is available, and the person needs to.

★ Why it matters

This structure is the grammar of institutional speech: we were told nothing is what a witness says, while nothing was told to us is what a lawyer writes when the absence is the point. The choice of subject decides who the sentence is about, which is rarely neutral.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech the person-first passive is overwhelming: I was given, we were told, she was sent. The thing-first passive with to appears mostly in writing, where a document or a sum is the topic.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The passive auxiliary carries the stress when the omission of the agent is the point: we WERE told nothing, though everyone knew.

Additional example bank
  • Person-first: The delegation was shown the draft before publication.
  • Thing-first: The draft was shown to the delegation before publication.
  • Single-option verb: The process was explained to us twice.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The plan was explained us (missing to with a single-option verb)

✅ Right: The plan was explained to us

❌ Wrong: A timetable was offered the board (person left without a preposition in a thing-first passive)

✅ Right: A timetable was offered to the board

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Distancing passive reporting · Verb + object + infinitive or gerund

Past tenses

Which past tense fits? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapmet

    gapwere meeting
    when the call came.
  3. We
    gaphad met

TIME RELATION→→ simple · continuous · perfect · perfect continuous
Level B2 Grammar

Past Tenses Review

Pick the past tense by what the sentence needs to show.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can choose between past simple, past continuous, past perfect and past perfect continuous.
Examples in context
  • They signed in June. Single completed event. — Past simple.
  • They were signing when the lawyers arrived. Event in progress. — Past continuous.
  • They had signed before the audit began. Earlier event. — Past perfect.

👀 What do you observe?

Four past tenses, four jobs. Past simple for completed events in sequence. Past continuous for an action in progress at a past moment, or for the background of a story. Past perfect for an event earlier than another past event. Past perfect continuous for a state or activity that had been going on before a past moment. The time expression usually decides: in 2019, when, before, for months.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which tense marks an event earlier than another past event?

2. Which tense shows an action in progress?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
past simple completed events in sequence they signed in June
past continuous action in progress, background they were signing when we arrived
past perfect earlier event they had signed before the audit
past perfect continuous activity continuing before a past point they had been negotiating for weeks
used to / would repeated past behaviour they used to meet on Fridays
past simple after when interruption of a continuous action when the call came, we were meeting

Formula / rule: Build the timeline first: which event is the reference point, which one came before it, which one was in progress. Then choose: reference event in the past simple, earlier event in the past perfect, background in the past continuous, prolonged earlier activity in the past perfect continuous.

★ Why it matters

Past tense control is what makes a report readable: an audit that says the file had been deleted before the review began tells you the sequence without a second sentence. Mixing the four tenses carelessly produces a timeline the reader has to reconstruct, which is where comprehension fails.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use the past perfect sparingly in speech and lean on before, after and then; in writing it does the work those words would do. The past perfect continuous is frequent in reports where a state had persisted.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The auxiliary is contracted in speech (they'd signed), so the stress falls on the participle when the order matters: they had SIGNED before the audit.

Additional example bank
  • Sequence: She opened the file, read the first page and closed it again.
  • Earlier: By the time the auditors arrived, the records had gone.
  • Prolonged: The team had been pressing for a decision since March.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: When I arrived, she already left (past simple for an earlier event)

✅ Right: When I arrived, she had already left

❌ Wrong: They were signing the contract before the audit began (continuous for a completed earlier event)

✅ Right: They had signed the contract before the audit began

209 Permission, Obligation and Prohibition

Rules

Who requires it, and how strong is it? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. Visitors
    gapmust not
    photograph the exhibits.
  2. Staff
    gapare required to
    wear badges.
  3. You
    gapneedn't
    book in advance.
  4. Contractors
    gapshall
    complete the work by June.
MODAL→→ strength and source of the rule
Level B2 Grammar

Permission, Obligation and Prohibition

Say what is allowed, required and forbidden, and who decided it.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use modals, semi-modals and formal structures for rules and duties.
Examples in context
  • Permission: You may use the archive on request. — Formal permission.
  • Obligation: You have to register first. — External rule.
  • Prohibition: You must not remove the files. — Absolute ban.
  • No obligation: You don't need to print it. — Optional.

👀 What do you observe?

The same obligation changes strength with its source: must imposes, have to reports, must not forbids, needn't releases. Read each example for who decided.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Does 'you mustn't' mean 'you don't have to'?
Mustn't forbids; don't have to makes it optional.
2. Which form marks an external rule rather than the speaker's authority?
Have to reports a rule; must often imposes one.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
must obligation from the speaker you must submit the form today
have to / has to obligation from outside staff have to wear badges
must not / be prohibited from prohibition visitors must not photograph the exhibits
needn't / don't have to no obligation you needn't book in advance
may / be allowed to permission you may use the archive on request
shall / is to be formal requirement in documents the contractor shall complete the work by June

Formula / rule: Obligation comes in two kinds: must and have to for what is required, with must usually expressing the speaker's authority and have to an external rule. Prohibition is must not or is not allowed to; don't have to and needn't mean no obligation at all, which is the opposite. Read the rule from two directions: is the action required or optional, and who decided it. In contracts, shall carries the obligation and may carries the permission, and neither is decorative.

★ Why it matters

A rulebook is read by people looking for what they may and must do, so the modal is the operative word: a prohibition written as you shouldn't is not a prohibition. In contracts the difference between shall and may decides who carries the risk.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers keep must for written rules and self-imposed duties, and use have to for everything institutional in speech: I have to file the report. Mustn't in speech is a warning from the speaker, which is why it sounds stronger than you're not allowed to.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Must is unstressed when it is a plain obligation (I must go) and stressed when it corrects (you MUST read it). Have to reduces to /hæftə/, and mustn't keeps a full /ʌ/ in careful speech.

Additional example bank
  • Notice: Bags must not be left unattended.
  • Contract: The lessee shall maintain the premises.
  • Colleague: You don't need to copy me in.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: You mustn't pay; entry is free (prohibition where no obligation is meant)

✅ Right: You don't need to pay; entry is free

❌ Wrong: You must to submit the form (modal followed by to)

✅ Right: You must submit the form

🔗 Connects to what you already know

210 Phrasal Verbs: Extended Patterns

Phrasal verbs

Can the particle move? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. We need to
    gapcall off
    the meeting.
  2. We need to call the meeting

    .
  3. The plan
    gapfell through
    .

VERB + PARTICLE→→ separable, inseparable or three-part
Level B2 Grammar

Phrasal Verbs: Extended Patterns

Separate the particles, keep the meaning, choose the register.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use transitive, intransitive and three-part phrasal verbs correctly.
Examples in context
  • They called off the meeting. Separable: particle after the object too. — Call the meeting off.
  • The plan fell through. Intransitive: no object. — Nothing separates.
  • They put up with the delay. Three-part: inseparable. — Put up with something.

👀 What do you observe?

Phrasal verbs come in three patterns. Separable verbs take the object between verb and particle, or after it: call off the meeting, call the meeting off, but a pronoun must sit between (call it off). Inseparable verbs keep the particle next to the verb: look after the file, never look the file after. Three-part verbs (put up with, get away with, look forward to) are inseparable and take the gerund after to.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

Element / structure Role in English Application example
separable object before or after the particle call off the meeting / call the meeting off
pronoun with separable always between call it off
inseparable particle stays with the verb look after the file
three-part inseparable, gerund after to put up with the delay, look forward to hearing
intransitive no object at all the plan fell through
register single Latinate verb in formal writing postpone, tolerate, investigate

Formula / rule: Learn the pattern with the verb, then the register. In a report, replace the phrasal verb with its single-word equivalent: postpone for put off, tolerate for put up with, investigate for look into. In speech, the phrasal verb is the natural choice, and the Latinate verb sounds stiff.

★ Why it matters

Phrasal verbs are where comprehension and production diverge: most learners understand put off and few produce it under pressure, because the meaning is not in the parts. Knowing the pattern also prevents the two most common errors, splitting an inseparable verb and keeping a pronoun after a separable particle.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers split separable verbs freely in speech (turn the light off) and prefer the noun-first order in writing (turn off the light). Three-part verbs are the ones dictionaries list as single entries.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The particle is stressed when it carries the meaning: call it OFF, the plan fell THROUGH. In three-part verbs the middle word is weak.

Additional example bank
  • Separable: They put the launch off until June.
  • Inseparable: She looks after the archive.
  • Three-part: We will not put up with further delays.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: They called off it (pronoun after the particle of a separable verb)

✅ Right: They called it off

❌ Wrong: She looks the archive after (inseparable verb split by its object)

✅ Right: She looks after the archive
