Level B2 Grammar

Possessive 's with Time Expressions

Use the possessive for time, distance and value.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can write a week's notice, two hours' delay and today's figures.
Examples in context
  • a day's work singular time expression — One day, so 's.
  • three days' work plural ending in s — Three days, so s'.
  • today's figures fixed time word — Today's, yesterday's, tomorrow's.

👀 What do you observe?

Time expressions take the possessive like people do: a week's notice, an hour's delay, two hours' delay, three months' salary. The apostrophe follows the normal rule: 's for singular, s' for a plural ending in s, and 's for irregular plurals (children's). Fixed words such as today, yesterday and tomorrow always take 's. The same pattern covers distance (a mile's walk) and value (a pound's worth).

Element / structure Role in English Application example

irregular plural + 's children, people a children's programme
fixed time words today, yesterday, tomorrow today's figures
distance the same pattern a mile's walk
value the same pattern a pound's worth

Formula / rule: Decide whether the time expression is singular or plural, then place the apostrophe: 's for singular and irregular plurals, s' for plurals in s. Keep the possessive only when the time expression is the owner (a week's notice), not when it is a plain adverbial (we met last week).

★ Why it matters

These possessives are frequent in business English (a month's notice, two weeks' notice, a year's budget) and the apostrophe is where they go wrong. Because the phrase often sits in a contract, the error is expensive: a six months notice clause is ambiguous about where the apostrophe belongs.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers say a week's notice but write the possessive inconsistently in informal text; the apostrophe is one of the first casualties of casual writing. In speech the possessive is audible only as a small /s/ or /z/.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The possessive ending is /s/ after a voiceless sound (a week's), /z/ after a voiced one (a day's), and /ɪz/ after a sibilant (a month's).

✅ Right: two weeks' notice

PREFIX→un- · in- · dis- · mis- · anti-
Level B2 Grammar

Prefixes & Negative Forms

Negate a word without changing its class.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can choose the right negative prefix instead of not + word.
Examples in context
  • unreliable The source proved unreliable. — un- before a native root.
  • illegal The payment was illegal. — il- before l.
  • misinterpret The press misinterpreted the ruling. — mis- means wrongly.

👀 What do you observe?

The prefix carries the negation, so the word class stays the same: reliable and unreliable are both adjectives. The choice among un-, in-, dis- and mis- is lexical, and in- assimilates to il- before l, im- before m and p, and ir- before r.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2

2. Which prefix fits 'legal'?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
un- negates, native roots unreliable, unclear, unfair
in- / il- / im- / ir- negates, Latinate roots incapable, illegal, impossible, irregular
dis- negates or reverses an action disagree, disconnect, disqualify
mis- wrongly misinterpret, misreport, mislead
anti- against anticompetitive, antidumping
non- not of that type non-binding, non-renewable

Formula / rule: Negate with a prefix when the word has a stable opposite (unfair, illegal, disagree). Use not when the negation is temporary or contrastive (the report is not finished, but not unfinishable). Never write unlegal or inlegal: the prefix is fixed by the root, so learn the pairs.

★ Why it matters

Prefixes are the fastest way to sound precise at B2. Misreport says the press got it wrong, while not report says it did not report at all; anti-competitive describes a design, while not competitive describes a result. The prefix carries the argument.

💭 Think like a native speaker

English has a few false negatives that look like prefixes: invaluable means extremely valuable, and inflammable means flammable. Trust the dictionary, not the prefix, for these.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Prefixes are unstressed except anti- and non-, so unreliable is /ˌʌn.rɪˈlaɪ.ə.bəl/ with the stress on the root, exactly as in reliable.

Additional example bank
  • un-: The evidence is uncontested but thin.
  • dis-: Two members disagreed with the ruling.
  • mis-: The figure was misquoted in three outlets.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The payment was inlegal (wrong prefix for the root)

✅ Right: The payment was illegal

❌ Wrong: The audit was not completeable (not + derived adjective)

✅ Right: The audit was incomplete

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Suffixes & word formation · Gradable vs extreme adjectives

Incomplete is the fixed pair.
2. Which word means 'quoted wrongly'?

213 Present Tenses Review

Present tenses

Which present tense fits? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. She
    gapworks
    in Leeds.
  2. She
    gapis working
    from home this week.
  3. She
    gaphas worked
    there since 2019.
  4. She
    gaphas been working
    all morning.
TIME FRAME→→ habit · now · experience · duration
Level B2 Grammar

Present Tenses Review

Choose between the simple, the continuous and the perfect present.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use the four present tenses for habits, current states, temporary actions and experience.
Examples in context
  • He works in Leeds. Permanent situation. — Present simple.
  • He is working from home this week. Temporary situation. — Present continuous.
  • He has worked there since 2019. Experience up to now. — Present perfect.

👀 What do you observe?

Present simple for habits, routines and permanent states (she works in Leeds, the train leaves at seven). Present continuous for actions happening now or around now, and for temporary situations (she is working from home this week). Present perfect for experience or a situation continuing to now, with for and since. Present perfect continuous for an activity that has been going on up to now, usually with a visible result.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which tense marks a temporary situation?
She is working from home this week.
2. Which tense goes with since 2019?

Element / structure Role in English Application example
present simple habit, routine, permanent state she works in Leeds
present continuous now, around now, temporary she is working from home this week
present perfect experience, situation up to now she has worked there since 2019
present perfect continuous activity up to now, visible result she has been working all morning
stative verbs no continuous form I know the answer, not I am knowing
timetables present simple for schedules the train leaves at 07:40

Formula / rule: Ask whether the situation is permanent, temporary, continuing from the past, or still in progress. Permanent goes to the simple, temporary to the continuous, continuing with for or since to the perfect, and in progress up to now to the perfect continuous. Keep stative verbs out of the continuous.

★ Why it matters

These four tenses cover most of what a report says about the present, and the choice between them is a claim about permanence: she works there says the arrangement is settled, she is working there says it may change. Getting the pair right is how a writer signals how much to trust a finding.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use the present continuous for irritations with always (he is always losing the file) and the present simple for narrative commentary (then she walks in and says nothing). In formal writing, the perfect continuous is rarer than the perfect.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The contracted auxiliary in the perfect forms is weak: she's worked, she's been working, with the stress on the participle.

Additional example bank
  • Habit: The committee meets on the first Monday of the month.
  • Temporary: The team is covering two regions while the post is vacant.
  • Experience: We have tested the system in three countries.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: She is knowing the answer (continuous with a stative verb)

✅ Right: She knows the answer

❌ Wrong: I work here since 2019 (present simple with since)

✅ Right: I have worked here since 2019

214 Reflexive and Reciprocal Pronouns

Pronouns

Reflexive or reciprocal? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The board
    gapitself
    approved the change.
  2. They blamed
    gapeach other
    for the delay.
  3. She taught
    gapherself
    to code.
  4. We consult
    gapone another
    before voting.
SAME SUBJECT→→ myself, yourself, itself · TWO PARTIES → each other
Level B2 Grammar

Reflexive and Reciprocal Pronouns

Use myself, themselves and each other where they belong.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use reflexive pronouns for the same subject and reciprocal pronouns for two-way actions.
Examples in context
  • She taught herself to code. Reflexive: the subject acts on itself. — Subject and object are the same.
  • They blamed each other. Reciprocal: two parties act on one another. — Each other for two, one another for more.
  • The board itself approved the change. Emphatic reflexive. — Adds emphasis, not an object.

👀 What do you observe?

A reflexive pronoun is used when the subject and the object are the same person or thing: she taught herself, the board itself approved the change. A reciprocal pronoun is used when two or more parties act on one another: they blamed each other, we consult one another. Reflexives are also used after certain verbs (behave yourself, help yourself) and in fixed phrases (by itself, in itself), but not after verbs that do not take an object.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which pronoun for two parties acting on each other?
They blamed each other.
2. What does the emphatic reflexive add?
The board itself approved the change.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
reflexive object subject acts on itself she taught herself to code
emphatic reflexive emphasis on the subject the board itself approved the change
reciprocal each other two parties, two-way action they blamed each other
reciprocal one another more than two, formal we consult one another
by + reflexive alone or unaided the system rebooted by itself
in + reflexive considered alone the delay is not a problem in itself

Formula / rule: Ask whether there is one party or two. One party acting on itself takes a reflexive: she taught herself. Two parties acting on each other take each other or one another. Use a reflexive for emphasis only when the subject is already present, and never use one where the verb has no object (she woke up, not she woke herself up).

★ Why it matters

The distinction matters in reports, where themselves suggests internal action and each other suggests mutual action: the departments blamed themselves is a very different finding from the departments blamed each other. Reflexives also carry responsibility, which is why a minute that says the board itself approved it names the body rather than the staff.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use each other for two and one another for more than two, but the distinction is soft and often ignored. Reflexives after verbs of movement are wrong: she sat down, not she sat herself down.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The reflexive ending is weak: /məˈself/, /jɔːˈself/, and the stress falls on self when the emphasis is the point: the board itSELF approved it.

Additional example bank
  • Reflexive: He hurt himself lifting the crate.
  • Reciprocal: The two teams briefed each other before the meeting.
  • Fixed phrase: The decision is not a problem in itself.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: They blamed themselves for the delay with two teams (reflexive where mutuality is meant)

✅ Right: They blamed each other for the delay

❌ Wrong: She woke herself up at six every day (reflexive with a verb that takes no object)

✅ Right: She woke up at six every day

🔗 Connects to what you already know

215 Relative Clauses: Review and Deepening

Relative clauses

Which linker does the gap need? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The report
    gapthat
    we commissioned has arrived.
  2. The consultant
    gapwhose
    figures we used has resigned.
  3. The office
    gapwhere
    the audit took place is closed.
  4. The evidence,
    gapwhich
    was never published, is now public.
NOUN→+ who / which / whose / where + clause
Level B2 Grammar

Relative Clauses: Review and Deepening

Attach a clause to a noun without breaking the sentence.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can define, add and shorten relative clauses at B2 level.
Examples in context
  • The analyst who wrote the note has left the team. — Defining: identifies which analyst.
  • The note, which was leaked, caused an outcry. — Non-defining: adds information.
  • The cost of which we spoke has doubled. — Preposition plus which in formal register.

👀 What do you observe?

A defining clause tells you which noun is meant and takes no commas: the report that we commissioned. A non-defining clause adds information and takes commas: the report, which we commissioned, has arrived. That never follows a comma; which can. Whose replaces a possessive, where replaces a place adverbial, and preposition + which replaces a prepositional phrase at the end of a formal clause.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which clause can take commas?
Commas mark added, not identifying, information.
2. Can the relative pronoun be dropped in 'the report that we commissioned'?
The report we commissioned has arrived is correct.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
who / that person, subject the analyst who wrote the note
which / that thing, subject or object the report that we commissioned
whose possessive the consultant whose figures we used
where / when place or time adverbial the office where the audit took place
preposition + which formal, replaces a stranded preposition the cost of which we spoke
reduced clause participle replaces the pronoun and verb the report commissioned last year

Formula / rule: Decide first whether the clause identifies (no commas, that allowed) or adds (commas, that forbidden). Then choose the pronoun by its role inside the clause, not in the main sentence. Finally, cut: if the pronoun is the object, delete it; if the clause is passive or progressive, reduce it to a participle.

★ Why it matters

Relative clauses are where B2 writing gains density: one sentence can carry a definition, a comment and a source. They are also where the most visible errors live, because the pronoun's role inside its own clause decides the choice, and the comma changes the meaning rather than the tone.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers drop the object pronoun without noticing (the report we commissioned) and use where for any place at all, including metaphorical ones (the point where we disagree). In careful writing, where should replace an adverbial of place, not of time or reason.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The relative pronoun is unstressed unless it is the subject, and the clause after a comma drops in pitch, which is how a listener hears that the information is an aside rather than a definition.

Additional example bank
  • Reduced: The figures collected in March are now suspect.
  • Non-defining with whose: The chair, whose term ends in May, will not stand again.
  • Prepositional: The meeting at which the decision was taken was not minuted.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The report, that we commissioned, has arrived (that after a comma)

✅ Right: The report, which we commissioned, has arrived

❌ Wrong: The analyst who he wrote the note has left (pronoun and subject both kept)

✅ Right: The analyst who wrote the note has left

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Participle clauses · Subject-predicate agreement

216 Reporting Verbs with Prepositions

Reporting

Which preposition does the verb take? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. They accused the supplier
    gapof
    delaying delivery.
  2. The board congratulated her
    gapon
    closing the deal.
  3. Critics blamed the ministry
    gapfor
    the delay.
  4. The auditor warned us
    gapagainst
    signing early.
VERB→+ preposition + -ing / noun
Level B2 Grammar

Reporting Verbs with Prepositions

Report what someone said with the preposition the verb demands.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can accuse, blame, congratulate and warn with the right pattern.
Examples in context
  • accuse somebody of doing something — accused the supplier of delaying
  • blame somebody for something — blamed the ministry for the delay
  • congratulate somebody on something — congratulated her on the result
  • warn somebody against doing something — warned us against signing

👀 What do you observe?

Each reporting verb owns its preposition, and the preposition decides what follows: of, for, on and against take a noun or an -ing form, while warn, remind, tell and persuade take an object plus to + infinitive. Blame allows both patterns with a change of focus: blame somebody for something, or blame something on somebody.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which pattern does accuse take?
They accused him of leaking the memo.
2. Is 'warn somebody against -ing' correct?
Both exist: warn somebody against signing / warn somebody not to sign.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
accuse somebody of names the offence accused of leaking the memo
blame somebody for / blame on assigns responsibility blamed for the delay / blamed the delay on the ministry
congratulate somebody on praises a success congratulated her on the result
warn somebody against / not to advises caution warned against signing / warned not to sign
criticise somebody for finds fault criticised for the tone of the reply
thank somebody for acknowledges help thanked the team for the analysis

Formula / rule: Learn the verb and its preposition as one unit, then check what follows: an -ing form after of, for, on and against; a to-infinitive after warn, remind, persuade and tell. Do not translate the preposition from your own language, because the mapping is arbitrary: accuse of but blame for, congratulate on but praise for.

★ Why it matters

In press reporting these verbs do the arguing: accused of is stronger than said to have, and warned against commits the speaker to a recommendation. Choosing the verb is choosing how much responsibility the sentence assigns, which is why lawyers read reported speech so carefully.

💭 Think like a native speaker

With blame, native speakers prefer blame somebody for when a person is the topic and blame something on when a cause is the topic. Blame is not used with to + infinitive, and accuse is never followed by that + clause in formal writing.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Accuse of links across the consonant: /əˈkjuːz əv/, and the -ing form after a preposition keeps its full vowel, which makes the pattern audible in fast speech.

Additional example bank
  • Warn: The regulator warned against relying on a single supplier.
  • Blame: The report blames the delay on the approval process.
  • Thank: The chair thanked the auditors for their patience.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: They accused the supplier to delay delivery (infinitive after accuse)

✅ Right: They accused the supplier of delaying delivery

❌ Wrong: Critics blamed the delay for the ministry (preposition reversed)

✅ Right: Critics blamed the ministry for the delay

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Distancing passives · Gerunds and infinitives

217 Rhetorical Questions & Parallelism

Persuasion

Which question does the paragraph answer? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. Why does the scheme
    gapkeep failing
    ? Because nobody owns it.
  2. Not only did costs rise,
    gapbut quality fell
    as well.
  3. We came to listen,
    gapto argue
    , and to decide.
  4. Is this the moment
    gapto retreat
    ? It is not.
QUESTION→→ answer it in the next sentence
Level B2 Grammar

Rhetorical Questions & Parallelism

Ask a question you will answer, and line up structures that match.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can build a persuasive paragraph with questions that lead and structures that balance.
Examples in context
  • What does the board actually want? It wants certainty, and certainty is expensive. — Question, then answer.
  • Not only did costs rise, but quality fell. Balanced correlatives. — Parallel halves joined by but.
  • We came to listen, to argue, and to decide. Three matching infinitives. — Same form three times.

👀 What do you observe?

A rhetorical question names the question the audience already holds, and the paragraph answers it in its second sentence. Parallelism repeats a grammatical shape - infinitive, infinitive, infinitive or not only X but Y - so that the reader hears the structure and expects the last item. Break the parallel and the sentence loses its grip.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What must follow a rhetorical question in a persuasive paragraph?
An unanswered question leaves the argument hanging.
2. What happens if the parallel breaks?
The break lands exactly where the emphasis should be.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
rhetorical question names the audience's question why does the scheme keep failing?
answer sentence pays the question off because nobody owns it
not only X but also Y balanced correlatives not only did costs rise but quality fell
three-part list same form repeated to listen, to argue, and to decide
antithesis parallel with contrast we came to listen, not to lecture
anaphora repeated opening we need clarity, we need ownership, we need time

Formula / rule: Ask one question and answer it, then build your list or contrast out of identical forms. For a three-part list, keep the same word class and the same length: to listen, to argue, to decide, not to listen, arguing, and a decision. Keep the strongest item last.

★ Why it matters

Persuasion in English leans on rhythm: the audience hears the shape before it judges the content. A balanced structure signals that the speaker has finished, which is why parallels close paragraphs and rhetorical questions open them. Rhetorical questions also carry risk, because an audience that already knows the answer may resent being asked.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, the question ends on a fall-rise and the answer starts on a step up in pitch; in writing, the question mark does the work. Parallel items usually shorten as the list goes on, and the shortest item carries the most weight.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The rhetorical question is marked by a fall-rise on the last stressed word, while the answer falls: Why does the scheme keep failing? Because nobody OWNS it.

Additional example bank
  • Question: What would a serious programme look like? It would name an owner.
  • Parallel: We need clarity, we need ownership, and we need time.
  • Antithesis: The choice is not between speed and care, but between ownership and drift.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: We came to listen, arguing, and to decide (the three items do not match)

✅ Right: We came to listen, to argue, and to decide

❌ Wrong: Not only costs rose, but quality fell (correlative half missing the auxiliary)

✅ Right: Not only did costs rise, but quality fell

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Cleft sentences and emphasis · Discourse markers

218 Speculation and Deduction

Deduction

How certain is the speaker? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The lights are off. They
    gapmust have
    left early.
  2. She
    gapmight be
    stuck in traffic.
  3. He
    gapcan't have
    signed it without reading.
  4. They
    gapshould have
    arrived by now.
MODAL + (have + participle)→→ degree of certainty
Level B2 Grammar

Speculation and Deduction

Say how certain you are about the past and the present.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use must, may, might and can't to reason about what happened.
Examples in context
  • Certain, past: The file must have been deleted. — The only explanation.
  • Possible, past: She may have missed the train. — One of several.
  • Impossible, past: He can't have known. — Logically excluded.
  • Expected, past: They should have finished by now. — Expected but not confirmed.

👀 What do you observe?

Deduction uses modals in a graded scale. Certainty: must (affirmative) and can't (negative). Possibility: may, might, could. Expectation: should, ought to. For the past, the modal is followed by have + past participle: must have left, might have left, can't have left, should have left. For the present, the modal takes a plain infinitive: must be, might be, can't be.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which modal excludes a possibility?
Can't have known means it is not possible.
2. What does should have finished add to 'they finished'?
Should have often implies it did not happen.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
must have + participle logical certainty about the past the file must have been deleted
can't / couldn't have + participle impossibility about the past he can't have known
may / might / could have + participle possibility about the past she may have missed the train
must be / can't be certainty about the present they must be stuck
should have + participle expectation, often unmet they should have arrived by now
seem / appear to have reported impression the plan appears to have failed

Formula / rule: Argue from the evidence to the modal: if the evidence leaves only one explanation, use must; if it excludes one, use can't; if several remain, use may, might or could; if you simply expected it, use should. Then set the time: plain infinitive for now, have + participle for before now.

★ Why it matters

This is the grammar of inference, and it is what makes a report read as reasoning rather than assertion. Must have signals that the writer has weighed the alternatives; might have keeps the file open; can't have closes it. Used well, the scale lets a writer commit exactly as far as the evidence allows.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, must have reduces to must've and might have to might've, which sound almost identical to must of and might of, a common misspelling. Could have is possibility, not ability, in this use, and can't have is far more common than couldn't have in British English.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The modal carries the stress when the deduction is the point: they MUST have left. In must've the auxiliary disappears and the participle carries the stress.

Additional example bank
  • Present certainty: The office must be empty; the lights are off.
  • Past possibility: The message could have been lost in the queue.
  • Expectation: The auditors should have signed off by Friday.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: They must left early (modal with past simple instead of have + participle)

✅ Right: They must have left early

❌ Wrong: He can't knew about it (can't with past simple)

✅ Right: He can't have known about it

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Distancing passive reporting · Permission, obligation and prohibition

Only one explanation: must have.

219 Subject-Predicate Agreement

Agreement

Find the head. Which verb form agrees? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. The list of candidates
    gapwas
    published on Monday.
  2. Neither the manager nor the drivers
    gapwere
    informed.
  3. The committee
    gaphas
    reached a decision.
  4. Each of the proposals
    gapneeds
    a separate budget.
HEAD NOUN→verb agrees with it, not with the noun next to it
Level B2 Grammar

Subject-Predicate Agreement

Make the verb agree with the real subject, not the nearest noun.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can keep the verb in agreement when long subjects and collective nouns intervene.
Examples in context
  • The number of complaints has fallen sharply. — The head is number, singular.
  • A number of complaints have been resolved. — Here a number of means several.
  • The team are arguing among themselves. — British English allows a plural verb for a group in dispute.

👀 What do you observe?

The verb agrees with the head of the subject, whatever sits between the two. Prepositional phrases, relative clauses and lists are noise. Collective nouns take a singular verb when they act as one body and a plural verb when the members act separately.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·b 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which word decides the verb in 'the list of candidates'?
List is the head; of candidates is a modifier.
2. Is 'a number of complaints have' correct?
The number of X is singular; a number of X is plural.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
the list of + plural noun singular verb the list of candidates was published
a number of + plural noun plural verb a number of complaints have been resolved
the number of + plural noun singular verb the number of complaints has fallen
neither X nor Y verb agrees with Y neither the manager nor the drivers were informed
each of / one of singular verb each of the proposals needs a budget
collective noun singular body, plural members the committee has decided / the team are arguing

Formula / rule: Find the head noun, then make the verb agree with it. Intervening phrases starting with of, with, together with, as well as and including never change the number: the list of candidates was, not were.

★ Why it matters

Agreement errors are the most visible kind of slip in formal writing, and long subjects are where they happen. A reader who sees the list of candidates were stops trusting the sentence, even if the point is sound.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, native speakers often say there's with a plural following (there's three options), and listeners do not notice. In writing, that same sentence is an error, so write there are three options.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The -s ending on a verb marks singular in the present tense, which is the opposite of the noun, where -s marks plural: the driver drives, the drivers drive.

Additional example bank
  • The report, together with its appendices, was submitted late.
  • One of the two proposals is still under review.
  • Neither the data nor the analysis supports that conclusion.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The list of candidates were published (verb agrees with candidates)

✅ Right: The list of candidates was published

❌ Wrong: Each of the proposals need a budget (plural verb after each)

✅ Right: Each of the proposals needs a budget

Relative clauses review · Compound nouns

220 Suffixes & Word Formation

Word formation

Which suffix completes the word? tap the line.write it on the line.

    gapimplementation
    of the policy took two years.

ROOT→suffix changes the word class
Level B2 Grammar

Suffixes & Word Formation

Build the word class you need from the word you have.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can turn a verb or adjective into the noun, adjective or adverb a sentence needs.
Examples in context
  • decide → decision The decision was taken in June. — Verb to noun with -sion.
  • rely → reliable The source is reliable. — Verb to adjective with -able.
  • care → careless The reply was careless. — Noun to adjective with -less.

👀 What do you observe?

A suffix fixes the word class: -tion and -ment make nouns, -able and -ive make adjectives, -ly makes adverbs, -ise makes verbs. The same root takes different suffixes with different meanings, and some combinations are lexical, not logical.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What class does -ness create?
Happy → happiness, a noun.
2. Is 'economical' the same as 'economic'?
Same root, different suffixes, different meanings.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
-tion / -sion verb to noun implement → implementation
-ment verb to noun agree → agreement
-able / -ible verb to adjective rely → reliable
-ive verb to adjective persuade → persuasive
-ly adjective to adverb remarkable → remarkably
-ise / -ify noun or adjective to verb modern → modernise, pure → purify

Formula / rule: Choose the suffix by the slot, not by the root: after a determiner you need a noun (-tion, -ment, -ness), before a noun you need an adjective (-able, -ive, -ous), and a verb needs -ise, -ify or -en. Then check the spelling shift: decide → decision, maintain → maintenance.

★ Why it matters

Word formation is where vocabulary and grammar meet: a sentence can be grammatically perfect and still wrong because the slot holds an adjective where a noun belongs. Suffixes are the cheapest way to expand what you can say at B2 without learning new roots.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers do not build words from rules in real time; they recognise whole words. Use the suffix rules to check a word you are unsure of, not to invent new ones, and note that -ly adverbs of manner are common but some are lexical (hardly means barely, not in a hard way).

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Suffix -tion is /ʃən/ (implementation), -sion after a vowel is /ʒən/ (decision), -ous is weak /əs/ (nervous), and -ly adds a syllable only when the adjective ends in -le or -ble.

Additional example bank
  • Noun: The maintenance of the fleet costs more than its purchase.
  • Adjective: The argument is persuasive but thin.
  • Adverb: The figures were remarkably consistent.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The decision was implement quickly (noun slot filled by a verb)

✅ Right: The decision was implemented quickly

❌ Wrong: She spoke with great confident (adjective where a noun is needed)

✅ Right: She spoke with great confidence

221 Used to, Would and Be Used To

Three forms

Which form does the meaning need? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. They
    gapused to
    meet on Fridays.
  2. The office
    gapused to be
    smaller.
  3. I
    gapam used to
    working nights.
  4. She
    gapwould
    sit by the window for hours.
USED TO + base→past state or habit, no longer true
Level B2 Grammar

Used to, Would and Be Used To

Separate past habits, past states and present familiarity.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use used to, would and be used to without confusing the three.
Examples in context
  • We used to meet on Fridays. Past habit, now stopped. — Used to + base verb.
  • The office used to be smaller. Past state, now changed. — States take used to, not would.
  • I am used to working nights. Present familiarity. — Be used to + -ing.

👀 What do you observe?

Used to plus the base verb describes a past habit or state that is no longer true: we used to meet, the office used to be smaller. Would describes repeated past actions in narrative but never past states: she would sit by the window, but not she would be smaller. Be used to plus -ing describes present familiarity, and get used to plus -ing describes becoming familiar.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which form cannot describe a past state?
Would sit is fine; would be smaller is not.
2. What does 'I am used to working nights' mean?
Be used to: present familiarity.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
used to + base past habit or state, now ended they used to meet on Fridays
would + base repeated past action in narrative she would sit by the window
would, not for states states need used to the office used to be smaller
be used to + -ing present familiarity I am used to working nights
get used to + -ing becoming familiar they got used to the new system
be used to + noun familiarity with a thing he is used to pressure

Formula / rule: Ask three questions: is the situation past or present, is it a habit or a state, and does it mean familiarity? Past habit or state: used to. Repeated past action in a story: would is possible, states excepted. Present familiarity: be or get used to plus -ing or a noun.

★ Why it matters

The three forms look alike and mean different things, which is why the error is so common and so visible: I am used to work says the speaker has not noticed that previous familiarity, present state and past habit are three different ideas. Getting them apart is a B2 marker.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers use used to freely and avoid would for states without thinking, and they often pronounce used to as /juːstə/, which hides the -ed and makes the written form look arbitrary.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

Used to is /ˈjuːstə/ in fast speech; be used to keeps the /d/ before a vowel (used to it), which is the one place the -ed is audible.

Additional example bank
  • Past habit: We used to hold the review on Mondays.
  • Past state: The team used to be much smaller.
  • Familiarity: She is used to presenting to the board.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: The office would be smaller in the nineties (would for a past state)

✅ Right: The office used to be smaller in the nineties

❌ Wrong: I am used to work late (infinitive after be used to)

✅ Right: I am used to working late

222 Verb + Object + Infinitive or Gerund

Verb patterns

VERB + OBJECT→→ to + infinitive / -ing / from + -ing
Level B2 Grammar

Verb + Object + Infinitive or Gerund

Choose the pattern the main verb requires.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use tell, ask, persuade, allow and prevent with the right complement.
Examples in context
  • They asked us to leave. Verb + object + to-infinitive. — Ask, tell, persuade, advise, encourage.
  • They allowed us to stay. Verb + object + to-infinitive. — Allow, permit, enable.
  • They prevented us from staying. Verb + object + from + -ing. — Prevent, stop, discourage.

👀 What do you observe?

The main verb decides the complement. Persuade, advise, tell, ask, encourage, allow, permit and enable take an object plus to-infinitive. Prevent, stop, discourage and prohibit take an object plus from + -ing. Verbs of perception (see, hear, watch, notice) take an object plus a bare infinitive or an -ing form, with a difference of completeness: I saw them leave, I saw them leaving.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. Which pattern follows prevent?
They prevented the error from spreading.
2. What does 'I saw them leave' suggest compared with 'I saw them leaving'?
Bare infinitive for the complete action.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
verb + object + to-infinitive persuade, tell, advise, allow they persuaded the board to delay
verb + object + from + -ing prevent, stop, discourage we prevented the error from spreading
verb + object + bare infinitive perception and let, make, help I saw them leave
verb + -ing verbs of liking and avoiding they avoided signing the deal
verb + to-infinitive agree, refuse, promise, manage they refused to sign
change of meaning remember, stop, try stop to check and stop checking

Formula / rule: Learn each verb with its pattern, then fill the slots in that order: verb, object, complement. Watch the change-of-meaning verbs, where the complement decides the sense: stop to check means pause in order to check, stop checking means no longer check.

★ Why it matters

These patterns carry the argument: preventing, allowing, persuading and discouraging are the four moves of negotiation, and each takes a different frame. A sentence that puts the wrong frame in place is understood, but it marks the speaker as translating from another language.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Native speakers prefer allow with to-infinitive (allow us to stay) and permit in formal contexts (permit them to enter); prevent from is so fixed that prevent to is never heard from a native speaker.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The to of the infinitive is weak /tə/ unless stressed for contrast, and from + -ing runs together: /prɪˈventɪd ðəm frəm ˈspredɪŋ/.

Additional example bank
  • Encourage: The chair encouraged the team to publish early.
  • Discourage: The cost discouraged firms from bidding.
  • Perception: We watched the auditors check every page.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: They prevented the error to spread (infinitive after prevent)

✅ Right: They prevented the error from spreading

❌ Wrong: She advised us waiting (gerund after advise with an object)

✅ Right: She advised us to wait

223 Whatever, Whenever, Wherever, Whoever, However

Open choice

Which -ever word fits? tap the line.write it on the line.

  1. gapWhatever
    you decide, we will support it.
  2. gapWherever
    the meeting is held, attendance will be high.
  3. gapHowever
    hard we try, the deadline will not move.
  4. gapWhoever
    signed the form is responsible.
-EVER WORD→→ open choice or concession
Level B2 Grammar

Whatever, Whenever, Wherever, Whoever, However

Leave the choice open, or concede the extent.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can use the -ever words for open choice, concession and degree.
Examples in context
  • Take whatever you need. Open choice, no limit. — Whatever as a pronoun.
  • Whatever the cost, we proceed. Concession. — Whatever + noun.
  • However late it is, call me. Concession of degree. — However + adjective or adverb.

👀 What do you observe?

The -ever words extend a question word to mean it does not matter which, where, who, when or how. Whatever, whoever and whichever work as pronouns or determiners; wherever and whenever work as adverbs; however is followed by an adjective or an adverb, never by a whole clause on its own. However also means but in formal writing, which is a separate job.

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·a

💡 Check your understanding

Score : 0 / 2
1. What follows however in a concession?
However hard we try, not however we try hard.
2. Which word is both a pronoun and a determiner?
Whatever you need; whatever reason you give.
Element / structure Role in English Application example
whatever any thing, open choice take whatever you need
whoever any person whoever signed the form is responsible
whichever any one of a set whichever option you prefer
wherever / whenever any place, any time wherever the meeting is held
however + adjective any degree, concession however hard we try
however as a connector contrast in formal writing the terms were fair; however, the timing was not

Formula / rule: Use an -ever form when the exact item does not matter to the statement: whatever you decide, whoever signed, wherever it happens. When the point is degree, however comes first and the adjective follows immediately. Keep however the connector apart from however the intensifier, since the first takes a comma and the second does not.

★ Why it matters

The -ever forms are how English says that a condition is not negotiable: whatever the cost means the cost will not change the decision. In negotiation and policy writing they signal that a variable has been taken out of the argument, which is why they are frequent in contracts and speeches.

💭 Think like a native speaker

In speech, whatever is often a dismissive one-word reply, and that use is hostile; wherever and whenever are neutral. However at the start of a sentence meaning but is common in writing and rare in speech, where but does the work.

🗣️ Pronunciation note

The -ever ending carries the stress: wherEVER, whenEVER, howEVER, and in whatever the stress falls on the second syllable.

Additional example bank
  • Choice: Whichever supplier you choose, the lead time is eight weeks.
  • Concession: Whatever the outcome, the process will be published.
  • Degree: However carefully we plan, the weather decides.
⚠️ Common mistakes to avoid

❌ Wrong: However we try hard, the deadline will not move (adverb after however in the wrong order)

✅ Right: However hard we try, the deadline will not move

❌ Wrong: Whatever decision you take it, we support you (object and pronoun both kept)

✅ Right: Whatever decision you take, we support you

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Clauses of contrast, purpose, reason and result · Discourse markers

C1–C2 Advanced Confusing Grammar Master Guide

Academic stance, information packaging (Theme-Rheme), ellipsis vs substitution, and sophisticated stylistic precision

👀 What do you notice?

Compare these two academic statements:

  • "This drug causes side effects." (Categorical / unhedged → risks overgeneralization)

Correct · Ellipsis leaves out redundant elements; substitution replaces them with pro-forms.

🧠 Logic Map: Core C1–C2 Advanced Grammar Contrasts

Concept AConcept BCore Precision DifferenceKey Examples
Categorical Claim Hedged Academic Claim Absolute fact claim vs. Evidence-based probabilistic claim Results prove X. vs. The data strongly point to X.
Ellipsis Lexical Substitution Silent omission of recoverable words vs. Replacing words with 'do so', 'one', 'such' She ordered tea and he [ordered] coffee. vs. He wanted tea and I wanted the same.
Loose Sentence Periodic Sentence Main clause first, details added vs. Main thought held until the end for climax He failed the exam despite studying all night. vs. Despite studying all night, he failed.
Given Information (Theme) New Information (Rheme) Starting with known anchor context vs. Placing the key new message at the end As for climate change, recent models indicate rapid sea level shifts.
⚠️ Common C1–C2 Precision Pitfalls
❌This study proves that all subjects behave identically.
tap to see the correct form

(Academic prose prefers hedged verbs like 'indicate' or 'tend to' over absolute 'proves')
❌He promised to submit the paper and he submitted the paper.
tap to see the correct form
✅He promised to submit the paper and did so promptly.
(Use 'did so' substitution to avoid awkward repetition)

C2 Confusing Grammar & Precision Master Guide

Fine-grained semantic distinctions, register shifts, archaic/legal connectors, and native-level syntactic control

🎯 Master Goal: Wield near-native precision across subtle adjective nuances, executive register shifts, statutory subordinators, and high-stakes rhetorical structures without introducing stylistic clash or ambiguity.

Compare these two sentences: "The board made an economic decision." (Related to economy/finance) vs. "The board made an economical decision." (Cost-effective / money-saving). One letter changes the financial implication entirely!

✎ ___ / 2✓ 1·a 2·b

💡 Check your understanding (CCQs)

Score: 0 / 2
1. Subordinator check: "The policy was enacted, notwithstanding public protest." What is the logical relationship between the policy enacted and public protest?
Correct · 'Notwithstanding' functions as a formal concessive preposition/prepositional subordinator meaning 'despite' or 'in spite of'.
2. Nuance check: Is a "historic agreement" an agreement that took place in history, or an agreement of major historical significance?
Correct · 'Historic' means famous or momentous in history, whereas 'historical' simply means pertaining to history or the past.

🧠 Logic Map: Core C2 Mastery Semantic & Syntactic Distinctions

Term / Structure ATerm / Structure BCore Logic / Register DistinctionKey Examples
Historic Historical Momentous / famous in history vs. Pertaining to history or events in the past a historic treaty vs. historical research documents
Economic Economical Relating to the economy or macroeconomics vs. Avoiding waste / cost-effective economic policy reform vs. an economical fuel-efficient car
Continual Continuous Recurring frequently with interruptions vs. Unbroken without any interruption continual complaints throughout the week vs. continuous flow of water
Classic Classical Timeless exemplar / typical vs. Relating to ancient Greek/Roman culture or traditional art music a classic mistake / classic design vs. classical music / classical literature
Notwithstanding Albeit Formal concession (despite / in spite of) vs. Reduced concessive clause (although it be) Notwithstanding objections, the motion passed. vs. He accepted the offer, albeit reluctantly.
Whereby Lest By which procedure/mechanism vs. In order to prevent / for fear that (+ subjunctive/should) a system whereby users vote vs. We took precautions lest the contract be invalidated.
Affect (v) / Effect (n) Effect (v) / Affect (n) Standard: affect = influence (v), effect = result (n) | C2 shift: effect = bring about (v), affect = emotion display (n) to effect systemic change | flat psychological affect

🗣️ Stylistic & Register Note

At C2 level, avoiding register dissonance is paramount. Combining high-register statutory subordinators like whereby or notwithstanding with casual informal vocabulary creates jarring stylistic incoherence. Maintain register integrity across the sentence.

⚠️ Common C2 Precision Mistake Flips
❌We bought an economic car that uses very little petrol.
tap to see the correct form
✅We bought an economical car that uses very little petrol.
('Economical' = thrifty / cost-saving; 'economic' = related to the economy)
❌The rain fell continually for 24 hours without stopping for even a second.
tap to see the correct form
✅The rain fell continuously for 24 hours without stopping for even a second.
('Continuous' = unbroken without pause; 'continual' = repeatedly stopping and starting)
❌They altered the terms lest where users could appeal.
tap to see the correct form
✅They altered the terms whereby users could appeal.
('Whereby' = by which mechanism; 'lest' = for fear that)

253 Ellipsis & Substitution for Native-like Economy

Level C2 Grammar · Part 2

Ellipsis & Substitution for Native-like Economy

Omitting predictable elements and employing advanced pro-forms to achieve concise, elegant discourse flow.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can streamline speech and writing by eliminating repetitive clauses using advanced pro-forms (do so, the former, such) and structural ellipsis.

Practice this topiccosylanguages.github.io/COSYlanguages/practice/index.html?lang=en&cat=Grammar&level=proficiency&theme=ellipsis-and-substitution-for-native-like-economy

Core Rule: Achieve native economy by replacing repeated verb phrases with do so, clause complements with so / not, and antecedents with the former / the latter, or by omitting shared subjects/auxiliaries entirely (Ellipsis).

Why this matters: Native speakers instinctively avoid verbatim repetition. Ellipsis and substitution create cohesive momentum, signaling absolute linguistic mastery.

Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.
Cohesive DeviceMechanismExample Transformation
Verb Phrase SubstitutionReplace full predicate with do soAny member wishing to resign may do so in writing.
Clausal SubstitutionReplace clause with so / notWill regulations tighten? I expect so. / I fear not.
Nominal ReferenceDistinguish antecedents with the former / the latterBetween growth and inflation, the former is preferable.
Textual EllipsisOmit redundant auxiliary or noun headSome favored expansion, others [favored] consolidation.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing Ellipsis & Substitution for Native-like Economy, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

  • The chairman recommended restructuring, and the board did likewise.

👀 Notice: In "...and the board did likewise", the verb phrase recommended restructuring is replaced smoothly without repeating a single word.

🧠 Think like English: English treats redundant repetition as a breach of elegance; once an idea is in the listener's head, erase or substitute it!

🧩 Language Signature: Pro-form Precision
`Repetition:` He promised to resign, and he resigned ➔ `Substitution:` He promised to resign, and did so.

Rhetorical StructurePattern MechanicsProse Example
Periodic SentenceHolds main idea until sentence conclusionDespite mounting opposition, declining revenues, and public skepticism, the CEO reaffirmed the strategy.
Balanced AntithesisSymmetrical clauses expressing opposing ideasNot that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more.

🧠 Think like English: Formal English uses sentence cadence like classical music—suspending resolution creates artistic weight and rhetorical impact.

`Loose:` We succeeded despite all odds ➔ `Periodic:` Despite all odds, we succeeded.
